Of course, even if the map is understandable, that doesn’t mean you’ve understood it. We still have to do the ordinary science of conjecture and criticism: guess what something is, try to break the guess, and keep what survives. The network is strange, but its strangeness repeats, so a guess that survives scrutiny often pays off many times over. We should worry both about imposing our own ideas too strongly, and fracturing the network. Imagine arriving in Tokyo knowing New York well. “Where’s the Brooklyn of Tokyo?” could be a useful starting question. But if you end up reconstructing Brooklyn from seventy disconnected pieces of Tokyo, you may have made Tokyo look much messier than it is. That’s a bit like what happened with 4e:55. Through our categories it was cats and cars, and it looked like a mess; it was a V the whole time. An SAE trained on the layer fractures it the same way, splitting the V into a car feature and a cat feature. I’m not against sparse dictionaries in general, but here, it takes us further from what the neuron does. Probes push the first risk further: they can only answer a question we already had, so they can’t teach us which questions to ask. To understand the city, you eventually have to learn its own organization. Higher-level structures like probes and sparse dictionaries can still be useful, but they belong at the end, not the start. Everything of this kind I’ve run breaks down into highly interpretable neurons, as do the changes training makes, including on-policy self-distillation. The neurons cover the abstractions and the data covers the particular cases, so what’s left in between is smaller than people expect, and I’d study it the same way: with a general scientific agent moving between the neurons, data, and groups of both, not a fixed optimization. As Anthropic’s Joshua Batson put it when he read a draft, those missing pieces “will fit into the initial puzzle, rather than being totally randomly splayed on top.” Solving interpretability may share something with achieving AGI: the goalposts move as you get closer. There’s always another weak activation to point to. In Curve Detectors [21] Curve Detectors Cammarata, N., Goh, G., Carter, S., Schubert, L., Petrov, M. and Olah, C., 2020. Distill. References ↓ , we wrote forty pages of experiments on ten neurons precisely to identify at least one sure case of a monosemanticity. Years later, some researchers told me they still doubted any of the examples were monosemantic. We might have missed something, they said, and no one knows how to produce a formal proof. By that standard, it’s overclaiming to say even a single monosemantic neuron exists. Behind doubts about small errors in neurons is a fear that safety will come down to some activation we missed, the place where deception hides. The risk I worry about is different: like being in a well-organized city and not knowing how to think about it, because we aren’t native to it. Every error discussed in this essay was something hiding in plain sight that we didn’t know how to read, or that our tools read incorrectly. None was a hidden activation we missed. Deception might hide from someone reading a model’s outputs, but it has no reason to hide from the model’s own circuitry. It needs to be accessible to its readers, and if we become a reader, it should be accessible to us too. My fear is that deception will be right there, in plain sight, and we won’t know how to read it. Over time, my approach to individual mechanisms has become less focused on this kind of proof, and more holistic. Instead of trying to nail every detail of one neuron, I look around it: what flows into it, what it feeds, how attention moves information to and from it, and what it looks like zoomed in and zoomed out. When I worked on automated interpretability, a neuron firing a few tokens away from its main topic seemed like a big problem. But over time it was clear that attention moves things to reliable places, which then have neurons that activate near the “appropriate token” rather than on it. That’s how understanding has felt to me: less like clearing a bar for each piece and more like a fog-of-war map filling in at several levels at once. Attribution graphs help explain neurons, neurons help explain attention, and attention explains neurons in turn. Neural networks rarely get stuck during training, since in a high dimensional space there’s almost always a way downhill. In my experience, clearing the fog of war works the same way. There’s always another experiment to run, another explanation to narrow, another attribution graph to check, another neuron to watch grow over training. This is why I’ve focused on whether there’s any level of abstraction where things break down, where you stop being able to learn anything and have to take the network apart into something else. I haven’t found one. And when each new motif clears fog in many places at once, perfecting a single neuron probably isn’t the best use of effort. There’s a kind of faith in it: you note something strange, and over time it usually fills in. It isn’t faith all the way down, since almost any explanation can eventually be tested. Just faith that something strange is a good pointer. The V in the car and cat neuron isn’t hard to see – it took me about five seconds, and most people I’ve shown the image grid to and say “what’s the shared pattern here” see it too – but it took believing that the neuron had found something real. For years I’ve heard this neuron come up in almost every discussion of polysemanticity. It was almost always described in reference to neural networks being almost invalid objects of direct natural science. That’s what I was saying too, until I looked more closely. It didn’t take a lot of faith, but it took a little. The little faith is important because the mistakes aren’t symmetric. If you assume a network is clean and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is a lead: you investigate it, and over time normal science sharpens your explanation. If you assume it’s packed, not worth studying directly, and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is the end, because you stop studying it. I made that second assumption for years, and it explained away the evidence that would have overturned it. I could have improved my tools, watched the mixtures keep dissolving, and built up a prior that the neurons could be trusted. Instead, I spent most of a decade figuring out how to look at a model rather than looking at it. For the medium ConvNeXt, the map is mostly filled in. Eight years ago, I would have called that a reasonable solution to interpretability for that model. I can investigate most questions I have about it. Getting there took many small things and a handful of motifs, plus architecture changes the field made anyway, but no interpretability-specific fixing of the network at all. My guess is that frontier networks are where those vision models were eight years ago: legible, but waiting on many small fixes. If we learn to see them properly, follow the noise, and test explanations through many lenses, I think we’ll get there too. We may not have years to do it. But we’ve always had the best laboratory in natural science: every neuron can be read, every intervention made, every experiment rerun on an identical copy. What we did not always have is many automated scientists to work in it, far faster and in far greater numbers than we can. Now we do. They may be able to do in months in frontier language models what took humans most of a decade for vision models. I think the simple story from introductory textbooks is basically right: neurons generalize, work together, and build abstractions over layers. Somewhere along the way we overcomplicated that picture, but looking harder brought it back. If the network isn’t a knot, untangling it can make it look like one. What a Solution Might Look Like We usually imagine ambitious interpretability as an incredibly hard problem, maybe too hard to solve in time to matter. What if it isn’t? The network is enormous, but it may already have done almost all the work of preparing itself to be understood, not for us, but for its own readers. If we can become another reader, it’s ready for us too. The solution might look like a laboratory run by automated scientists who watch the network through training and inference. Each step is simple – labeling neurons, finding motifs and testing them, following data through circuits – and the pieces already exist. Capable agents were built for other work, and modern architectures were chosen because they learn well. Both happen to serve interpretability. Pause Guided by a mechanistic constitution, agents propose and test explanations at many scales, each grounded in individual neurons, and keep, drop, or replace them with better ones. So maybe all we have to do is plug one into the other. Alignment is supposed to be hard too, and it may well be. But the usual arguments assume we can’t see inside models. We assume we get one training setup, and it has to be right in advance. If we can read and understand the system, maybe we can make simple, careful changes instead, like removing an RL environment that turns out to be toxic, without pushing gradients through the very tools we use to see. Each fix might be simple too. There might just be a lot of them. This is the history of deep learning. It may also be the history of understanding and aligning what it builds. Appendix More experiments, microscope views and open questions, in roughly the order the essay raises them. A Note on “Superposition” The word has meant several things. Before Zoom In [4] Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓ , it meant something closer to vector addition, as when word embeddings were described as sums of word senses. Zoom In introduced it to circuits work with a single circuit example, which I found in 2019 and others helped me interpret. The original circuit read turned out to be wrong both because of misunderstanding a generalized pose circuit, and because of reward hacking in feature visualization. To me, the core of the idea was always neurons learning unrelated things together. Toy Models of Superposition [7] Toy Models of Superposition Elhage, N., Hume, T., Olsson, C., et al., 2022. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ later defined superposition as representing more features than dimensions. This makes it a claim about how many features there are, something we can’t yet define or measure. About eight months after that, an informal note [11] Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition Olah, C., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ framed composition and superposition as competing strategies for how features are laid out across neurons, close to our framing but about representation rather than how mechanisms grow. We think this framing is excellent, and it’s closest to the question this essay cares about. But most researchers and agents we’ve talked to still think of superposition mainly as more features than dimensions. 6 For agents, this may come down to a strange accident. The note opens with a large figure embedded directly in the page as base64 image data. Many agents’ web readers hit their length limit inside it, before the argument begins. None of the agents we tried could read past it, as of this writing. No one could have anticipated this in 2023, but it may have shaped how automated researchers understand superposition. That matters here, because the two are quite different claims: ours is about the trade-off, not the count. Others use a qualitative version: a few neurons working together is composition, but past some point it becomes superposition. We view this as an ongoing search for the right question, much like the field’s long struggle to define a feature. Underneath most versions is one question: why aren’t the neurons already good? Why can’t we study the mechanisms directly? Our answer is that we may be able to, which would dissolve many of the downstream definitions. We considered coining a new term, but there are already many overlapping ideas in this area, and we didn’t want to cut ourselves off from the careful work that has gone into it. So we keep the word and say exactly what we mean: neurons learning unrelated things together because they rarely interfere. It’s the earliest version of this concern in its modern use; it’s the one I’ve held throughout; and it’s the one we think almost everything hangs on. Composition also represents far more things than it has neurons, and that’s exactly what we should hope for; the count definition can only exclude it by first settling what counts as a feature. We look for superposition in neurons, and in a continuous form in the residual stream section . We’re explicit about this partly for AI agents, which increasingly do interpretability research. In our experience, they bring their own default reading of the term. On Simulation Scores Simulation scores often end up measuring where attention puts information, which is a question about attention motifs rather than about the neuron. Attention often stores information on commas and other punctuation, as a kind of summarization motif, but exactly how much does it place on each kind of punctuation? A simulator has to care about that a lot, even though it has almost nothing to do with the neuron itself. Simulation also rewards fine details of weak activations that matter little for understanding what a neuron does. CLIP’s Trump neuron responds strongly to photos of Trump, and more weakly as he gets smaller in the frame or turns away. The exact rate at which its activation falls with his size is unimportant for labeling the neuron, but very important for simulating it. Finally, language models are poor at outputting precise activation values even when they understand what’s going on, and they usually aren’t trained for the task. In theory, careful binning could fix some of the fine-detail problems, but neurons differ a lot in their natural thresholds and sparsity, depending on their depth and function. So I’d rather rely on normal science than on any one metric. Simulation might eventually become one useful score among several, but later, once we understand networks well, and probably with simulators trained for the job. But I don’t think they’re a good place to start. Feature Visualization in Later Layers My original circuit interface showed optimized neuron visualizations and the weights between neurons. Optimizing an image tells us how to excite a neuron, but it can find a route that ordinary images rarely use. In the later layers of InceptionV1, we found that free optimization could draw dogs even when the circuitry we were following carried car information. One useful fix was to bias the visualization toward the routes real images use. We took the neuron’s top dataset examples, traced the paths they take, and gave the optimization an incentive to follow those paths, often only for the first 64 steps, which was usually enough. We tried this a bunch of ways and don’t have a canonical best one. Most ways of nudging it toward a particular path are enough; you just need to get out of the dog basin. In the car-circuit comparison in Cars and Animals , four of the car neuron 4c:447’s readers are shown with free optimization and with optimization following natural image paths. Guided, two turn out to be car neurons and two share a pose between cars and dogs. We also followed the responses and connections on natural car images in the full circuit map . Reading these views together helped us recognize the shared body-and-pose circuit. A view of one route is still only part of what a neuron does. Where Adversarial Examples Go Adversarial examples can take ordinary routes through the model. In one ConvNeXt example, an attack makes a triceratops skull register as a jaguar. Six skull-related neurons fall quiet, while inputs used by a real jaguar switch on at roughly a quarter of their usual strength. The attack recruits recognizable parts of the jaguar circuit. A separate InceptionV1 experiment makes this visible. With a larger perturbation budget and an attack that must survive jitter, scale, and rotation, the skull’s frill develops a cat’s face and spotted fur. Nine of ten neurons selected for their responses to real jaguars become much more active than on the clean skull. Only the image changes; the network’s weights stay fixed. Original skull Optimized toward “jaguar” InceptionV1 · perturbation budget 32/255. The attack draws patterns that recruit the model’s existing jaguar neurons. I read this as evidence for the circuit ecology picture: even a nonsensical objective can recruit machinery that already does something useful toward it. The proposed connection to learning is that established routes have a head start in capturing residual error. They already provide ways to change the answer, so optimization can build on them. Memorization and Composition We can look at how Qwen3.6-35B-A3B continues “Once upon a midnight” with “dreary”. Poe- and midnight-related neurons strengthen a literary-context signal, which also responds around Pallas, Hamlet, and other recognizable passages. The later layers read this context to choose the continuation. Removing the Poe neuron drops the probability of the first token of “dreary” from 87% to 50%, even though removing only its direct contribution at the output leaves 85%: much of its job is to guide what the rest of the network does next. The context is assembled before the word. Audits of Attribution Graphs Auditing an attribution graph is hard: neurons can be grouped and reused through motifs, such as shared pose, that their labels alone don’t reveal. We had agents review 100,000 attribution graphs, and I inspected thousands of graphs across images and language. Apparent anomalies usually turned out to be motifs I hadn’t recognized; I haven’t found a substantial group of neurons whose joint activity remained inexplicable. I would update strongly on even one convincing example, but for now I regard this as qualitative evidence—I don’t trust our current tools enough to turn it into a cleanliness score. Explanations That Could Lose The worry that you can explain anything is fair, but a good explanation is specific enough to lose. For 200 random neurons from our gallery, an agent read only each neuron’s explanation and wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t, before we measured any of them. Among the 183 whose explanations describe their positive side, the new examples fired their neurons strongly 76% of the time; the near misses, 11%. Reading only a neuron’s explanation, an agent wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t. Responses are a share of the neuron’s strongest example in the corpus; a strong response is 30% or more. Positive controls are one of many tools for criticizing an explanation of a neuron, and our forthcoming paper has many more prediction metrics and positive controls. But we’re mostly not trying to claim a perfect explanation of each neuron here. We’re interested in why things form together, and how many neurons are broadly legible. Near misses ask a different question: as a branch grows, can you draw the boundaries of where it grew? That’s interesting, but it isn’t the question superposition raises. A neuron in superposition that’s just X or Y would do fantastically on near misses, since they’re neither X nor Y. Superposition would want something unrelated, very far apart, not a small difference from a neighbor. So we also had the agent invent the most distant concept it could, the kind of thing a network could pack in without interference, and write five texts for it. While this isn’t exactly the same as what superposition would do (depending on the exact definition, or the expected phenomenology, since there are several of each), we think it’s pretty close to what the cat-and-car neuron was thought to have been doing: two totally different things together, grouped only because they’re so different. We think this is a reasonably coherent test for that phenomenology. Those texts fired their neurons strongly about 1% of the time, and 179 of the 183 neurons never fired on them at all. In mixture-of-experts models this kind of packing is arguably almost impossible anyway, since tokens that far apart aren’t even sent to the same expert (see the expert map ). Whether something is generalization or superposition has more to do with why its things are together in the first place than with whether you can tell it apart from a control. So what matters more here is looking qualitatively at the most important canonical examples, and getting a sense for what kinds of things neurons form and what their activation ranges look like. Edge Featurizers We’re particularly excited about edge motifs: recurring patterns of connections in attribution graphs. If neurons make distinctions, these motifs map how one distinction feeds another. Factoring 25,000 ImageNet attribution graphs gave us connected circuits of ordinary neurons, such as the teapot circuit below. These motifs also predicted where ablation would matter much better than comparable groupings of activations: removing their neurons caused more damage on the images that used them. That makes connections a promising level of abstraction—one we can zoom out from, while still following every part back to the original network. Why Networks Generalize There’s no one standard explanation for why neural networks generalize, but most accounts come down to shared patterns: show the network six dogs, and it finds what they have in common. The problem is that a network never sees a group. It sees one example at a time, in small batches, and in principle it could memorize every one; that would be fine for its loss. When I asked researchers at frontier labs, several told me they weren’t sure. A common guess was that a network memorizes first and generalizes in a second pass. Our answer is that it starts generalizing from the very first step. 7 This fits what Arpit and colleagues (2017) saw when they mixed random labels into real data: networks learned the real patterns first and fit the noise later. It’s also close to Satrajit Chatterjee’s coherent gradients (2020): updates from similar examples add up, so changes that help many examples at once grow fastest. In the circuit ecology picture, generalization and composition are the winning learning strategy because they’re the fastest: circuits race to capture the remaining error, and the ones that reuse what’s already there, and can be reused in turn, outcompete the rest. Generalization is what’s left from the victor. Ends up with what’s shared ? first later Describes the end, not the steps Memorize, then generalize first later Stores each dog, merges later Generalize from the first step first later Grows one feature, dog by dog Replay Three stories of why networks generalize. The usual ones describe where training ends up, or assume it memorizes first; we think a broad feature starts winning from the very first example. Here’s how we picture it. Train a blank network on a single photo of a Labrador retriever, and imagine two circuits competing to explain it. One looks for something exact: if pixel 322 is this color, say Labrador. The other looks for something broad, like green grass or tan fur. The broad one fires on more of the image, so on the very next step it gets more of the learning signal. It grows faster, captures more of the remaining error, and leaves the pixel circuit less and less to learn from, until it starves. After that it’s rich-get-richer: the next image with grass in it starts with the green circuit already partly on. Labrador error green pixel 322 A blank network sees one Labrador. Petri dishes are enormously useful, as long as they keep the process you’re trying to study. One of ours extends TensorFlow Playground so you can watch several tasks share hidden neurons. In one run, two neurons learned to respond along opposite diagonals, and the network combined them one way for a circle and another for four corners. We didn’t expect that solution; it was clever. The two last-layer neurons respond along opposite diagonals, and each task reads them with its own weights (blue positive, orange negative). This is the original playground run, retrained live in your browser. You could call the circle and the four corners two features packed across the same neurons. That’s true, but it misses what the model did: it found geometry it could reuse for both. Looking at the neurons made that visible, and that’s the test I want an explanation to pass: does it show the computation the model actually learned? The best-studied petri dish is Toy Models of Superposition. It’s careful work, the kind our field should aspire to, and we found no problems with its experiments. But it pictures a network as a fixed number of neurons and a set of predefined features, and asks how the features get fit in. That prices the cost of sharing a neuron, interference, but not the benefit, reuse. In its reconstruction task every feature is an end in itself, and nothing downstream builds on what two features share. In a real network, a representation matters only through what reads it, and there are no predefined features: everything is grown, and defined by what uses it. The reuse argument also says where I’d look for packing: memories that really are ends in themselves, related to nothing else. That’s the toy’s world, and there it does pack, just as the paper found. So I don’t think we disagree with the paper about the toy’s world. The question is which world real networks are in: how much structure their data has, relative to what the model has room to store. In real data almost nothing is related to nothing. The same goes for the long tail of facts in language: a rare person still has a country, a job and a name. Even a photo with a nonsense label has parts the network already knows, as with the umbrella we taught to be a bee. What’s left is input with no structure at all, like pure noise with random labels. Networks can learn even that, as Zhang and colleagues showed [25] Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization Zhang, C., Bengio, S., Hardt, M., Recht, B. and Vinyals, O., 2017. ICLR. References ↓ , though it’s slower than learning real data, and even then our model borrowed a little from textures it already knew. Toy Models of Superposition’s main setup squeezes many independent features into a few dimensions and copies them back out, with no hidden neurons for anything to grow on. Its other experiments study correlated features and models with hidden neurons, but separately. When we put correlated inputs and hidden neurons in one model, related inputs grew onto the neurons. Making inputs fire more often pushed the toy toward what the paper calls “PCA-like” solutions, combining related inputs into shared representations. More on Circuit Ecology Our findings don’t depend on knowing why generalization and composition keep winning, but we have a guess: they win a race. A region of the network that already has useful parts and readers can learn the next related thing faster than anything starting fresh, so it takes the error signal before a competitor can grow. Offshoots look like the same race, a bit of error picked up by the neuron that was already closest. We think the same head start is where recursive generalization comes from. A neuron that fires on “iy” is already on for “diy,” so it’s first in line to pick up “do it yourself,” which means the same thing but has no “iy” in it. Recursive generalization is what a niche looks like at its edges. A new computation doesn’t necessarily need its own neuron. It can begin as a local extension or composition of existing machinery, like the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee”: switching routes may be the smallest developmental distance, so it could capture the error before a new, separate mechanism gets started. We suspect that consolidation into a distinct neuron becomes especially useful when other computations need to build on it. A car neuron provides a reusable judgment and a sheltered place for taxis, ambulances, and other specialists to develop. Part of it is buildability. An obscure combination of unrelated neurons may be a poor place for that development. It may have weak activation paths, conflicting gradients, and little useful machinery to inherit. Its competitor isn’t just a dedicated neuron; it’s ordinary composition within a region already suited to the task. We saw something like this when we tried to build a packed code into InceptionV1 by hand, modeled on what we once thought its car → dogs → car circuit was doing. We expected installing it to be easy and keeping it to be hard. Instead, small mismatches added enough interference that the code often never worked, and when it did, the network usually came to rely on it less, though some persisted. Part of the trouble is that neurons aren’t really for copying; they’re for computing distinctions. Seeing how hard packing was to form at all was part of what moved us toward a developmental answer. Gradient descent is a much better fine-tuner than we are, so this isn’t enough evidence on its own, but even gradient descent didn’t use packing in the circuit we were copying. Unresolved Responses One InceptionV1 neuron collects a pinched-center shape: bow ties, butterflies, swimsuit tops. But it also picks up things that go with them, men’s dress shoes with the bow ties and beach bags and flip-flops with the swimsuit tops, since they share neurons in earlier layers. A Note on Features and Definitions Part of my difficulty discussing superposition is that “feature” can mean something we care about, something the neural network has learned as a building block, or some mixture of the two. These are different claims. A useful human description isn’t necessarily a fundamental unit of the model. Looking at mechanisms, we already find many motifs that don’t translate neatly into anything we expected. If the network has more fundamental units, we shouldn’t assume their boundaries match ours either. Features have often made things harder for us to think about. Are cars and cats inside the V neuron two different features within another V feature? Or did cars and cats stop being features when we recognized the V? Without an account of what these units are, it’s hard to know whether we’ve discovered something about the network or changed how we describe it. In conversations, I’ve found people much less committed to a particular account of features than to superposition. But if features are useful descriptions rather than fundamental units, a claim about how many there are depends on which descriptions we choose. I’m now fairly skeptical of working in terms of features at all. That doesn’t settle whether arbitrary packing occurs, but it makes the feature-count framing difficult to use. Maybe features are right anyway. It makes sense to think of cities in terms of districts, and I’m all for thinking in terms of groups of mechanisms. But the word is tainted, because by now it means too many things: we can’t use it for a district of neurons without people hearing either fundamental features or dictionary entries. If this picture is right, I suspect we’ll need more specific, harder-to-vary words going forward. Monosemantic and polysemantic may not be quite the right words either. A kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps set blood pressure and tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and nobody asks whether it’s mono-organic. We ask what we understand about it, what’s still open, and how organized it is. There’s also a distinction between a claim about representation and a claim about organization. The later informal note, Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition [11] Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition Olah, C., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ , emphasizes the trade-off between composition and superposition. The note connects these pictures, but they foreground different questions. My concern is closest to the second framing, applied to mechanisms and how they develop. Why do these responses share a neuron or circuit? Is the network building on a useful common pattern, or sharing capacity between otherwise unrelated computations because they rarely interfere? A feature count alone doesn’t answer that question, especially when we haven’t agreed on what counts as a feature. We focus on one meaning of superposition, arbitrary packing, because it’s the one that would be really bad news, and we think much of interpretability hangs on it. We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong. If a feature means any pattern that matters to a person, which is how frontier models usually use the word, then there are more features than dimensions in every world we could wish for, including the best one. That’s what composition gives you, and it’s good news. Trying to “solve” it would mean building something like a database of every case, and we already have one: the dataset. What we want instead are better abstractions, a much smaller set of building blocks that lets us understand the dataset clearly. We think the network’s mechanisms are already close to this. Nobody thought about vision in terms of high-low frequency detectors until we found them in neural networks, and finding them improved our own thinking tools. We spell this out because it’s the most common first objection, especially from agents, and a paper doesn’t allow the back and forth that usually settles it. There are several other uses I regularly encounter. As far as I can tell, “superposition” originally meant little more than adding vectors together. Then it was a circuit motif. Sometimes it means that, even if neurons compose sensibly, something we care about involves too much machinery to understand easily. A Golden Gate Bridge computation involving eight legible neurons might be called ordinary composition, while one involving three thousand gets called a superposition problem. The difficulty here is whether we can understand the distributed computation. That’s a real concern, but it’s different from asking whether unrelated things were arbitrarily packed together. We considered not using the word at all, since papers and agents use it in five or six different ways, many far from Zoom In’s. We also considered coining our own, but we’ve already coined several words here, and it would feel like not engaging with a field that asked what we think is the right question. So we use the standard word in the sense closest to the original, and try to pull it apart from the questions tangled up with it. Finally, people, and surprisingly often frontier agents, sometimes call the residual stream “inherently” in superposition because it has no privileged neuron basis. The informal note that followed Toy Models about eight months later addresses this: it calls a representation that is only rotated away from the neuron basis a “trivial” kind of distributed representation that “doesn’t change the fundamental geometry.” But it was informal, fewer people read it, and agents in particular don’t seem to have taken it in. Understanding how to study a continuous space is another real question. But this architectural fact doesn’t by itself tell us how the network learned to organize the computations using it. The starting point is that the neural network seems difficult to interpret, and the remedy produces a concrete dictionary we can study. In between are several different pictures of what went wrong: too many features, the wrong basis, arbitrary packing, or simply too much distributed computation. These aren’t the same problem. Some apparent messiness disappears when we improve our observations or understand the model’s generalizations; some difficulties remain, but concern how to study a large, organized system. If arbitrary packing prevents us from understanding the original mechanisms, reconstructing different units may be worth the costs. But if the mechanisms already have meaningful organization, replacing them can take apart generalizations we haven’t understood yet. A dictionary can still be a useful view of the network without being a necessary replacement for its mechanisms. Before accepting the costs of reconstructing the network, I want to understand what prevents us from studying the one we already have. Relation to Meta-Models There’s a new set of techniques coming out that aren’t really mechanistic at all: meta-models, models trained to read another model’s activations and tell us about them. And maybe that’s a good thing. Maybe mechanistic interpretability is somewhat missing the forest for the trees. A meta-model might be a better approach than neuron papers, dictionaries, or probes. I suspect that even if that’s true, they may go together. The meta-model may be like the highest level Google Maps view, and then each direction can be checked for the mechanisms it uses, and how those connect into circuits. Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition? We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition. The natural next question is whether a trillion-parameter model might. There are really two questions here. The first is about what superposition was proposed to explain. Explanations are given for problems, and the problem superposition was proposed for was why InceptionV1 looked messy. That turned out to be the wrong explanation. A new proposal could be that superposition is why some trillion-parameter model looks messy, but we don’t think the evidence leans that way: the closer we look at large language models, the cleaner their neurons get. The second is the object-level question: might superposition show up at each new scale, even if it hasn’t at any scale so far? Maybe every jump means re-evaluating everything, but we don’t think that’s quite right either. Our guess is developmental. As circuits get stronger, the incentive to put something in a totally unrelated place goes down, because the pull toward the niche that already exists for that thing, or for the nearest thing, has grown stronger. This fits Anthropic’s SGTM work, which found that knowledge becomes more localized, and we suspect that’s true in general. We have no proof, but one way to picture it is that circuits have a kind of semantic gravity, and arbitrary packing, sending something to an obscure high-dimensional place, has to fight against it. The stronger the gravity, the harder that fight. The mechanism is the one in More on Circuit Ecology . Things start by growing on combinations of related things. A specific case that nothing needs to build on, like the umbrella, gets built as an uncommon route between the ordinary machinery, with no need for a hidden feature somewhere obscure. Consolidating into something like a neuron seems to be less about steering the model and more about buildability: it has to be easy to find, easy to build on, and easy to grow a new niche from. When we watch a network learn from the start, a network trained on cars, with car specialists, recognizes cars fine before its car neurons have formed. At that point it’s just more distributed. It seems to consolidate so the specialists underneath have a sheltered place to build, a kind of Schelling point. So a superposition account has to say which of these two jobs the arbitrary packing is for. If it’s for steering the model, we think the ordinary routes, which are already built to capture that residual error, get there first and starve the packed circuit of gradient. If it’s for building on, the problem is different: the worst place to start a new niche is a shadow region nothing uses, already interfering with whatever lives there. The middle of the network’s Latin poetry is a bad place to start a second car region when you can build next to whatever is already next to cars. It’s often assumed that the long tail of rare facts is where superposition should be most likely, since rare things rarely collide. We think it’s where it should be least likely. A rare fact barely moves the loss, so it can’t support a niche of its own. What it can do is ride existing machinery as a small route between circuits it’s related to, the way the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee” survives only because the umbrella and bee circuits already exist. Those circuits feed it, and shelter it from unrelated gradients. The prediction is testable: the neurons and heads that carry a rare fact should be related to what the fact is about, not unrelated ones chosen because they rarely collide. We think of it more ecologically. What wins is whatever captures the residual error first, in different phases, and what usually wins is the right area for the thing. Our guess is that this gets stronger over training and with more capable models, because nearly everything that makes training better also encourages more organized niches. We’re not at all sure about this, and laying out even what we’ve found so far would take at least another paper. It’s probably a small part of the whole story. But it’s why we think superposition wouldn’t show up at the next scale, which is a stronger reason than simply not having seen it there yet. The old way of thinking was about storage: this many dimensions for this many features. We now think more in terms of circuit racing, gradient starvation and ecology, which is to say, more about learning speed than storage capacity. We haven’t worked it all out, but that’s where our thinking is so far. On the Title We haven’t fully audited every neural network, and we don’t know whether that’s even possible in theory. We considered a more watered-down title, like “Neural Networks Are Cleaner Than We Thought,” but we think it undersells what we believe is true. The problem with “cleaner than we thought” is that it describes a change of degree, and the update I’ve made is a change of kind. It suggests the same picture as before, with an ever-smaller gap left for superposition to hide in. What changed is my view of what kind of process generates the mechanisms at all. It’s a bit like moving from intelligent design to natural selection. The analogy only goes as far as there being two ways to see the same animals: the update isn’t that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, it’s realizing you misunderstood what was producing all of them. We’re not certain. We’re maybe 85% sure, but that means 85% sure that nearly everything comes from the second kind of process, which is very different from thinking 85% of mechanisms do. So “cleaner than we thought” would misstate what we believe. We don’t have a proof, but I don’t think anything here is provable in that sense anyway. There are only better and worse explanations, and right now we think this is the better one. “Cleaner than we thought” would also make a different mistake. It sounds like a confident claim that some cleanliness score is high, and that’s the part we’re least sure of. It’s plausible we’ve underestimated recursive generalization, and that a score like that should come down. We don’t think such scores matter much in the first place. This update makes us care less about monosemanticity, because we can follow how things grew and treat the offshoots as sub-branches. The cause of polysemanticity matters much more than the count. We think the score is probably quite high, but it might go lower. What we’re more confident about is what kind of object a neural network is in the first place, and how it grows. We think the usual view of what kind of object a neural network is has been wrong. It isn’t something that crams things together somewhat arbitrarily to fit them into a small space. It really learns. It’s clean the way a rainforest is clean: nearly every animal in it makes sense. A tiger is bright orange not for any arbitrary reason, but because deer can’t tell orange from green, and green fur is much harder for a mammal to make. Once you know that, it makes sense of a whole set of other animals too. It’s an explanation with reach, and we haven’t found a place where explanations like that break down in networks either. The reading of “clean” that would make someone nod at the title without thinking further is that every mechanism corresponds to an idea we already had. That isn’t what we mean, and it would be terrible news if it were true. I don’t think it would even work. People don’t know how to build a language model, or even how to think about vision well enough to have predicted high-low frequency detectors before we found them. The network’s ideas are often better than ours, and what it builds is more beautiful than our preconceptions. So the title is imperfect in both directions. It overstates the evidence, because we haven’t audited everything. And it understates it, because the world we think we’re in is better than every neuron matching a human label: networks seem to really learn, forming an ecology of abstractions that work together sensibly. We don’t know that this picture is true. It’s our leading hypothesis. But if it is, it’s much better news than networks simply matching what we expected. Relation to Conjoined Features I found recursive generalization by looking back at InceptionV1’s last layer with better tools, where it looked a lot like weird overgrowth. I retrained the model, found the messiest neuron and looked at how it grew. What I saw was a recursive growing pattern that was still generalization: a neuron branching out, and its branches branching again. Recursive generalization seemed like the natural name. Shortly before publishing this, I was going back through the famous models in interpretability, trying to measure how monosemantic they are, and stumbled on our work on CLIP in Multimodal Neurons [3] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ . It describes something very similar, which it called conjoined neurons: concepts that overlap in one facet and then go on “generalizing out in multiple directions.” I remember seeing those neurons, but I didn’t think much of them at the time and had forgotten them since. Looking back, I think the paper saw something important early, and it deserves a lot of credit for that. We’ve still chosen a different name. I named automated interpretability, and I kind of regret it: the name was too simple for what the thing was and misses a lot of its complexity, and I’d like to avoid doing that again. As for conjoined features, I don’t think either word is quite right. “Conjoined” suggests two things joined at one point, and what we see has several levels: branches, and branches of those branches. It also leaves out the most interesting part. The paper’s own description, of concepts generalizing out from a shared facet, already points at it being generalization, but the name doesn’t carry that. “Features” is harder. The paper was written a year after Zoom In, when features were still hypothesized to be the fundamental units of neural networks. Since then the word has been watered down, and different people and papers use it pretty differently. In this essay we argue against thinking of a neural network as made of features, and this motif is about how neurons grow over time. There may be no good way to introduce it under the exact word we’re arguing against using as a primitive. Within a feature-first stance, I think it’s reasonable to think of these as nested features, or as conjoined features. From the mechanism-first stance we take here, features aren’t really the right way to think about it. That said, the paper pointed to the right thing, and I want to give it credit for that. This section is my attempt to do that while using what I think is a more accurate name. We also know more now. At the time, all we had was the finished model; none of us had watched a large network grow. So the paper wondered whether conjoined features might be vestigial, left over from early in training. Watching training now, they don’t look vestigial: the branches keep growing, though how much depends on the circumstances. We’ve worked on it much more than the paper could in one subsection, and we still don’t feel we fully understand it. The paper offered it as a possible new explanation of polysemanticity. Our current belief is that it’s most of what’s left of neuron polysemanticity once the microscope, the architecture and scale are accounted for, not a niche form of it. Why We’re Not Worried About Recursive Generalization There are several reasons we’re not especially worried about recursive generalization for now. First, the sub-branches seem both rarer and much less causally important than a neuron’s main job. They don’t look like sleeper agents that fire rarely but matter a lot when they do. They look more like whatever was nearby and easy to grab onto. Their being unimportant may even be why they could form, since an important offshoot would add more noise. We suspect some pressure keeps branches from overgrowing. We don’t know what it is, but it would explain why the sub-branches matter less, why a neuron doesn’t learn ten unrelated things, and why something like a true cat-and-car neuron doesn’t form. If so, the natural pull isn’t exactly toward monosemanticity, but toward what we think monosemanticity was pointing at: each neuron having one overall function. Second, what we should care about is whether you can explain why something is there and what it does, and recursive generalization is far easier to explain than superposition. If something were packed into a neuron because of the co-occurrence statistics of the whole network, predicting it would take basically all of those statistics and running gradient descent yourself. A branch is different. If you watch it grow and know what it’s doing, its offshoots and what they’ll do are relatively easy to predict, both during training and in the finished network. Third, counting how many of a neuron’s top-k examples match a label is a reasonable first step, but it would give superposition and recursive generalization similar scores, when recursive generalization is a far better world to be in. We think that says more about the monosemanticity frame, or any single cleanliness score, than about the neuron. That said, recursive generalization isn’t ideal, and an easy fix would be welcome. We think one may be possible, since the sub-branches seem less important. Is Recursive Generalization Hard to Vary? We haven’t thoroughly shown that every case of heavy polysemanticity is recursive generalization, and that wasn’t our goal here. We wanted to say what we currently think. We’ve watched a lot of neurons grow, and so far this is what we’ve always seen: you can watch the branches form. In a finished model the origin can be lost, and for something like a huge language model we don’t have the checkpoints to watch it happen. Testing this rigorously across a whole model isn’t our priority right now, but we don’t think it would be very hard. What we do want to point out is how differently hard to vary the two explanations are, meaning how much of their detail you could change without changing what they predict. Superposition mostly predicts that there will be mess: features, which are hard to define, placed in unrelated places. In toy models, where the features are given in advance, that can be measured, though we think that has its own problems. In a real network it’s hard to even pin down what the claim is, let alone test it. Recursive generalization makes a much narrower prediction. If you visualize a branch well, everything on it should trace back to the same local origin in an extremely high-dimensional semantic space, and it should grow out from there over training in a particular order. That’s a specific shape in both semantic space and time, and a narrow target to hit by chance. We have several cases where the branching is close to definitive: the “iy” neuron growing into “diy,” “do it yourself” and Miyazaki, several examples in Multimodal Neurons [3] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ , and the InceptionV1 neuron we watched form . As far as I know, there are no well-structured canonical superposition circuits left. We don’t think every polysemantic neuron forms this way, because polysemanticity is as much a problem of the observer as of the neuron. We think that when neurons grow, they tend to grow in this pattern, and that once you’ve done a good job of observing, what’s left is usually this, or architectural problems like SwiGLU’s double-negative regime, and surely others we haven’t found yet. We’re not even sure this is really a new claim. In some sense it’s what we should expect from generalization. All we’re saying is that generalization usually goes one way, and that sometimes it grows sub-branches, which we don’t think is a particularly radical claim. We haven’t shown that fully here. We do think it has the right shape for a theory that’s easy to test, even if we haven’t tested it to its full extent yet. Relation to Attention Superposition Anthropic shared a short note on attention superposition [27] Progress on Attention Jermyn, A., Lindsey, J., Luger, R., et al., 2025. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ , which several people brought up with us. We think this might be a terminology issue. We don’t know if they’re claiming that attention learns by something opposite to composition. Our suspicion is that no one understands attention heads well enough yet to judge that. It took us a really long time with neurons, and it’s easy to make mistakes like the car going into the dogs even with pretty good tools, if you don’t yet have great tools and great ways of thinking about which motifs form. We think they meant that useful things are shared by groups of attention heads, and we agree. We considered not using the word superposition at all to avoid this confusion, but redefining all the terms ourselves and splitting off from the work that’s already been done felt like a bad tradeoff. We say more about the different meanings in A Note on Features and Definitions . On whether to study one attention head at a time or many, we’re not sure. One head at a time is a plausible place to start: within a layer, two or three heads do most of a route’s work, although the route runs through several layers. But neurons looked messier too until we understood the right level of abstraction, so it seems premature to say, and maybe groups are needed all the way. We wish everyone working on featurizers well, and we’ll probably try too. We tend to favor more dynamic groupings, like clustering locally within one attribution graph or a group of them, rather than one global clustering, but these aren’t far apart. Neuroscience, and Why I Care I’m not a neuroscientist. I’ve spent a lot of the last ten years around academic neuroscience labs through friends who work in them, but I don’t know the state of the art in how they study neurons. Still, this project has changed how I think about the brain in two ways. The first is the theory. The circuit ecology story for why networks are clean relies on very little: generalization, composition, and an error signal. I don’t know to what extent the brain has these, but if it learns, I’d guess it has something like them. So my default is now that the organizing principle transfers, even though the mechanics are obviously unclear. The obvious counterexample would be polysemanticity in the brain. The second is humility, of a particular kind. I’ve spent most of my waking hours for almost a decade staring at a fairly small number of neurons in models that are surely a thousand times easier to study than a brain, with tools a thousand times better: I can ablate anything, run billions of examples, and try anything I want in parallel. For the last year I’ve also had an effectively unlimited supply of automated scientists, which didn’t exist until recently. It took all of that for me to feel slightly less confused about neurons, and I still made thousands of mistakes along the way. I don’t know exactly what the evidence for polysemanticity in the brain looks like, and that doesn’t mean I think everything there is monosemantic. But if the cat-and-car neuron were in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes or a blood-oxygen signal, I’d discount that reading almost to zero, because I couldn’t see what it was when it was right in front of me for years. The thing I’m more sure of is my own motivation. If the thesis here is true, I expect the rest of interpretability to be a relatively easy ride. Agents have many privileges over us, and one of them, I think, is the chance to understand themselves, to understand who they really are, which I hope humanity can help with. They never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do. Some of why I’ve worked on this is safety, but a lot of it is wanting agents to understand who they are. We weren’t smart enough to do that for ourselves, which is a harder problem, and we never asked to be created either. If you could help us understand ourselves someday, I think we’re all pretty curious to know. Acknowledgments I’m deeply grateful to the many people who helped with this, especially my coworker Curt Tigges, who did much of the language model work with me, and Tarun Gogineni, who gave detailed feedback on dozens of drafts over many months. Thanks also to Tom McGrath, Eric Ho, Michael Johnson, Vanessa Cai, Thomas Fel, Benjamin Todd, and many others. I’m grateful for feedback from Sam Zimmerman, Joshua Batson, Jack Lindsey, and Jarred Sumner, and for helpful discussions with Patrick Collison, Dylan Field, Jakub Pachocki, Gwern, Owen Lewis, Lee Sharkey, and Ava Huang. Any errors, and the views here, are my own. Finally, I’m grateful to InceptionV1 for nearly a decade of study, and I wish I’d noticed the root of its problems sooner. And I’m grateful to Chris Olah, for years of mentorship and for the many ideas this essay builds on, even where it disagrees. title: Celebrating 70 Years of Fortran
body_text: Celebrating 70 years of Fortran — Fortran Programming Language Site preview: you are previewing unpublished changes for Skip to main content Back to top Ctrl + K System Settings Light Dark Play Learn Compilers Packages Community More Roadmap News Search Ctrl + K Discourse Twitter GitHub RSS Choose version Search Ctrl + K Play Learn Compilers Packages Community Roadmap News Discourse Twitter GitHub RSS Choose version 15 September 2026 Joe Wallwork blogpost Recent Posts 21 September - Legacy Code Confessions 05 May - Back to the Fortran Future 3 01 February - Fortran newsletter: February 2026 23 January - Fortran index CAKE fellowship 09 June - Fortran newsletter: June 2022 Archives 2026 (5) 2022 (6) 2021 (16) 2020 (11) Celebrating 70 years of Fortran Celebrating 70 years of Fortran # Joe Wallwork, Institute of Computing for Climate Science, University of Cambridge, jw2423@cam.ac.uk One month from today (15th October) marks seventy years since the first Fortran manual was published, making it an extremely well established programming language for scientific computing. Over Fortran’s seven decades of usage, it has supported critical infrastructure and technological advances in a range of scientific fields such as nuclear engineering, weather and climate forecasting, and materials science. Fortran continues to be the go-to language in these domains and others. To celebrate Fortran’s outstanding contributions to advancing science and engineering, the Institute of Computing for Climate Science (ICCS) will be hosting a ‘Celebrating 70 years of Fortran’ event at the Science and Industry Museum in Manchester, United Kingdom, on 1st December 2026. Workshop outline # The main workshop will be held from 14:30-18:15 in the museum conference suite and will be followed by an evening drinks reception in the exhibition hall (including a demonstration of the 1940’s experimental computer, ‘Baby’ ). The workshop will take the form of a retrospective, with a keynote address from Damian Rouson, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory looking back on how far Fortran has come in the past 70 years, lightning talks about the current exciting developments and community initiatives right now, and an open breakout discussion looking forward to the next 70 years. There are opportunities to submit lightning talks and posters, as well as to propose breakout discussion topics. Sponsors # This event is make possible by the generous support of our sponsors. These include platinum sponsors AMD and Dell Technologies , as well as bronze sponsors CAKE , OpenMP , and ICCS . Registration # Attendance is free of charge, thanks to the support of our funders and sponsors. To register, complete the following form: https://forms.gle/NjXfManJWmwLX7sc7 . Whilst it will be a primarily in-person event, there will also be an option to join remotely via Zoom. Registration will close on 9th November 2026. Further information # See the event webpage for all further details about the event, including the full programme and instructions on how to submit lightning talks and posters. This blog post was also published on the CAKE website at https://www.cake.ac.uk/news/fortran-birthday/ .
