See RELEASE-NOTES.md . I've created a Discord server! You can also report bugs and submit ideas for new features here! link : https://discord.gg/xR5f7Xs49 DEsk is D esktop E nvironment and desk in one word -- a name that came from the Reddit community. It used to be called DeskWM: the commands are now desk , desk-session , desk-settings and so on, and what was set up for DeskWM (its settings, its data, DESKWM_* variables) carries over by itself. A Wayland desktop for Linux in realistic skeuomorphism -- the kind iOS 6 had, where everything on the screen is drawn to look like the real thing. Here the desktop is a desk. Windows are sheets of paper on a walnut desk. The dock is a drawer, your apps are filed in binders on a bookshelf behind the desk, notifications arrive in a post box, and the system controls are a panel built into the back of the desk. The room is ray-traced, and one desk lamp lights all of it. Status: beta. DEsk is used day to day on its author's machines and has been checked carefully (see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md , section 9), but this is its first release: expect rough edges, and expect things to change. Your settings and data will be carried forward. Install Download the latest release from the Releases page and unpack it (or clone this repository). Then, in its folder, run the line for your system: Debian 13 sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 (and Linux Mint, Pop!_OS) sudo sh scripts/install_ubuntu.sh Arch Linux (and EndeavourOS, Manjaro) sudo sh scripts/install_arch.sh Fedora 43 / 44 (and Nobara) sudo sh scripts/install_fedora.sh Then log out and choose DEsk on the login screen. It shows what it will install and asks first. --yes takes the suggested answers; --no-apps installs DEsk without the recommended programs. The first login draws the room once: a few seconds on a GPU, longer without one. After that it starts at once. To update, get the new release and run the same line again. Your settings are kept. Something went wrong? See Reporting a problem . More options, building by hand and running DEsk in a window are under Build and Run . What's on the desk Nothing here is a symbol for a thing on a desk. As in the realistic skeuomorphism of iOS 6, each is drawn to look like the real thing set down there -- its material, the light on it, its shadow and the wear of use. Windows are paper. Each window sits on a cream sheet with real fibre, thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close: crumpled into a ball and tossed). Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet. The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D ). It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that opens Shell Settings. The bookshelf holds your apps ( Super+A , or the ALL APPS plate). Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring. Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book : every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the page to type into (input methods via IBus work). The post box is the notification centre ( Super+N ). Letters show the sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk. The Control Panel ( Super+C ) is a valve-era machine built into the back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too), a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along). A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light only while a camera or a microphone is in use. The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it. Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock counts how far in glowing red. Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger things. More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its windows on one that is left. X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames sit on paper too. The screen lock is the front door ( Super+L , or logind): you walk up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with PAM, as at login. Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean, Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is, and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces. Standard programs DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there: app.terminal , app.browser , app.files , app.editor in shell.conf (a .desktop id), the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order: ~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list (what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and the same two in the system's folders, ending with the desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open and GIO give, the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on), any program filed under the right category. A tour The corner of every window: Fold, Unfold, Discard. The drawer: the dock. A folded window, lying on the desk under the others. The bookcase behind the desk. ALL APPS, every program from A to Z ... ... and a line to type into. The Control Panel. The post box: notifications. The desk calendar and its notes. Shell Settings. Documentation docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -- how DEsk is built: the programs, the compositor, the ray-traced room, threads, files. docs/MODDING.md -- changing DEsk: words and languages, settings, borrowed programs, sounds, the room, things on the desk. docs/CONFIGURATION.md -- every setting, file and environment variable. RELEASE-NOTES.md -- what is in v0.1.2 and what is known not to work yet. docs/design.md -- the full development log (in Japanese). As a desktop DEsk draws the desk; the work done on it is done with free software that already exists. It reaches completeness by borrowing, and keeps a firm line between what it makes and what it borrows: DEsk makes both: DEsk draws it, something else does the work borrowed what what is drawn as the room and handled as its things; what only the compositor can do programs, system settings panels, background helpers examples windows as paper, the drawer, the bookcase, the clock, the Control Panel, the post box, the front door, the calendar and memo pad; keyboard, pointer and their keys (volume and media keys too), the screens and their power, remembering their arrangement, going idle, the lock; Shell Settings volume knob and mute (PipeWire/PulseAudio), brightness (logind), Wi-Fi and Bluetooth levers, the post box (the desk is the notification daemon), the tray's slips (the applets' own items), the clock's MEDIA page (MPRIS), screenshots (grim), the input method (a bridge to IBus) network connections, Bluetooth devices, sound devices, display arrangement, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, polkit agent, keyring, portals -- and the programs themselves The rule for new cases: make only what is drawn as part of the room or can only be done inside the compositor; otherwise find an existing program that works as it is under a wlroots compositor, and make something only as a last resort. KDE's System Settings and kcmshell (which do not work outside Plasma), Xfce's and MATE's X11-only dialogs, and Xfce's display and appearance dialogs (which need xfsettingsd, and xfsettingsd overwrites GSettings with Xfce's defaults as it starts) are not used. sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # DEsk and the whole set (install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh) sh scripts/install-desktop.sh # only the programs (shows them, then asks for sudo) sh scripts/install-desktop.sh --extras # and the office suite, mail... install-desktop.sh works with apt, dnf, pacman and zypper. On Debian and Ubuntu the same set is also one package: equivs-build packaging/debian/desk-desktop.equivs . For What comes terminal, files, text Xfce Terminal, Thunar (with tumbler and thunar-volman), Mousepad the web Firefox (Firefox ESR on Debian, the snap on Ubuntu) pictures, documents, music and video Ristretto, Atril, Parole tools Engrampa, GNOME Disks networks, Bluetooth, sound NetworkManager with its applet and editor, Blueman, PipeWire, pavucontrol displays, looks, defaults wdisplays, nwg-look (GNOME Tweaks on Ubuntu 24.04 and Fedora), Xfce's MIME settings printing system-config-printer, CUPS notices udiskie (memory sticks mounted, with a letter), poweralertd (low battery; batsignal on Arch; none on Fedora), package-update-indicator (updates; Debian and Ubuntu) looking after the machine QDirStat (disk usage), LXQt's date and time and users, Mugshot (your name and picture), Seahorse (passwords and keys), gnome-packagekit (adding and removing programs), Back In Time (backups), Xfce Task Manager, hardinfo2 (about this computer); baobab and Deja Dup on Arch; no Mugshot on Fedora passwords MATE's polkit agent, GNOME Keyring plumbing xdg-desktop-portal (wlr, gtk), Xwayland, xdg-user-dirs, xdg-utils, wl-clipboard, grim, curl looks Qt's GTK platform theme, so Qt programs match the GTK ones typing and fonts IBus (and Mozc for Japanese), Noto (CJK, emoji), the URW base 35, Klee One (not on Arch or Fedora) --extras LibreOffice (drawn with GTK), Thunderbird, Galculator, Xfce Task Manager, Simple Scan The classic GTK programs of Xfce and MATE come first because they are the kind of window the desk's paper is cut for -- a menu bar, plain tools and the document -- and they are light, start quickly and run on Wayland as they are. GTK 3 asks the compositor for its frame through KDE's server-decoration protocol, so they lie on DEsk's paper with its printed heading and no GTK title bar. Windows with a header bar (GNOME's programs, Firefox) keep their own frame, inside a paper margin. Shell Settings ( desk-settings ) holds DEsk's own settings -- windows, the size of things, how much is drawn, language, clock, your birthday and the weather, when the screen goes off and whether the desk locks then -- on its Shell tab, and on its System tab rows that open the borrowed programs (network, Bluetooth, sound, displays, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, disk usage, colour profiles, the input method, date and time, your name and picture, users, passwords and keys, adding and removing programs, backups, what the computer is doing, and the Experience Index), classic-looking programs first, each with the program's own icon and its name -- "Displays (wdisplays)" -- so you can see what does the setting. A row whose program is not installed is printed faint with the package to install, by this distribution's name. The two tabs sit on the sheet like a folder's index tabs, and in each pocket is a wire-bound pad with a sheet to each part of the form and a sticky note on each sheet's edge; taking hold of a note turns the sheets over the wire to it, as on the desk calendar (Page Up and Down too). Changing tab (a click, Ctrl+Tab or Ctrl+Page Up/Down) draws the other pad up out of the folder from below, and the pad comes up the same way when the window opens. Started as a session ( desk-session , from a login screen), DEsk tells D-Bus and systemd where its display is, runs the XDG autostart entries (leaving out the ones that would fight it, such as another notification daemon or an X screen locker), and starts an authentication agent, the keyring, the input method and the network applet with whichever free program for each is installed. The input method's candidates come up under the text being written -- in a program's window as on the desk's own pages -- and leave the keys where they are. It turns the screen off when nobody is at the desk (locking first, by default), lets video players keep it on, and speaks wlr-output-management (wdisplays, wlr-randr, kanshi), remembering a display tool's arrangement for each set of screens. Logging out, restarting and powering off ask every window to close first, so a program with unsaved work can ask about it; a window that does not close holds it up and is put in front. Shell Settings also sets what only a Wayland compositor can: tap to click, natural scrolling, pointer speed and left-handed buttons (through libinput), the keyboard layout, a second layout and the keys that change to it, and key repeat -- applied at once to what is plugged in. How much the desk draws is a setting too, Graphics: Ultra (the room traced finer, and wider where a GPU can, and nothing drawn coarser while it moves), High (as made, the default), Medium, Low, and 2D Fallback -- for a machine without a GPU or a virtual machine rendering on its CPU: no shadows, nothing fading, blurred or moving, nothing ray-traced as it moves, and the room traced once, small and plain. On two CPU cores without a GPU the first start goes from nearly ten minutes to about a quarter of a minute, and a frame from 2 ms to 0.5 ms. The installer takes a quick look at the machine ( desk-index --suggest : the graphics, or the processor, for a couple of seconds, the threads and the memory, and how long the processor takes to draw a sheet of paper folding) and picks the level for it, as the machine's default ( /etc/xdg/desk/shell.conf ); each user's own choice wins. Where the screen is drawn by the processor -- no GPU, a virtual machine without 3D, a GPU without its driver -- the desk runs in 2D Fallback unless you choose a level yourself, and says so: a letter in the post box (check the graphics drivers, or the virtual machine's settings) and a line in red beside Graphics in Shell Settings. 2D Fallback is the same desk with its effects off, not a second one, its room traced at a sample a pixel and softened. And a first start, which traces the room from nothing, leaves a letter in the middle of the desk saying it may take a minute or two, more on some machines, and that the desk can be used meanwhile. It is meant to stay light on old machines. Measured on a machine held to about a 2010 laptop's pace (a quarter of a core each on two cores, 2 GB, no GPU for the room): a later login shows the desk in under half a second and has the light on in 1.4 s; the very first one, which has to trace the room on the processor, shows a soft first look and the light within seven seconds instead of a minute and a half in the dark; folding a sheet costs 5 ms a frame at Low. The traced room is kept across updates, and paper in motion is drawn finer or coarser by the level (whole at High, half at Low). Programs on the desk are dressed for it too: DEsk's own icons, drawn to look like the real things set down on the desk, the way iOS 6 drew them -- manila card folders with papers in them, a typed page with its corner turned down, a letter signed in blue ink, a ledger, slides in their mounts, instant photos, a record sliding out of its sleeve, a film slate, a taped carton for an archive, a deck of punched cards for a program, a block of wood type for a font, a wire wastebasket you see through, a brass globe for the network, a drive in its aluminium case -- with the grain of paper, card, wood and brushed metal and the shadows they cast; and a GTK theme of paper, ink and brass. They are set in a dconf layer of DEsk's own over the user's, so another desktop on the same machine keeps its look. When something on the desk gets stuck: Ctrl+Alt+Del twice puts everything of the desk's own away and draws it all again (the windows stay as they are); three times logs out. desk-ctl reset and desk-ctl logout do the same from a terminal or another VT. The DEsk Experience Index desk-index rates the machine at what the desk asks of it, the way the Windows Experience Index did: processor, memory, 2D graphics (the desk's own drawing), 3D graphics (the room's shader, checked against the CPU) and disk, each 1.0-9.9, on brass-rimmed meters; the base score is the lowest. desk-index --text prints the same in a terminal. Requirements The simplest way is the installer for your distribution (below), which brings everything. To build it yourself: wlroots 0.18 (Debian 13 has it, and Fedora 43 and later as wlroots0.18 ; Ubuntu 24.04 has 0.17, Ubuntu 26.04 only 0.19 and Arch only 0.20, so the installers build 0.18.3 from its release into /opt/desk-wlroots , used by DEsk alone through its run path) wayland, wayland-protocols, xkbcommon, cairo, pixman, fontconfig, libdrm, PAM libsystemd (optional): the notification daemon and the system tray. Build with -Dpost=disabled to leave them out. libpulse (optional): the desk's sounds ( -Dsound=disabled ) libinput (optional): touchpad and mouse settings EGL, GLES, gbm (optional): ray-trace the room on the GPU. Without them the CPU does it. Xwayland and xcb (optional): X11-only apps. Fonts: the URW base 35 ( fonts-urw-base35 ) and Noto CJK ( fonts-noto-cjk ); fonts-klee for the memo pad. At run time: grim for screenshots, curl for the weather at the door. Minimum and recommended Measured with the CPU, GPU and memory cut down ( systemd-run CPUQuota and MemoryMax, taskset ; nested, 1440x900, the same hand moves every run). Once the room is traced, even one core without a GPU dropped no frames; a frame costs about 2 ms. Only the first login traces the room: 6-9 s on a GPU, about 10 minutes on two cores without one (then it is cached). minimum recommended CPU 2 x86-64 cores (1 works) 4 cores or more memory 4 GB (DEsk itself 200-450 MB) 8 GB or more GPU none needed (a long first login) OpenGL ES 3.0 with GBM (Mesa Intel, AMD, Nouveau; VMware's SVGA3D) screen 1366x768 1440x900 or more disk about 1 GB ( --bare ; --no-apps adds what Shell Settings opens) 2-2.7 GB with the whole set system Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 LTS, Arch Linux, Fedora 43 / 44 the same Build meson setup build meson compile -C build Run Inside your current session, as a window: ./build/desk -s foot As a session of its own, picked from the login screen (GDM, SDDM, LightDM), use the installer for your system ( Install ). All four take the same options: sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # or install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --no-apps # DEsk, what it needs and what Shell Settings opens sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --bare # DEsk and what it needs, no programs (containers) sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --prefix /opt/desk sh scripts/install_session.sh picks the right one by itself and keeps what it says in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log . Each installer does the same (derivatives such as Mint, Pop!_OS, EndeavourOS, Manjaro and Nobara are recognised): packages, a release build in build-install , the PAM file, the login entry, and the removal of what the old name, DeskWM, left behind (after asking). Every program Shell Settings' System tab opens is installed, --no-apps or not, and at the end desk-settings --check lists what each row opens (or which package would bring it). On other distributions, install the requirements and run scripts/install.sh . Or from a TTY: desk-session . To update, get the new copy and run the installer again the same way ("this updates it", it says): what is installed is replaced, the last build is reused (or made afresh when it cannot be), and your settings and the traced room stay. All the installer says is also kept in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log (the last run's) -- the thing to look at, or send, if it stops part way. A copy made for passing round carries SHA256SUMS, and the installer checks every file against it before building: a copy damaged on its way says which files are wrong and stops (copy it again; if a fresh copy is damaged too, suspect the machine's memory or disk -- memtest86+). A Japanese locale gets the Mozc converter among the suggested programs; IBus itself is installed for everyone but only runs for languages typed through an input method, or when one is set up. The first start at a new screen size spends a little while ray-tracing the room, on the GPU the screen is drawn with: the desk first, then the bookcase, the Control Panel and the post box, each there to turn to as soon as its picture is, and last the films of the camera moves to them (until a film is done, the move to its view is a cut). Each part is cached as it is done, so a first start cut short picks up where it stopped. What DEsk says as it runs is kept in ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (the session before in session.log.old ); its desk: room: lines say what the room was traced on and how long each part took -- the thing to send if a start is slow. A GPU is tried once, in a child process, before the room is traced on it; one that fails says why ( failed its trial: ... ), and the processor traces the room instead -- at High's quality even where Ultra is chosen, Ultra's being a GPU's to trace. Keys Key Super+Enter terminal Super+Q / Alt+F4 close the focused window Super+M fold / unfold the focused sheet Super+D open / close the drawer Super+A look up at the bookshelf Super+C the Control Panel Super+N the post box Super+Tab / Alt+F1 cycle windows Esc back to the desk brightness keys the screen's backlight (or, with none, the lamp) volume, mute and media keys the mixer and the player playing (as the clock's MEDIA page) Print / Alt+Print screenshot of the screen / of the window in front Super+L lock the screen: the front door; type the password, Enter (or click the key) Super+Esc / Alt+Esc log out (asking the windows to close first) Reporting a problem The quickest way: run this in a terminal (any desktop, or a console -- DEsk need not start), and attach the file it writes, ~/desk-report.txt : desk-report It gathers DEsk's version, your Linux, your graphics card and driver, the last session's log and whether DEsk crashed, with your user name, home folder, machine name and network addresses taken out. Read it through before sending it. Say too what you did and what happened. Without it (an older DEsk, or one not installed), attach by hand: ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (and session.log.old if the problem was in the session before) -- what DEsk said as it ran; if the installer stopped, its last lines from the terminal (or ~/.local/state/desk/install.log when it was run through install_session.sh ). Both are plain text; look them over before sending them. If the desk is stuck, desk-ctl reset from a terminal (or another VT) draws everything again without closing your windows. How it was made DEsk was built with the help of AI. Much of the code and the documentation was written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) under the author's direction: the author decided what DEsk should be and how it should look, tested it on real machines, and reviewed what went in. Reports and patches are welcome all the same. License MIT About No description, website, or topics provided. title: What I Self-Host
AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
body_text:
Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware - The Citizen Lab Skip to content Opens in a new window Opens an external site Opens an external site in a new window --> Our Work Research Publication Directory Tools & Resources News & Events Expert Insights In the Media Events News About Who We Are Contact People Donate Search by keyword Search for: Our Work Research Publication Directory Tools & Resources News & Events Expert Insights In the Media Events News About Who We Are Contact People Donate Focus Areas App Security & Privacy Artificial Intelligence Censorship Digital Transnational Repression Disinformation Law & Policy Mass Surveillance Targeted Surveillance Subscribe to our newsletter Search by keyword Search for: Research → Targeted Surveillance Exposing AdFection How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware This is the first-ever public confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered via targeted ads. We call the technique AdFection, and show how it was used to infect devices at Al Jazeera with Candiru’s spyware. We also uncover Discover-Tech, and show how the company helps mercenary surveillance vendors track and hack devices around the world. Date Published October 15, 2026 Authors Bill Marczak , Wolfie Christl , John Scott-Railton , Astrid Perry , Siena Anstis , and Ron Deibert Topics Targeted Surveillance advertising intelligence , spyware , targeted ads Share Citation Bill Marczak, Wolfie Christl, John Scott-Railton, Astrid Perry, Siena Anstis, and Ron Deibert. “Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware,” Citizen Lab Report 195, University of Toronto, October 15, 2026. Contents Key Findings 1. Introduction 2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click Works 3. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform 4. Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors  5. Uncovering Discover-Tech’s Billion-Bid Scale Ad Targeting 6. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser 7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate Network 8. Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru’s Corporate Networks 9. Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising Industry 10. Discussion: AdFection Shows that Online Ads Are a Cybersecurity and Privacy Crisis 11. Recommendations: How to Stop AdFection Attacks Correspondence with Companies Key Findings Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection . The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. Discover-Tech operates a platform called Controlium that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack. Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy.  A separate threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report. Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union. Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report. We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage.  We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. Other ad vendors we found to be involved in Discover-Tech’s operations did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. We are also actively working with vendors to mitigate DARK CARTOGRAPHER ’s mass-deanonymization attack. This report is co-timed with an investigation by Confiant . Read the Executive Summary of this report 1. Introduction This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech. The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad. Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps. Figure 1 Basic architecture of the online advertising ecosystem. Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem: The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit bids for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers. The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves may contain code from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referred to as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally. Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports have uncovered vendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection. There has been some reporting about the intersection between spyware and the advertising ecosystem. However, the specific ways mercenary spyware companies plug into the ads ecosystem to target particular users have remained largely secret. This report exposes zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads, which we call AdFection , and is the first technical demonstration that mercenary spyware is being distributed via targeted advertisements. Discover-Tech is a Bridge Between Mercenary Spyware Companies and the Advertising Ecosystem We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users. The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them. Figure 2 The website of Integrity Labs (the rebranded Candiru), one of the mercenary spyware companies working with Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm. What is Discover-Tech and How Does It Operate? Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa. Discover-Tech appears to place advertisements using several techniques. Firstly, the company operates a platform called MyDSP, which interfaces with online ad vendors including Google, Yandex, Vungle (Liftoff), and Sunteng. Secondly, separately from MyDSP, it purchases ads via the ad vendors Eskimi and Comcast-owned Beeswax (Freewheel). A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a script tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “ NOAS server ” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads. Figure 3 Discover-Tech bridges the mercenary spyware industry with the online advertising ecosystem. As detailed in Section 9 , Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale. As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms.  Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains. Report Overview: Exposing Discover-Tech’s AdFection Pipeline  In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network. In Section 2 , we show how Candiru works with Discover-Tech to conduct AdFection attacks, and describe one such attack: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with Candiru’s mercenary spyware. In Section 3 , we examine Controlium, a Discover-Tech platform that provides a control-panel style interface enabling mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads.” In Section 4 , we examine links between Discover-Tech and mercenary spyware companies Candiru/Integrity Labs and Bindecy. We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as DARK CARTOGRAPHER , which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers. In Section 5 , we analyze where Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. These records show that Discover-Tech ads were served in almost 200,000 different Android apps, iOS apps, and websites in many countries. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions. In Section 6 , we use technical analysis to examine how Discover-Tech deploys ads, tracks users and exchanges user identifiers with other ad vendors, including with Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad system Xandr. In Section 7 , we present our research on Discover-Tech Ltd, its corporate network, key persons linked to the company, the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology, and its connection to the wider advertising ecosystem. In Section 8 , we summarize what is known about the mercenary surveillance firms Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos, and we further examine their activities and corporate networks in the context of the findings presented in our report. In Section 9 , we explore how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, including Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, Sunteng, and Xandr (Microsoft). In Section 10 , we discuss the implications of AdFection for user security and human rights. In Section 11 , we provide recommendations to lawmakers, regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to mitigate and block threats from AdFection-style attacks. The Citizen Lab sent requests for comment to 13 companies; their responses are included in full in the ‘Correspondence with Companies’ section. 2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click Works This section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware . We refer to this type of attack as AdFection . Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware. What AdFection Looks Like The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in Figure 4 , though in some cases the ad may render in the background. Figure 4 Discover-Tech ads that could have infected users with spyware. We were served these ads while browsing the CBC and Yahoo websites, and while using a Sudoku app on Android. When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is not selected for targeting, and the server will not return any JavaScript to be executed.  Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address. Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech Ads In 2024 and 2025, international news network Al Jazeera was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by Figure 5 . Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface. Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called Controlium that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress. As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend. 2 We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface.   In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this. Authentication Vulnerability While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems. Figure 15 Controlium incorrectly derives the authentication token from encrypted user metadata, instead of the signed JWT returned by Okta. The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s Auth0 product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with Auth0 , a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by Auth0 , and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate user object as a token to the backend server. The user object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform. Interestingly, the correct code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code. Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors  This section examines links between Discover-Tech and the mercenary spyware companies Candiru and Bindecy . We also illustrate that, beyond facilitating mercenary spyware delivery, Discover-Tech is linked to ADINT firms, including Intelos. Discover-Tech also supports mass-deanonymization of internet and app users by a threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER , which exploits vulnerabilities in mobile networks to unmask users’ phone numbers. Links with Candiru/Integrity Labs We observed that Discover-Tech sends encrypted ad impression data to Candiru using Controlium’s “Ad URL OpSec” feature. We identified several 2024 and 2025 Candiru infection links to at least six domains matching Fingerprint V1 and that also contained a parameter “?q=” whose value was 16 bytes of data in Base64-encoded form. In every case, the value of the “?q=” parameter was correctly decrypted with the “V1” AES-256 key published on a page called “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” on the website myipinfo[.]io . The website myipinfo[.]io is clearly linked to Discover-Tech: passive DNS data shows multiple overlaps in IP addresses and CNAME records with other Discover-Tech websites, including powerium[.]net and myweb3id[.]io (see also Section 7 ). One case of a Candiru infection link bearing a Discover-Tech Ad URL OpSec parameter is listed publicly on VirusTotal. The “?q=” parameter decrypts to an IP registered at the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, indicating that organization as a potential target of Candiru spyware via Discover-Tech ads: Figure 19 Discover-Tech’s “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” shows that a Candiru infection link submitted to VirusTotal bears opsec data indicating the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs as a likely spyware target. We assess that this opsec data is included to facilitate a secure handoff from Discover-Tech to an attacker. The attacker presumably compares the visitor IP for the infection link against the IP encrypted by Discover-Tech, to make sure the link from the ad impression was not silently swapped to a different device (as a security researcher might want to do to capture an exploit). DARK CARTOGRAPHER: Mass-Deanonymization With Ads We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue , which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices. One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content. We taxonomized the issues into five types, exploited by attackers across numerous mobile providers in more than 30 countries in North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and disclosure to companies is in progress. Once the disclosure process is complete, we will release our subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks. Notably, DARK CARTOGRAPHER ’s infrastructure links to both a mercenary adtech vendor and a U.S. government contractor. It is rare to see such direct overlaps between mercenary vendors and U.S. government or intelligence contractors. We assess that this attacker has been exploiting MSISDN leak issues since at least 2019, fronted by a variety of mercenary adtech companies. Our investigation into this threat actor is ongoing. Ad Impression Data Highlights Systemic Risk Our review of the ad bidding data indicates that Discover-Tech ads were shown on devices in national-security-sensitive networks around the world. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity. An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but can also carry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag . A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel , also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors. Our analysis of ad tags, tracking pixels, and ID syncing activities associated with Discover-Tech’s ad delivery is based on an analysis of publicly available code, browser testing and ad transactions archived by the web investigation tool urlscan. While ads displayed in mobile apps similarly carry code that connects to ad vendors, this section focuses on Discover-Tech ads displayed in the web browser. Discover-Tech’s Ad and Tracking Tags We found two versions of another app related to Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform named “Banner Tester” published on the sites bt.myweb3id[.]io and bt.platc-tester[.]com . User ID Syncing with Other Ad Vendors Unlike apps on mobile devices, web browsers do not allow websites to access a universal device identifier. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code. We found evidence showing how Discover-Tech engages in ID syncing with Comcast’s ad system Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad platform Xandr. Discover-Tech appears to use its myweb3id[.]io domain for ID syncing with Yandex. This domain is highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites. Starting in May 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to the domain events.myweb3id[.]io , most of them occurring during visits to Russian websites. A recent urlscan record shows an example of a typical request chain that involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s events.myweb3id[.]io domain and the following Yandex endpoint: an.yandex.ru/mapuid/discovertechis an . yandex . ru / mapuid / discovertechis The URL component “discovertechis” indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Yandex. Discover-Tech appears to use another domain, tracookiepixel[.]xyz , which is associated with myweb3id[.]io via DNS links and which is also highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites, for ID syncing with Beeswax. Starting in July 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to tracookiepixel[.]xyz , many of them occurring during visits to popular websites including IMDb and New York Times . A recent urlscan record shows an example request chain that was initiated during a visit to the website of The Guardian, which involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s tracookiepixel[.]xyz domain and Beeswax’ tracking domain bidr[.]io . The requests contain the parameter “bee_sync_partners=dtech”, which indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Beeswax. These ID syncing activities typically take place during website visits even when a user was not served a Discover-Tech ad. We are unsure how exactly Discover-Tech uses its browser ID syncing capabilities. Generally, being able to synchronize and correlate user identities across vendors is considered a precondition for individual-level ad targeting in the web browser. The Controlium platform, as examined in Section 3 , offers to upload lists of Beeswax identifiers for ad targeting in its “cTargeting” module, among mobile advertising IDs, IP addresses, and other identifiers, based on our analysis of the source code. We conclude that many websites make constant requests to Discover-Tech’s domains events.myweb3id[.]io and tracookiepixel[.]xyz in the background. These requests serve the purpose of ID syncing with Beeswax and Yandex, and Discover-Tech’s domains receive, in addition to user identifiers, at least the website visitor’s IP address and information about their browser and operating system. Discover-Tech’s Tracking Pixel Separately from Discover-Tech’s large-scale ID syncing on many websites, we found JavaScript code for a “tracking pixel” that was loaded during recent visits to only a few sites including myipinfo[.]io , cookiesurfer[.]com , and Discover-Tech’s corporate website, discover-tech[.]io (all three archived on urlscan ). These sites loaded versions of the tracking pixel code, both broadly similar, from the following URLs: js.tracookiepixel.xyz/myipinfo/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr.js js.tracookiepixel.xyz/dt/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr_enhanced.js js . tracookiepixel . xyz / myipinfo / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr . js js . tracookiepixel . xyz / dt / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr_enhanced . js Based on our analysis of the source code, the tracking pixel serves the purpose of storing, retrieving and synchronizing user identifiers across Discover-Tech, Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex. Once loaded on a website, the code stores user identifiers associated with Discover-Tech, Beeswax, and Xandr in the user’s web browser in order to retrieve them again during subsequent visits to websites that load the same code. The code is designed to initiate the ID syncing process by sending Discover-Tech’s user identifier to Beeswax and Yandex in order to receive corresponding Beeswax and Yandex identifiers. Additionally, the code retrieves the user’s Xandr identifier. Request chains archived on urlscan show Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel in operation, including ID syncing with Yandex and the retrieval of user identifiers from Beeswax and Xandr. When the tracking pixel code detects that a website visitor is located in a region where the GDPR applies, based on geolocating the user’s IP address, it uses IAB Europe’s Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) to process user “consent” signals for the three TCF vendors Discover-Tech Ltd, Xandr Inc, and BeeswaxIO Corporation. This demonstrates how Discover-Tech utilizes its listing as a registered and approved ad vendor by IAB Europe, as discussed in Section 9 . The code also clearly maps the acronym “ZUID” to Xandr’s user identifier. As detailed in Section 4 , several Controlium modules refer to an option labeled “Detect ZUID”. We are unsure how Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exactly utilizes this identifier. As the “Detect ZUID” option is among a few “Add Ons” that can be activated when setting up an ad campaign, it may serve the retrieval of Xandr user identifiers either for ad targeting or for tracking targets. Xandr (Microsoft Advertising) did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Generally, the purpose of Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel is unclear. As a large share of Discover-Tech ads are designed to lead users to the site myipinfo[.]io when clicking on those ads, the tracking pixel loaded during the site visit then correlates a target’s Discover-Tech user identifier with their Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex identifiers. Records archived on urlscan show that the MyIPInfo website loaded a version of the tracking pixel from another domain associated with Discover-Tech in the past: js.cookie-sync.xyz/myipinfo/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr.js js . cookie - sync . xyz / myipinfo / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr . js 7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate Network Discover-Tech has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the digital advertising industry for years. In this section, we further investigate Discover-Tech, key persons affiliated with the company, related companies, and the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology. Adtech with a Background in Spytech Discover-Tech purports to be a typical digital advertising firm, offering a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), which facilitates the delivery of targeted ads. On its website, it claims to have “unrestricted access to top-ranking apps with 1+ billion daily active users” via a “worldwide ad exchange”. In addition to its DSP, Discover-Tech offers “monetization” solutions to mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers, which we discuss further below. Israeli company records we reviewed link Discover-Tech’s website, discover-tech[.]io , to the company Discover-Tech Ltd registered in March 2020, with Dekel Boni listed as its initial director and sole shareholder. In the two months after its incorporation, Eric Banoun, who is a major figure in the Israeli surveillance technology industry, joined Discover-Tech’s board of directors, and the shareholder base was expanded. From April 2020, the company’s shareholders included Dekel Boni, Guy Lants, Yaniv Basil, Zfanya Leib, Sergei Bartashevich, and Chaia Services Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. Eric Banoun left the company’s board of directors in January 2025 and Chaia Services Ltd ceased to be a shareholder in March 2026. As of July 2026, Discover-Tech is directed by Dekel Boni and owned by Boni, Basil, and Lants. Eric Banoun co-founded the cyberespionage firm Circles, a close NSO Group affiliate , and Senpai Technologies, which is part of the Intellexa consortium. We could not access corporate registration information on Discover-Tech’s shareholder Chaia Services Ltd. However, a Haaretz investigation reported that one of Chaia’s directors was Sara Hamou. Hamou managed Intellexa’s corporate network and was sentenced to eight years in prison (pending appeal) by a Greek court for her role in the Predatorgate scandal. Eric Banoun was listed as a director of a similarly named U.S.-based company, Chaia Services Tech LLC , which was dissolved in 2025. Based on the links to Eric Banoun and Chaia Services Ltd., we conclude that Discover-Tech was linked to the spyware industry for almost six years, according to Israeli company records and other publicly available information. Discover-Tech’s other shareholders, including Dekel Boni who is now the company’s sole director, have a background in digital advertising, previously working for adtech firms like Digital Turbine and Taptica, according to their LinkedIn profiles . 3 Boni lists himself as Discover-Tech’s CEO, Guy Lants as its “Director of Product”. Yaniv Basil lists himself as the company’s “Chief Technology Officer” between 2020 and 2023. Ad Vendor Registrations with Google and IAB Europe Despite information about Discover-Tech’s links to figures in the spyware industry that could be readily obtained from a review of corporate records, major advertising industry organizations added the company to several lists of “certified” or “approved” ad vendors, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitated its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale. As discussed in Section 9 , Google listed Discover-Tech among its “Ad Manager Certified External Vendors”, “Ad Technology Partners”, and “Ads Personalization Providers” from 2020 until 2026. The advertising industry association IAB Europe listed the company on the “Global Vendor List” for its “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), also from 2020 until 2026. In Section 9 , we examine the implications of Discover-Tech’s ad vendor registrations with Google and IAB Europe in detail. Both the Google and IAB vendor registrations consistently refer to the Israeli company Discover-Tech Ltd and the domain discover-tech[.]io . In addition, Google’s list of “Ads Personalization providers” clearly links Discover-Tech to the domains  mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io , which it listed among “domains which can be attributed to the provider” Discover-Tech Ltd. Tracing the Origins of Discover-Tech’s MyDSP Advertising Tech As discussed in Section 5 , the domain mtrtb[.]com and the ad system MyDSP ( mydsp[.]io ) play key roles in Discover-Tech’s ad targeting. According to historical whois information, Discover-Tech Ltd took ownership of both domains in 2020. While domain registration data became anonymized in 2022, mydsp[.]io redirected to discover-tech[.]io until early 2026. Both mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io can be “attributed” to Discover-Tech Ltd according to Google, as discussed in Section 9 . MyDSP was launched by the Israeli adtech firm Matomy in 2016. In 2018, MyDSP was “connected” to Matomy’s MobFox subsidiary, had “access” to 50 billion daily ad impressions and was able to target 500 million users, according to its website. Also in 2018, Matomy sold MyDSP to the Cypriot firm Marketcom Technologies Ltd, which belongs to the e-commerce firm Market Group owned by the Israeli billionaire Teddy Sagi, as confirmed by public filings , business data , media reporting , and whois information for the domains mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com . A 2019 version of the mydsp[.]io site confirms that MyDSP ultimately became part of Glispa, a Berlin-based adtech firm also acquired by Market Group back in 2015. We are not aware of any robust information that shows how Discover-Tech Ltd eventually took over MyDSP, but whois information confirms that Discover-Tech Ltd, founded in March 2020, took control of the domains mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com from Marketcom Technologies Ltd at some point between June and October 2020. According to a Google record , the ad provider with the ID ‘3036’ changed from MarketDSP ( advertising.market[.]com ) to “Discover-Tech Ltd” ( discover-tech[.]io ) on July 31, 2020. While the company names and websites changed, the list of additional domains attributable to this Google ad provider stayed identical: ( mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com ). JavaScript code related to MyDSP’s admin interface for customers, published on admin.mtrtb[.]com , details a list of ad vendors MyDSP was connected to at an unspecified point in time ( archived code ). The list includes Google, Yandex, Vungle, and Sunteng. Thus, it confirms the connections with the ad vendors we found in Discover-Tech’s bidding records ( Section 5 ). In addition, the list suggests that MyDSP was or is also connected to the ad vendors MobFox, Inneractive, MoPub, PulsePoint, RhythmOne, GumGum, Pubmatic, Smaato, Sonobi, NativeAds, Unity, Q1Media, and Applovin. Offerings for Mobile Carriers and Device Vendors Discover-Tech Ltd itself can be traced back to a company named RelevanTech Ltd (relevantech[.]com), founded by Discover-Tech shareholders Dekel Boni and Yaniv Basil in 2015, according to their LinkedIn profiles and Israeli company records we reviewed. Like MyDSP, RelevanTech was also acquired by Market Group’s Glispa in 2017, and became Glispa Discover . Boni and Basil then worked for Glispa, before creating Discover-Tech Ltd in 2020. The descriptions of the services provided by RelevanTech ( 2016 ), Glispa Discover ( 2017 ), and Discover-Tech Ltd are very similar. The current discover-tech.io site promises to help mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers benefit from “sponsored and tailored app recommendations”, in addition to the company’s DSP offering. The 2022 version of the site explained that Discover-Tech would “place” mobile apps on new mobile devices “from the moment” they are “turned on” and provide “operator certified installs” of apps on new devices. We are not aware of any robust information that shows how Discover-Tech’s founders regained control over what was left of RelevanTech from Glispa, but whois information confirms that Discover-Tech Ltd regained control of the domain relevantech[.]com in July 2020. In 2021, Discover-Tech Ltd operated a mobile app on behalf of the Serbian subsidiary of the mobile network operator A1 Telekom Austria, according to a terms of use agreement, which explains that the app would provide A1 customers with content from both A1 and Discover-Tech. The description on the 2021 version of the Serbian A1 website suggests that the app, named “Moy A1” (“My A1”), enabled A1 customers to check their mobile plan, download invoices, and buy additional credits. Put differently, Discover-Tech was sitting inside the official app of the third-largest Serbian mobile operator. We do not know for how long Discover-Tech was involved in operating this app. The 2020 version of the Discover-Tech lists A1 and device manufacturers like Samsung, Tecno, and Wiko among the company’s customers. We did not further investigate Discover-Tech’s mobile carrier and device manufacturer business, which may or may not be active anymore. In conclusion, we believe that Discover-Tech emerged from both RelevanTech and MyDSP, both previously owned by Glispa. While MyDSP and additional software for the delivery of malicious ads appear to be operational in 2026, an asset sale discussed in the next subsection suggests that Discover-Tech may not offer its services for mobile carriers and device manufacturers anymore. A Sale of Assets Leaves Open Questions  In 2021, the Dubai-based firm Affle MEA FZ-LLC, part of the mobile advertising group Affle, based in Singapore and India, acquired “business assets” from Discover-Tech Ltd, according to public filings . Publicly available financial statements refer to the acquisition of a Discover-Tech “business segment” including “brand, IP, domain, business relationships and goodwill”. Public filings further specify that Affle acquired Discover-Tech’s “mobile device marketing platform” that provides “initial device customization” including “dynamic app discovery and recommendation at initial boot or reset of a device” through its integrations with device manufacturers and mobile network operators. An Affle press release quotes Discover-Tech founder Dekel Boni stating that he was “proud” that Discover-Tech’s “technology” that “powers the first interaction a user has with his new device” would become part of the “app discover offering” of Appnext, another company acquired by Affle. Based on the information available to us, we believe that Discover-Tech Ltd sold its offerings for mobile carriers and device vendors examined in the previous subsection, to Affle. We have no reason to believe that Affle has any control over Discover-Tech’s malicious ad operations that we investigate in this report. However, the exact scope of this asset sale remains unknown to us. Affle did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru’s Corporate Networks This section provides an overview of Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru, and provides details on what we know about their corporate networks and business identities. Furthermore, we present additional links between Discover-Tech and Intelos. Intelos and Its ADINT System AdHoc In 2023, the trade press website Intelligence Online and Haaretz first reported about Intelos, a new Israeli ADINT vendor that provides a surveillance system based on data from digital advertising named “AdHoc”. Intelos was reportedly founded by Eric Banoun, who is “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel” according to Haaretz. Israeli company records reviewed by us confirm that Banoun has been a shareholder in Intelos Ltd from its registration in 2018 until present, and he is listed as the company’s director. The email address he uses in corporate filings, [email protected] , clearly links Intelos Ltd to the website intelos.io. The fact that Banoun was also listed as a director of Discover-Tech Ltd (see Section 7 ), already suggests a potential connection between the ADINT vendor Intelos and Discover-Tech. In addition, the websites intelos[.]io and discover-tech[.]io were published by the same entity until at least February 2026, according to technical analysis discussed in Section 7 . While we cannot assess the exact scope of the collaboration between Intelos and Discover-Tech, the technical analysis discussed in Section 4 indicates that the two work together. Besides a few media articles and the company’s website, there is almost no public information available about Intelos. The company’s AdHoc product is not mentioned on its website. According to Israeli company records reviewed by us, Intelos Ltd’s shareholders include Eric Banoun, Senpai co-founder Roy Shloman, Thai businessman Charoenrath Vilailuck, and a Liechtenstein-based firm named SAR Investments International Ltd, among others. On its website , Intelos purports to be a “marketing intelligence” platform that monitors “worldwide digital signals, actions, and preferences”, including “subtle changes in behaviour”, by processing 16 billion “daily data sets” across 50 countries. Much of the promotional language on the site sounds like the company’s products are built for customers in digital marketing, but could also describe an ADINT vendor. Intelos promises to “map behavioural patterns across audiences” and to build “profiles of audiences and groups” in order to “map relationships, track behavioural shifts, and anticipate collective action”. It also provides “location intelligence” based on a “proprietary index of the physical world” with “every relevant location classified, mapped, and weighted for significance”. Another system named “Nexus AI” could transform “raw data into structured insights” based on “live and historical datasets” in order to “map behavioural clusters” and “detect relationships”. Haaretz and Intelligence Online reported that Intelos provides ad-based geolocation surveillance but also the delivery of spyware via ads, without providing details about the latter. Its technology was reportedly offered to the Shin Bet in Israel and sold in Thailand. According to Haaretz, Eric Banoun presented an ADINT product named “Havoc” that included the AdHoc logo to an Egyptian customer. An agreement related to his presentation mentioned a U.K. firm, whose director is also the director of another U.K. firm named “Havoc”, which sold an unnamed cyber system to an unnamed country over a period of three years at a cost of about $42 million. Based on the media report, it remains unclear whether AdHoc was sold in Egypt or not. Intelos did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Both sites offered a “Data Marketing (DM) platform” and the “AI Edge” product using a number of identical sentences. According to the current website , Tekma purports to have access to data on 3.5 billion devices, which can be utilized “across major DSPs”, and is based in Dubai, with regional offices in Greece, Cyprus, and Spain. The 2024 site includes Tekma contact information referring to “Chaia Services” and mentions another regional office in Hong Kong. Another older but also almost identical site, tekma[.]io , includes Tekma contact information referring to “Chaia Ltd” in “13&15 GR. Afxentiou Street, Mesa Geitonia Limassol, Limassol 4003 CY”.
