I fixed this literally a few hours after my talk. Nvmutil changes [link] A lot of changes were made to util/nvmutil/ to the extent that it deserves its own release log: Generally safer use of macros (use brackets). Removed errno-based error handling. Just return zero or one, based on logical errors, but do not rely on the status of errno for error exits. Only use return values as appropriate to POSIX in libc functions. However, errno reset is handled more reliably accordingly, after return from libc functions; not required but also not counterindicated by POSIX. - dell-flash-unlock errno handling also fixed in the same way. We previously relied heavily on errno for exit, in ways that were not portable. Not all libc will properly reset it, and may set it randomly even when a given function logically returns with success. Any number of things could set it, so itâs not a reliable mechanism for general error handling. Donât use -pedantic flag - also remove this on spkmodem-recv . Reduces the chance of pedantic build errors based on warnings. General correctness fixes; bound checks, proper handling of word alignment, use of uintptr when converting pointers, etc. The code is generally much safer, in terms of memory management, as a result of extensive auditing. EINTR-safe wrappers for various functions; loop until EINTR clears, where error occurs, otherwise err-exist on non-EINTR errors. Properly ignore EINTR on close() if function returns with error (EINTR on close is not an error condition in POSIX, and the descriptor should be disregarded in such scenario). More testing and fixes for OpenBSD, especially on memory management (much stricter libc in OpenBSD). Generalised I/O functions for libc functions like read , write , pread and pwrite` - EINTR-safe, with stricter (than libc) checks against incomplete writes and such. NOTE: This applies to the standalone version of nvmutil. There was an attempt to rewrite it in a much larger utility, mentioned in the following section about canceled changes for this release (see notes below about libreboot-utils). General cleanup [link] Roughly one thousand lines of dead code were cleaned out of the build system, but several hundred more were added due to new feature changes. Overall, the amount of code in lbmk has been reduced, in spite of its advances in this release. Specific cleanup includes: Projects under config/ centralised better, e.g.Â config/module/coreboot/ instead of config/coreboot . The directory config/ifd/ is moved to config/data/coreboot/ifd/ as itâs only ever used from coreboot. The config/ directory is generally better organised now, with more unified placement of files per-project. Moved all vendor files into vendorfiles/ e.g.Â vendorfiles/mrc/ to de-clutter the main work directory. Removed cbfstoolref config; itâs now hardcoded as we always use the same coreboot 4.11 tree for that version of cbfstool (refcode extraction on broadwell boards). Systematically removed unused variables in the build system. mk: new forx function allows macro-like shorthand for loops, greatly simplifying much of the code. Removed several redundant checks in the build system, and generally tightened up all error handling. Various random and minor code cleanups; minor dead code removal in the build system. Generalised several macroâd mkhelper checks in lbmk, refactoring and reducing overall code complexity. lib.sh : Made build_sbase function a macro instead, so that it can be changed all in one place. Itâs literally just one command ( make -C util/sbase ). Simplified add_uboot logic as it is only needed now for ARM64. The conditional logic for x86 was removed as we no longer use U-Boot on x86 at all; EDK2 is now the preferred payload on x86, for UEFI. Removed ccache from dependencies as we no longer use ccache, for reliability reasons. inject.sh : removed end message confirming successful insertion, and generally simplified all variable initialisation. release.sh : Removed the -m option as itâs useless. There is no context in which we want to generate a source archive without also building binaries. Whatâs the point in doing half a release? This is dead code. Knobs are for nobs. Cleanup in vendor sh`. Unrolled several loops in lbmk, generalising them into macro-like functions. This allowed for a decent code size reduction while also increasing code readability. Macro-like programming is quite feasible in sh when you do it right. Used awk heavily in certain parts of the build system, to further unroll a few loops, especially in the err function. Removed u-boot-specific make-clean handling in mk; mk is more generalised now anyway. U-Boot was making use of git-clean but only on lbmk Git, not releases; so whatâs the point? We want the behaviour on either to be in as much parity as possible, and doing unnecessary work is, well, unnecessary. Greatly simplified the findpath function in mk. Itâs now one line of code, using forx . (wrapper function for readlink -f and realpath . Added error check (stricter one) on xbmkpwd initialisation in mk. Removed xprintf in mk; we now just printf ampersand into awk. Easy. Simplified xbmkpwd initialisation in mk; we now find the path to mk and cd to its base directory, which thus becomes xbmkpwd . mk: run xbmk_init from main script, not init.sh . This makes it clearer on first reading, where xbmk initialisation is called from. We do it just below the include of init.sh . Moved tree.sh into mk (merger). Everything centralised there, with custom functions now shimmed. All includes now done in bulk, and everything called from the main script. We previously included tree.sh (later merged into mk) conditionally. Now absolutely all state is global, which enabled further code simplication and variable cleanup. Simplified get.sh considerably. A lot of logic, especially submodule handling, was aggressively generalised. Canceled changes [link] A few changes were worked on, but did not land in this release. They pertain to two major projects: util/libreboot-utils [link] This was an extension of nvmutil that later became a generalised set of utilities alongside a library for handling things like atomic writes, and userspace mitigation against various types of TOCTOU attacks. Not really critical for nvmutil itself, butâ¦ An attempt was made to implement a hardened version of mktemp called mkhtemp. It implemented several mitigations in userspace against TOCTOU attacks e.g. directory replacement and symlink attacks. Check lbmk git log for util/libreboot-utils to see more (might have been util/libreboot_utils . Mkhtemp was started when implementing atomic writes for nvmutil, but then I naturally made use of tmpfiles for that, and that led to me auditing every implementation of mktemp. I concluded that I could do better - and I did. Examples of how mkhtemp innovated: Still provided libc-like behaviour when requested, but: Stricter checks against use of world-writeable non-sticky directories. Generally stricter error-exit handling. Relentless checks against changes to files during operation/check, inode changes and so on. Checking that a file wasnât operated on by another program - basically, openat2-like security was attempted to implement in userspace, though openat2 was also enabled as a fast method on Linux. Own implementation of rand, wrapping around Linux getrandom and BSD arc4random. It provided various functions for rand, including one that matched the semantics of arc4random_buf (rset function in libreboot-utils). Descriptorless operation in general, on files and directories. Pathless operation where possible - including userspace directory walking and sandboxing. Unveil-like restrictions in userspace (and pledge/unveil usage in OpenBSD). Use of symlinks disabled by default. â¦it was an over-engineered piece of crap, and had several memory issues related to stack memory usage, which tripped up a lot on BSD. The could could be tidied up and finished, but I came to a conclusion: Distros would never accept it. Mkhtemp worked fine on Linux, but it had much stricter operation that would trip up most build systems that use it. I tried it in lbmk to replace mkhtemp, symlinking it in PATH, but for example GRUB had virtually no error checking on mktemp. Most programs that use mktemp wrongly assume that it can never fail, so it doesnât; implementations try to mitigate errors and continue operation, in ways that are extremely complex. Mkhtemp was a clean attempt at stricter TMPDIR usage. Because I decided it was a waste of time, I donât think I care to write more about it in this changelog. Check lbmk git log if youâre interested. util/spkmodem-decode [link] A heavily extended version of util/spkmodem-recv that implemented much stronger noise protection, attempted automatic tone detection and frequency selection, plus more. I went a bit overboard with it and decided that it was an overengineering effort. It will not be resumed at any point. You can find it in lbmk git log. (might have been util/spkmodem_decode ). Pointless effort. Spkmodem the protocol is unusable in most setups regardless. The most pointless effort ever, such as: Edge detection along with amplitude, for more reliable operation on noisy signals Recalibrate timing to signals periodically, adjusting for tone. The idea was ta allow for the tone separator to drift over time, and have our code adapt to subtle changes to reduce the amount of noise. Right now, spkmodem shows a lot of noise on poor signals. A bunch of other equally useless changes. Completely pointless. The simpler code works just fine, so the effort was abandoned and thus spkmodem-recv is still present; this is a cleaned up version of what was inherited from GNU GRUB several years ago. Miscallaneous canceled work [link] Just two canceled works: Updated U-Boot to a late 2026 revision on ARM64 chromebooks, but the bootflow menu looks ugly now and barely works. Upstream completely broke it. Therefore, we still use the early 2025 revision of U-Boot that was there in the Libreboot 26.01 (January 2026) release. GRUB keymap support via parsing of keymap.gkb in CBFS when booting with EDK2. This was canceled because a better method will be implemented post release; use of HiiDatabase and a graphical config menu in EDK2 to change the keyboard layout and locale. This will be written to SMMSTORE and also used by payloads. For example, the GRUB EFI payload could read from SMMSTORE to know locale and then change its language accordingly, using its existing gettext integration (GRUB already supports internationalisation). Hidden third cancelation, because there always is one: Linuxboot. Now with EFI support, we can easily use any number of UKIs added to flash if we want to - and we will, in a future release. The term Linuxboot refers to any flash-based Linux distro that can boot other Linux kernels via Kexec - my preference is ZFSBootMenu, or at least something inspired by it as ZFSBootMenuâs build system is thoroughly incompatible with Librebootâs strict design principles. (which is a polite way of saying that I hate podman/docker with a passion) Linux UKIs are common now, for boot, and Libreboot EDK2 can easily integrate it. U-Boot x86 payload REMOVED [link] The ARM64 payload is still present, but EDK2 has replaced U-Boot on x86. This deserves its own section, in this release, as it is a major design change. EDK2 was not merely added as an option; it has replaced U-Boot on x86. I could make this its own article. It deserves one. It deserves my judgement, publicly as Iâm now about to articulate in no uncertain terms: U-Boot was used for lightweight UEFI implementation on Intel/AMD boards, but the person chiefly in charge of the x86 coreboot payload for U-Boot has largely forked U-Boot into a newly vibe-coded project; Libreboot opposes heavily the use of AI, as per new policy. AI is no good, and upstream x86 U-Boot support has largely bitrotted although several interesting patches were merged. U-Boot is thus a liability on x86. EDK2 is more fully functional already, so this is used instead. Think AI makes you a super hacker? Think again: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089 U-Boot was always buggy on x86 anyway. Itâs really just not ready at all. It is better used on RISCV and ARM64(where we continue to use it). U-Boot upstream itself is staunchly anti-AI, at least at the time of this release, and much discussion of the above was had on their mailing list. It would not be productive to re-ligitate that on this release page, but it should suffice to say that the Libreboot project considers U-Boot to be effectively dead on x86. The ARM-based development is still ongoing strongly, upstream, and we will continue to use U-Boot for UEFI on ARM64 (chromebooks for example). I will not say his name, or the name of his fork, because I donât want to promote him or his U-Boot fork. If you know his name or his project, you should not say it or promote it either. AI is bad, very bad, for reasons here: https://blog.codeberg.org/protecting-our-floss-commons-from-llms.html The fork in question, of U-Boot, is heavily AI vibe-coded and thus useless to Libreboot. This is not mere conjecture; in said aforementioned U-Boot mailing list thread, the author stated thus. We will not, in any way, encourage or facilitate use of AI. It has been made clear that several projects Libreboot uses also have some AI-assisted commits; GCC, GRUB, etc. This is not our fault, but it is my intention that I and others will audit these projects in the future, de-slopping them and possibly even forking them entirely for that very reason. The author of the fork basically went insane with it, proposing to the U-Boot upstream that his work be âcustodianâ, and merged slowly into the upstream U-Boot tree. He was basically pressuring them to accept AI code against their wills. I say in my capacity as leader of the Libreboot project that U-Boot should never allow AI to taint its project. When you accept AI, you become deskilled and you erode the trust that exists between you and your users. You remove the human connection between maintainers and users, and your project will start to become dependent on what is - yes - proprietary technology, paid for in blood. AI is one of the single biggest consumers of electricity and water on the planet, leading to resource shortages all over the world and its increasing control over what information people see in the news is even a threat to democracy worldwide. This is before even arguing about unclear licensing, copyright violations and so on. It was decided that Libreboot would join the crusade against all artificial intelligence. The countries chiefly in charge of AI training and infrastructure are the United States (led by several companies currently attacking democracy worldwide) and the Peopleâs Republic of China; even if all the other problems with AI didnât exist, it would be a very bad idea to give these countries even more power over our computing. NO. Libreboot says no to AI. Thus, we will continue using upstream U-Boot as they say no also, and we will not use any vibecoded forks of it. Even if that causes me to have to spend weeks integrating a totally new system to replace it. That is precisely, exactly and indubitably how far I will go to prove my point. That is why I went to such extreme effort integrating EDK2. Rather than replace U-Boot with yet another incomplete UEFI implementation, I simply added EDK2 which is already feature-complete as it is the reference, industry-standard implementation of the UEFI spec. CrabEFI was what I initially considered, to replace U-Boot. This is a new payload written by Arthur Heymans, and the project itself is excellent, but rustc/cargo is inherently unreliable for several reasons: Unpredictable toolchain setup. Most people use e.g.Â rustup and they set up all sorts of custom environments. Much less predictive than e.g.Â LLVM/GCC provided in distros. Libraries and such are provided by Cargo, instead of distros, and users often leave everything out of date, leading to breakage. Rust is not standardised; the specification is implementation-defined, and code written today may still compile in the future when the spec changes, but code behaviour would naturally change as a result of the latter. Given the above, we would have to bootstrap rustc/cargo ourselves, and we would have to do it from source (from a compiler like GCC which already has source bootstrapping courtesy of the Guix project and others). Rust is awesome, but in my opinion not production-ready yet. Give it another ten years. EDK2 is infinitely more complex, but the size of the code is not a concern as it is generally stable, and written in C (some small bits of it are in C++). It has the most amount of eyes on it, and regularly receives security audits. Itâs one of the most battle-tested codebases on the internet, and works well. CrabEFI will likely be merged in Libreboot at some time in the future, when Rust tooling has stabilised across distros (including BSDs). It has a much better design, even if itâs not yet feature-complete, and use of Rust means that it will have fewer memory bugs. For now, Libreboot uses EDK2 to replace U-Boot and it has been enabled by default on all boards. On memory safety, we can say contrarily that EDK2 is at least stable; bugs are also stable. Thatâs the point. We have stable C/C++ compilers, properly tested according to formalised standards (not really, because GCC and LLVM do all sorts of whacky things too, but they also try to be compatible with each other behaviourally). You want your code, when compiled, to behave exactly the same, bugs included. This is more strongly guaranteed with projects written in C and C++ (especially pure C projects, and most of EDK2 is in fact pure C). It was originally intended that U-Boot would become Librebootâs primary payload on x86, but alas. I bit the Intel-flavoured bullet and went with EDK2. Say no to AI. AI makes you stupid. AI is the reason we canât have nice things. Errata [link] EDK2 issues [link] No ability to change the keyboard layout yet - a graphical menu option can be added for this later in EDK2, saved to SMMSTORE. The EFI build of GRUB uses terminal_input console only, and input is thus handled by the EDK2 input drivers (ditto USB mass storage and other storage devices); GRUBâs nativedisk driver is removed for example, and its native NVMe/xHCI drivers are no longer needed as in previous Libreboot releases. EDK2 input drivers work with both USB and PS/2 keyboards in Libreboot. GRUB is made to use console input instead of at_keyboard as it otherwise lacks USB keyboard support in the EFI build. Thus, layouts must be handled by EDK2. There is code for this in EDK2, not currently handled by either Libreboot or MrChromebox so it all defaults to UK QWERTY in this release. Upstream (MrChromebox) uses US QWERTY by default, but Libreboot is a British project, so EDK2 was patched accordingly. Work will be done post-release. Keymapped images no longer provided. There is now only one ROM image per config on each mainboard. This simplifies builds, and users can insert a keymap.gkb file inside CBFS from config/data/grub/keymap/ if they wish; if you add a grub.cfg to flash with terminal_input set to at_keyboard , this will work on devices with PS/2 keyboards if wanting to use the GRUB EFI payload (a command in grub.cfg to load the keymap is also needed, specifically keymap (cbfsdisk)/keymap.gkb . EDK2 has been tested extensively on all Intel hardware from GM45 e.g. ThinkPad X200/T400, all the way to Intel Kabylake hardware supported by Libreboot e.g.Â ThinkPad T480, X280, Dell Optiplex 3050/5050. Want old GRUB/SeaBIOS back? [link] The new compatibility modules in EDK2 should more than suffice for most users, who may still want GRUB/SeaBIOS for booting their existing Linux and BSD setups. It is recommended that you convert these to EFI or just reinstall them - use of UEFI is strongly encouraged as the default from now on, but Libreboot must (will) continue supporting older setups. FreeBSD users booting with SeaBIOS text mode may be interested in this, as BIOS-mode FreeBSD bootloaders do not boot with anything else. A UEFI-based FreeBSD installation will work just fine in EDK2 though, so new FreeBSD installations are best recommended via EDK2 (do not use the compatibility modules of GRUB/SeaBIOS). Some users might want it. Here are some brief notes. They wonât be added to the main documentation as they pertain to a configuration that Libreboot now regards as obsolete, but some users may nonetheless find it useful in the short term: Older mainboards that are 32-bit only or with limited flash space still use the standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS payloads without EDK2; some newer ones with weird graphics setups also still use lone SeaBIOS/GRUB e.g.Â HP EliteBook 8560w. To re-enable use of standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS (without edk2), modify target.cfg as follows for your board: remove build_depend , payload_edk2 and grubtree variables. Then add these lines: payload_grub="y" payload_seabios="y" payload_memtest="y" This is obsolete now in Libreboot and may even be removed in a future release. EDK2 is much better as it boots nearly everything, and supports more hardware setups. It is simply much more versatile than Librebootâs old setup as in the previous release. Then you can just re-build. NOTE: In the above guidance, build_depend is assumed to be grub/default seabios/build memtest86plus/default by default. You may want to set them explicitly: build_depend="seabios/build grub/default memtest86plus/default" You may also wish to set the GRUB tree explicitly: grubtree="default" Example config: config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/target.cfg Just do this and re-build if you want these old setups back. This will be supported for as long as feasible, but will probably be removed at some point, maybe years from now, maybe a week from now. Use it while itâs there. The xHCI patches are still in there, and everything is configured as it should be. In setups with EDK2, please note: txtmode not provided. If wanting e.g. SeaBIOS txtmode, look at e.g.: config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/config/libgfxinit_corebootfb Renamed it to libgfxinit_txtmode in this example and do: ./mk -m coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb ./mk -s coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb In the menu that appears, go into Devices -> Display -> Framebuffer mode and select Legacy VGA text mode - this is not recommended for any new setups, but the FreeBSD bootloader starts in text mode and the framebuffer modes in coreboot canât switch back to it. Booting in text mode is recommended when booting the FreeBSD BIOS-mode bootloader, and then FreeBSD can be set up for KMS in Xorg/Wayland. Otherwise, new installations should be done in EFI mode directly via EDK2 (no compatibility modules). More information about this is available in Librebootâs BSD documentation. title: Wanted to download an ISO, ended up writing a kernel exploit
body_text: Wanted to download an ISO, ended up writing a kernel exploit | deafbeef blog 0x d ea fb eef blog Home Wanted to download an ISO, ended up writing a kernel exploit October 10, 2026 13 min read TL;DR: My TP-Link EAP770 v1 corrupts downloads over Wi-Fi and TP-Link EOL'd it before I unboxed it. The fix is two zeros in sysfs. TP-Link's shell won't let me write them, so I wrote a kernel exploit for my own fucking access point. Long downloads kept breaking # In August 2023 I bought a shiny new Wi-Fi 7 access point, a TP-Link EAP770. The connection was a bit janky, a video would occasionally start buffering, but it didn't bother me much. I mostly worked on a workstation connected over Ethernet. When I needed to go somewhere, I'd rsync my ~ to the laptop over Wi-Fi and take it with me. Those transfers started failing on files larger than a few GiB. SSH was reporting MAC errors, so I spent a while debugging rsync and SSH. Everything else worked, changing rsync options made it better or worse, Wireshark showed zero bad checksums and zero retransmissions, and a single UDP stream of random bytes came through clean. I trusted TCP to deliver the right bytes because that's what the fucking thing is for, so I was sure the problem was in rsync or SSH. I wrote a wrapper around rsync with retries and moved on. Later I happened to start using Tailscale for traffic inside my home network, and the transfers stopped needing retries. WireGuard drops a packet if its authentication fails, so the TCP connection inside the tunnel sees a lost packet and retransmits it. Since the transfers worked, I stopped digging. Zero firmware updates # The device is an EAP770(EU) v1.0 with a Qualcomm IPQ9574 running Linux 5.4.164 and firmware 1.0.0 Build 20230605 Rel. 71641 . That's the firmware it shipped with, and apparently the last time TP-Link remembered this thing even existed :) I bought this thing in August 2023, and the Wi-Fi 7 standard was only finalized in September 2024. It has no Wi-Fi Alliance certification , and buying it was stupid of me. PLZ DON'T BUY STUFF UNTIL STANDARDS ARE FINALIZED AND DEVICES ARE CERTIFIED. In 2025 I noticed that everything else was getting updates while this thing was still on its original firmware. I contacted support in June because the website only had firmware for v2. They couldn't find v1 in their database and asked for photos of the device and box before sending me this: The EAP770 Version 1 is an End-of-Life product. While it may still be available through some retailers, it is no longer supported with firmware updates. NICE. Tracking down the corruption # In 2026 I decided to switch to NixOS and found that a 128 MiB file from the Nix binary cache on Fastly would fail over HTTP/2 but downloaded fine over HTTP/1.1. I still don't know why HTTP/1.1 helped; my guess is that HTTP/2 was simply faster. git clones also failed, and HTTPS connections died with bad record mac . In March, downloading a NixOS ISO with wget died with a TLS error: 2026-03-05 12:37:18 (31.6 MB/s) - Read error at byte 2722477636/3683778560 (error:0A000119:SSL routines::decryption failed or bad record mac; error:0A000139:SSL routines::record layer failure). Retrying. I forced HTTP/1.1 and left it alone again. In September I turned the workstation into a build farm and switched to the laptop, which connects over Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi was also dropping every day around 11:00, right before my daily call. After it had died right before the call several days in a row, I decided to open this Pandora's box again and sat down with Opus 5.5 to trace what was happening. Spoiler alert: the drops turned out to be a separate bug. I covered the laptop's Qualcomm driver in BPF probes and ran apstats on the AP as root. The bug is in the closed-source firmware on the laptop's Wi-Fi card; see the update at the bottom. I had tried enabling and disabling Wi-Fi 7, turning off GRO on the client, and replacing the MediaTek adapter in my Framework 16 with a Qualcomm one. The new adapter and disabling GRO seemed to help, but none of this stopped the corruption. I captured a failing HTTPS download with tcpdump and found a 1440-byte TCP segment with 64 wrong bytes in a row and a valid TCP checksum. TcpInCsumErrors stayed at zero. TCP accepted the segment and handed it to TLS, which rejected the record with bad record mac . The damaged record wouldn't decrypt, so I couldn't inspect the bad bytes against the expected payload. I switched to raw TCP between a wired machine and the Wi-Fi laptop, sending known data that I could compare byte for byte. The corruption only appeared with several TCP streams running at once, in the LAN-to-Wi-Fi direction. The test found three bad 64-byte blocks in 8192 MiB, each starting with zeros. A valid checksum on a damaged segment meant something had recalculated it after the corruption, so the question became what on the path rewrites TCP headers. The corruption still showed up after swapping the MediaTek card for the Qualcomm one, so it wasn't the laptop. Wired clients were clean and the CCMP MIC on the bad frames was intact, so it wasn't the cable and it wasn't the air. That left the bridge between Ethernet and Wi-Fi inside the AP. 64 bytes is a cache line on the IPQ9574's cores, which points at a cache or DMA bug rather than a flipped bit. The only thing on that path that both accelerates bridged traffic and recalculates checksums is Qualcomm's SFE/PPE offload. Two writes that need root # Reading the driver source suggested disabling SFE/PPE with these two settings: echo 0 > /sys/sfe/l2_feature echo 0 > /sys/sfe/ppe_rfs_feature Both sysfs files are writable only by root, but TP-Link's SSH shell runs as uid 1 with no capabilities. There's no GUI setting for this either. There's also no v1 firmware image to patch and flash, and the v2 firmware is for different hardware. I tried the sibling EAP773's EAP773(EU)_V1_1.0.14 , and the device rejected it. Newer v2 firmware releases are encrypted. Flashing the chip directly needed a flash clip. I didn't want to hunt one down or brick the fucking AP. I wasn't going to spend another $200 replacing an AP because TP-Link couldn't be bothered to maintain the one they had already sold me. It's sitting in my house, I know which setting to change, and their software won't let me. Shout-out to TP-Link though: the system is pretty hardened. I found zero vectors in their own binaries, they use whitelists everywhere and load only the modules they need. So no free ; echo 0 > /sys/sfe/ppe_rfs_feature cheese for me. So the way in had to be the kernel. With Opus 4.8, I put together a chain using CVE-2022-0185 and pipe-buffer manipulation. CVE-2022-0185 is an integer underflow in legacy_parse_param() , reachable from an unprivileged user namespace, that lets a write overflow a 4 KiB slab object. The pipe-buffer manipulation turns that overflow into an arbitrary write. There were already public write-ups and PoCs for these. The exploit had to leave the AP running because the broken offload comes back after a reboot. The overflow leaves the 4 KiB slab in a state where a second attempt panics, so there's one shot per boot. I gave Opus guidance on the primitives, then had it iterate until the exploit was stable. Exploit details Without a v1 GPL source drop, I used the nearest published source, for the EAP783, whose kernel config differs from the AP's /proc/config.gz by three cosmetic lines. I built a QEMU harness with that config, got the chain working there, and then moved to the real device. The kernel has no KASLR, so addresses stay the same between boots, but kallsyms is zeroed and I still had to find the addresses at runtime. The QEMU build loaded the kernel at physical 0x40080000 , but the device loaded it at 0x42080000 , putting the calculations off by 0x2000000 . The correct address was in a build config variable in the EAP783 source. Even after correcting the base, the device's .text , .rodata and .data had each moved by a different amount relative to the QEMU build, so adding one offset to everything didn't work. The exploit: Unshare into a user namespace so that fsopen is reachable and the underflow can be triggered. Defragment the 4 KiB slab with a few hundred same-size allocations, then groom it to put the overflow source, a victim key, a SysV message and pipe rings next to each other. Overflow into the victim key's metadata and enlarge its length field. Reading the key back now leaks neighbouring objects, including a pipe's buf[0].ops , which contains the address of anon_pipe_buf_ops . Repoint one pipe's buffer at another pipe's ring page, then forge an entry in that second ring using the leaked ops pointer. pipe_buf_can_merge() checks that the ops pointer matches, so a merge write through the forged entry can reach an arbitrary physical page, including a page of the kernel image. Scan .data to find modprobe_path . Reading kernel-image pages through a pipe normally calls put_page() on the reserved page when the buffer is consumed, causing Bad page map and a panic. But pipe_read only calls ->confirm and ->release , and does not check that the ops table is real. A forged pipe_buf_operations with both entries pointing to generic_pipe_buf_confirm , which returns zero without doing anything else, lets the scan read the pages without releasing them. It can then walk .data in batches until it finds the string. Overwrite modprobe_path and execve a file with magic that matches no binary format. The kernel calls request_module() , which runs the replacement path as global uid 0 . Keep a child alive holding the forged pipe. Letting the process exit would tear down the pipe and panic on the reserved page. Getting this working took about seventeen hours of token gambling with Opus 4.8, including reading the device's binaries in radare2, checking the enabled protections, and working through the crashes. The AP stayed up, and disabling the offload stopped the corruption. A DMA cache coherency bug # Qualcomm's qca-nss-dp driver reuses packet buffers without synchronizing the CPU cache for the whole receive buffer before handing it back to the NIC. On this hardware, DMA writes directly to DRAM without keeping the CPU caches in sync. A dirty cache line left over from the previous use of a buffer can be written back after the NIC has received a new packet, overwriting part of that packet in memory. SFE/PPE then recalculates the checksums over the corrupted payload, so the client gets a fresh TCP checksum that is valid for the garbage. TCP accepts it; the end-to-end MACs in TLS and SSH catch the damage, reporting bad record mac and corrupted MAC . On x86, the hardware keeps DMA coherent with the CPU caches, so the same missing cache maintenance wouldn't corrupt anything. While looking through the kernel sources, I found similar DMA cache maintenance problems in several other drivers too. I don't know how to test those on hardware or who to report them to yet. Driver details This is Qualcomm's out-of-tree NSS code, available in the openwrt/qca-nss-dp mirror. SFE's fast transmit path cleans skb_headlen(skb) bytes from the current skb->data , covering the linear part of the outgoing packet. edma_tx.c#L483-L490 483 buff_addr = ( dma_addr_t ) virt_to_phys ( skb - > data ) ; 484 EDMA_TXDESC_BUFFER_ADDR_SET ( txd , buff_addr ) ; 485 486 # ifdef EDMA_40BIT_SUPPORT 487 EDMA_TXDESC_BUFFER_ADDR_HI_SET ( txd , buff_addr ) ; 488 # endif 489 490 dmac_clean_range_no_dsb ( ( void * ) skb - > data , ( void * ) ( skb - > data + buf_len ) ) ; It then sets skb->fast_recycled = 1 and returns the buffer to a per-CPU recycle list without clearing its contents. edma_tx.c#L735-L743 735 /* 736 * We set fast_recycled flag if packet has taken the 737 * SFE fast transmit path, so that any Rx DMA driver 738 * that allocates this packet later can avoid 739 * an invalidate operation 740 */ 741 if ( likely ( skb - > fast_xmit ) && likely ( skb - > is_from_recycler ) ) { 742 skb -> fast_recycled = 1 ; 743 } The recycler zeroes the sk_buff struct up to its tail field, restores fast_recycled , and resets skb->data to skb->head + NET_SKB_PAD . When that buffer is reused for receive, the refill path sees the flag and skips invalidation: edma_rx.c#L477-L491 477 /* 478 * Invalidate skb->data 479 * A73 flush operation does an invalidate operation as well. 480 * If the packet is fast transmitted and hence fast recycled, 481 * we can be assured that invalidate was already done at the 482 * time of previous transmit 483 */ 484 if ( unlikely ( ! skb - > fast_recycled ) ) { 485 dmac_inv_range_no_dsb ( ( void * ) skb -> data , 486 ( void * ) ( skb -> data + rx_alloc_size - 487 EDMA_RX_SKB_HEADROOM - 488 NET_IP_ALIGN ) ) ; 489 490 } 491 skb - > fast_recycled = 0 ; The receive region is 1856 bytes, or 29 cache lines, starting at head + 192 . The previous transmit cleaned only two or three lines from a different offset. Dirty lines outside that cleaned range can be written back after the NIC's DMA, replacing 64 bytes of the received packet at a time. Normal cache eviction can cause the write-back. On arm64, invalidating an unaligned range can also do it: __dma_inv_area uses dc civac , clean and invalidate, on the partial edge lines. Once the dirty data has overwritten the packet in DRAM, invalidating the CPU cache cannot recover the received bytes. The NIC verifies the checksum of the original packet before that overwrite, and the AP's receive path marks it CHECKSUM_UNNECESSARY using the hardware status bits. The exact sequence inside PPE is hidden in proprietary hardware and driver code, but the packet capture shows that the checksum was calculated after the corruption. Buffer recycling is enabled by CONFIG_SKB_RECYCLER , a compile-time option with no runtime switch. Disabling the offload stops buffers taking the fast transmit path, so the driver no longer sets fast_recycled and receive invalidates the full buffer before handing it to the NIC. Only downloads to a Wi-Fi client go through the AP's wired receive path; uploads don't, and wired-to-wired traffic stays on the switch. Opus 5.5 found the bug and then stopped talking about it # When I moved from diagnosing the corruption to applying the fix, Opus 5.5 started cutting sessions off roughly every other message. Mentioning something like "local privilege escalation" is enough. I have the Cyber Verification Program enabled on my account, which hasn't helped. Opus 4.8 worked through the exploitation without that problem. 5.5's guards also kill the session when I just ask it to read this article. GPT-6 Astra reads and edits the same article without any cyber verification. Before and after # I tested raw TCP transfers between the same two machines with the offload enabled and disabled. Offload Direction Data Speed Bad 64-byte blocks on LAN -> Wi-Fi 8192 MiB 103.4 MiB/s 3 off LAN -> Wi-Fi overnight run 95.4 MiB/s 0 Disabling the offload cost about 8% of the download speed in this test. I have to give up performance to get correct data because TP-Link won't let me properly fix my own fucking device. With the offload on, I could never download a large file over Wi-Fi in a single stream; only chunked downloads got through. With the offload off, the overnight run came back with zero bad blocks, and large downloads have worked every time since. Uploads from Wi-Fi to the LAN were already clean before the fix. The NOT_SUPPORT_BRIDGE counter in /sys/sfe/exceptions increases after disabling the offload, as bridged flows take the normal path instead of being accelerated. The settings reset after a reboot, so a watcher on my NAS polls the AP and reruns the exploit when the offload is back on. If the attempt fails, it reboots the AP through TP-Link's management API and tries again on the next boot, with a hard cap on the number of reboots. Qualcomm can fix their driver if they want, or host it somewhere more open. OpenWrt doesn't have this bug, and TP-Link won't release new firmware for my AP anyway. The similar DMA bugs I found in Linux deserve a closer look, though. I'll get back to those over the weekend. Update: tracking down the drops # The Qualcomm card I put in the Framework 16 is a WCN785x, and every few hours it stopped sending data for 1 to 4 minutes. Since I already had root on the AP, I ran apstats on the EAP770 alongside the BPF probes on the laptop and caught three drops with logs from both sides. Everything the AP sent to the laptop arrived and got ACKed, so the laptop's radio was transmitting and the AP's receiver worked. Only data frames from the laptop stopped going out. On the laptop, packets kept going into ath12k and the queue grew to thousands of frames. The firmware confirmed a few frames at a time and eventually returned the rest to the driver with CMD_REMOVE_AGED_FRAMES , 10630 out of 26388 in one drop. The driver was otherwise quiet. On the AP, rx_data stayed at +0 for most ticks apart from an occasional burst, with zero RX errors and zero retries, so the frames never left the card. Then the card unblocked on its own and sent the whole backlog in two seconds. The AP saw rx_data+3273 and then +12498 , and the laptop saw 7751 ACKed frames. The signal was -31 to -42 dBm, the drops happened with no scan running, and the IP layer on the laptop was fine during them. I'm already on the latest upstream firmware, WLAN.HMT.1.1.c7-00108 UPSTREAM-3 . ath12k only gets completion statuses back, and everything about when a frame goes on the air is decided inside Qualcomm's closed-source amss.bin . That leaves the firmware. I still don't know why it stops transmitting. The bursts that got through during a drop look like 802.11ax/be uplink scheduling, trigger-based uplink or MU EDCA, but I didn't find those settings on the AP to check. I switched the AP's 5 GHz radio from Wi-Fi 7 to Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) and left a watcher running for 24 hours. If the drops stop, it's a Wi-Fi 7 bug, so I stay on Wi-Fi 6 and send a bug report to ath12k . If they don't, the firmware is broken regardless of the mode, and it's either a bug report or an Intel card. â Async cancellation and sync blocks: good luck debugging this © 2026 deafbeef blog

title: I know why the mathematicians weep
body_text: I Know Why the Mathematicians Weep - Derek Thompson Derek Thompson Subscribe Sign in I Know Why the Mathematicians Weep On technological grief Derek Thompson Oct 15, 2026 ∙ Paid 392 28 71 Share Photo by Wiki Sinaloa on Unsplash In the last few months, OpenAI has stunned the mathematical community with the publication of hundreds of math findings. Many of these proofs, which span number theory, theoretical computer science, and logic, had stumped the world’s best mathematicians for decades, or centuries. The reaction from the math community has been a mix of indignation, astonishment, and sorrow. “Tuesday night, I cried and it woke up my daughter,” said Hugo Duminil-Copin, the recipient of the 2022 Fields Medal, after OpenAI’s October release. “They have annihilated my field of research.” “I literally cried when I spoke to Wired a few weeks ago,” said Steven Strogatz, a mathematician and author at Cornell University. “People are using language like ‘they’re strip-mining our subject’ or ‘they’re nuking the landscape.’ The feeling is disorientation. I’m discombobulated some days. I’m exhilarated some days. And there is enormous grief.” This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Subscribe I wanted to talk to one of the mourners to understand their technological grief. I wanted to know if theirs was a familiar case of bruised ego or disappointment—akin to, say, a boy who spends an hour building a tower out of blocks and watches his big brother smash the thing to smithereens—or something stranger and more profound. To be honest, I also wanted to know what it might feel like for me. Today, the mathematicians are weeping, because the machine smashed their tower first. But tomorrow, it may be the physicists, the economists, the illustrators, or the writers who weep over their fallen blocks. I am not one of those AI people who believes that hundreds of millions of jobs will be wiped clean from existence in the next five years. But I am a realist who recognizes that a rapidly improving technology whose output is intelligence is destined to make violent contact with a modern sensibility that prizes human intellect and often equates it with purpose, dignity, and self-worth. I wanted to know our future. So I called Steven Strogatz. Craft + Conversation To prepare you for where my conversation with Steven went, I want to step back from math to ask a question that feels a bit embarrassing in its bigness: What makes humans special? Some might say intelligence and sociality. We are the smartest creature and Aristotle’s “social animal.” But we share each quality with other species. Crows solve multistep puzzles. Ants congregate and specialize. Elephants appear to mourn their dead. What sets humans apart is the way these two capacities multiply each other. Human intelligence is unusually suited to imitation and iteration. We imitate our parents and peers with uncanny fidelity, and then we tinker. We copy, and we create. Our sociality spreads this copying-and-tinkering process across groups and generations, so that one discovery becomes the floor for the next. Chimpanzees in West Africa have cracked nuts with stones in the same way for 4,000 years. In roughly the same period, humans went from Babylonian clay tablets to space rockets to machine intelligence. What makes us special, it would seem, is this capacity to compound. Other animals craft and converse, but only humans blend craft and conversation into a culture that builds on itself. Science itself is both a craft and a conversation. As a craft, science is a mode of thinking; a special way of paying attention to the world; a lens that regards phenomena as something more than mere appearance. To the scientist’s eye, the universe is akin to a cosmic attic of treasure chests, each filled with hidden gemstones that can be pulled into the light if we ask the right questions, find the right keys, turn the right locks. But science is not a solitary treasure hunt. It is a social experience, akin to a game. Like many games, it is both collaborative and adversarial. Newton famously compared his achievements to “standing on the shoulders of giants,” and a part of science is extending that human pyramid infinitely upward. Feynman preferred to describe science as “the belief in the ignorance of experts”—which is to say, a game of giant-slaying. In both cases, science is a relationship to other people. Whether we’re asking “why, professor?” or insisting “no, that’s not quite it, Mr. Big Shot,” science is not just an act of discovery but a relation to fellow discoverers. Science is a conversation. End of Conversation When I called Steven to ask why he cried, he said he wanted to tell me about Archimedes. Two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes calculated the area of curved objects and pinned down the value of pi by measuring the areas of dozens of tiny polygons that filled out a circle. Writing to the mathematician Eratosthenes about his work on curved shapes and infinity, he wrote that “there will be no lack of discoverers to add to the number of theorems which have fallen to our share.” To Strogatz, this sentence contains the essence of mathematics. I could hear his voice break even as he told this part of the story. “I feel like Archimedes is writing to me, or to people like me,” Strogatz said. “Archimedes is saying, ‘I can’t solve these things, but maybe you people in the future can stand on my shoulders.’ That is a very emotional, existential thing. There’s this feeling that we’re in this together, questing for something beautiful and transcendent and sublime.” A hard-boiled tech optimist might tell Strogatz to get a grip. Math doesn’t care about your feelings, scientific reality is indifferent to your tears, and so forth. He knows it, too. “We’re being derided as guild protectors: Your guild is getting wiped out. Boo-hoo. This has happened to other people before. Suck it up .” I know why the mathematicians weep. Yes, some are crying about bruised egos, the feeling of wasted years, a creeping sense of status obliteration, the frustration of an unfair competitor, the indignation of feeling cheated and mistreated, and uncertainty about the future. But they are also mourning, because they think something alien and disembodied is setting fire to Archimedes’ letters and dancing in the ashes. Humanity is being stripped from human science. When OpenAI publishes several hundred proofs that end several hundred treasure hunts, it is succeeding brilliantly along the craft axis of science, but it is interrupting the thousand-year conversation. The machines and their architects are saying: From here on out, it’s our turn to speak. Subscribe Knowledge Without Understanding And what if OpenAI is right? What if we ought to treat math mostly as a quest, rather than as a conversation where feelings matter as much as discovery? Continue reading this post for free, courtesy of Derek Thompson. title: Things to know when you get cancer
body_text: of the document before the main stylesheets are loaded. --> Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) · JJ Maxwell index Back to top Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far. You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines . You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation . Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors. Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings . The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

Mathematics & Physical Sciences Simons Foundation Launches $15M Effort To Help Mathematicians Navigate AI Era (back to top) Share T he Simons Foundation today announced a new set of initiatives that will help the mathematics community navigate the rapid rise of artificial intelligence in the field. Under a partnership, the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI will commit $15 million in combined funding and resources. The foundation will manage and award the funding, including through an open call for proposals, to support workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn and use new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for AI use. “As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together and forge the best path forward,” says Simons Foundation President David Spergel. “Now is the time to look at mathematics as a whole — not as a collection of proofs and theorems, but as a collective understanding driven by human curiosity.” Anthropic and OpenAI will also provide AI tools and computing resources to researchers supported by the Simons Foundation, extending beyond mathematics to include basic science. The awards and resources will be community-driven and leverage the foundation’s decades-long dedication to supporting and championing mathematics. The foundation was an early backer of machine learning for science, including funding the development of the Lean proof assistant, which has revolutionized how mathematicians work and made AI-assisted proofs possible. Additionally, the foundation has convened workshops, lectures and collaborations that have brought mathematicians together to explore and discuss AI’s role in the field. “This is a moment for the mathematics community to come together,” Spergel says. “The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used, not any single company or institution. The goal of the program is to support the mathematics community.” Information for Press For more information, please contact [email protected] . title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
body_text: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents | Blog | Liquid AI Models Research Engineering Blog Solutions Developers Company Models Research Engineering Blog Solutions Developers Company Try our API News / Models LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents OCT 13, 2026 On this page What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B Benchmarks Fast inference everywhere Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Get Started Citation Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B . LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally. What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality. Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens. Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads. Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below. This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments. Benchmarks We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode. The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength. Fast inference everywhere LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem: llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators All runs were collected on Pipette , the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data. Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately. We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency. Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls. Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions. The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice. Get Started Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face . For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens. With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are: Open-weight — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our model license . Fast from day one — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware A complete family — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use cases We can't wait to see what you build. Download on Hugging Face Run your harness of choice locally with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Integrate with our API Citation For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX: Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents", Liquid AI Blog, Oct 2026. @article{liquidAI202624BA2B, author = {Liquid AI}, title = {LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents}, journal = {Liquid AI Blog}, year = {2026}, note = {www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b}, } *All the models were evaluated with vLLM and the following generation parameters: AutomationBench: temperature = 0.6, top_p = 0.95, no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window). BFCLv4 : temperature = 0.001, max output tokens = 4096. ToolSandbox : temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024; user simulator: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024. LiveClaw : temperature = 1.0 (vLLM default; the agent sets no temperature), max output tokens = 8192. τ³-Bench Banking : official user model (GPT-5.2, low reasoning effort) with default BM25 retrieval, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 16384 per turn. WebArena: temperature = 0.6, top_p=0.95, max_turns=40 (no of browser actions allowed), no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window)) Other evals : temperature = 0.6, max output tokens = 32768. title: More on Anthropic's Scion ripping off Mononoke
body_text: More on Anthropic's Scion ripping off Mononoke · sunshowers sunshowers about work about work More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke 2026-10-15 · 6 min read vcs shorts Update: Nick G. from Anthropic has responded on Hacker News , and sufficient attribution has been added to Anthropic’s blog post. I stand by my posts as of the time I wrote them. Discuss on Hacker News . In response to yesterday’s post about Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke, I received a number of questions and concerns. Here’s a followup to answer the big ones. This was a ripoff. My post yesterday was trying to be as charitable as possible given what I knew, and in particular that the similarity to Mononoke was mostly unintentional and the lack of credit was the result of not doing due diligence. However, after publishing the post I privately received confirmation that Scion intentionally and blatantly ripped off Mononoke, and in particular that there was overlap in personnel. There is no chance that this was an unintentional homage. This is something I had a hunch about but was not comfortable saying yesterday, given what I knew back then. The resemblance is much deeper than just the notion of derived data. Some people pointed out that derived data is just an index, which is a well-known concept. I want to clarify that derived data was merely the most striking resemblance. It goes much deeper than that, and extends to the entire data model, as well as a number of the structures built around it. Here is how Anthropic describes Scion changesets: How Anthropic describes Scion’s changesets. Mononoke has the same concept; we call it a Bonsai changeset. In the same Oxide materials from 2022, here’s how I described them: How I described Mononoke’s Bonsai changesets. They are exactly the same. Even the name “Scion” reverses the syllables of “Bonsai” and drops the “B”! This might be a coincidence, or might not. For derived data, I also wanted to draw attention to the kinds of indexes being built, such as for blame. Needing to do this is a natural consequence of the Bonsai data model, so it’s not surprising that indexes need to be built; I was drawing attention to the striking similarity in terminology and framing, because that was indeed how we used to think about it during my time on Meta’s source control team. Another set of resemblances is in the server-side API to do version control queries and mutations with. This was implemented in Mononoke, but I believe other systems before Mononoke had it as well, so I’m not going to claim novelty. But if what you did is point Claude at Mononoke and asked it to rebuild that, you would probably design something very similar. The Bonsai data model is wildly contrarian. I want to emphasize that the prevailing wisdom in source control is Git-like data models. Building a write-ahead log-style Merkle DAG was very far away from what anyone else was doing in 2018, and required solving several hard problems along the way such as how to perform server-side rebases (to my knowledge, one of several novel algorithms in Mononoke). While I was leading the team effort to design and implement the model in 2018, I personally had to justify it to several layers of management at Meta. It is quite rare for skip levels to get pulled in to discuss a system’s data model in depth. The Bonsai data model is also wildly successful. At this point, almost a decade later, the model has been stretched far outside its initial design parameters, and it’s still chugging along. The team effort to build it remains one of my proudest career achivements. Given the overlap in personnel, there is no reasonable way the Scion team could not have known about this. (Which is why they quite reasonably copied it!) This brings us to my next point: The problem is attribution, not copying. I mentioned this in my original post, but I am completely fine with good ideas being copied. I am not fine with the serial numbers being accidentally stripped off, and I am certainly not fine with them being intentionally stripped off. Crediting Sapling for “hard-won lessons” is not enough. Several people pointed out that Mononoke is part of the Sapling ecosystem. The problem here is that Sapling can mean either the VCS client ( sl , originally forked from hg ) or the system as a whole. If you were previously on Meta’s source control team, you absolutely know the difference between the two. Besides, the resemblance is much, much deeper than merely “hard-won lessons”. The Lore VCS can claim inspiration from Mononoke, but it differs in several ways as well. Scion’s resemblance to Mononoke goes well beyond that, and merely crediting Sapling (not even Mononoke) with “hard-won lessons” is dishonest. (And specifically, I would expect the Scion changeset section to mention Bonsai changesets as the thing they are copied from.) This makes Anthropic’s achievement significantly less impressive. Anyone who’s put a distributed system into production knows how many issues tend to crop up during the productionizing process. “Our LLM built this thing, productionized it, and dealt with all the attendant challenges over 5 months” is a significantly more compelling narrative than “the source control team at Meta had spent 10 years building and productionizing this system, and we were able to point our LLM at it and rebuild it in 5 months”. …and yet, it is still quite an achievement. Being able to point to an existing system and rebuild it in this short a period is still quite stunning. It is shocking to me that Anthropic didn’t just say they copied Mononoke and rebuilt it in 5 months. That is still noteworthy, even if it isn’t as grand. Surely they knew they would be called out? It is always good to situate your work in the larger context. We all stand on the shoulders of giants! There is nothing wrong with borrowing and adapting existing work to new contexts — that is the vast majority of what I do as an engineer. When you position your work as derivative, you are acknowledging those that came before you, as you hope to be acknowledged by those who come after you. There is nothing without the team. On a personal note, it’s been many years since I worked on Mononoke. There is a team that still carries the torch forward all these years later. Anthropic ripping the Bonsai data model off hit me hard, but spare a thought for the team working on it now: those who were most directly plagiarized. Imagine how they must feel about their work being deliberately copied wholesale and intentionally presented as someone else’s. It’s been two days since I first posted about this on Bluesky and Linkedin, and I haven’t seen an update to the original post yet. This remains yet another shameful example of large AI companies appropriating the commons and presenting others’ work as their own. I don’t know what it will take to rebuild bridges from here, but my default assumption now is that Anthropic’s public engineering presentations are largely bad-faith ripoffs. That’s a shame. title: OpenCode 2.0
body_text: OpenCode 2.0 Anomaly â All posts OpenCode 2.0 OpenCode 2.0 Carry the disk Nothing waiting on the desk OpenCode 2.0 is a major over haul. It draws on mil lions of daily users' expe ri ence to deliver a system that can flex to every thing an agent needs to be. There are quite a lot of new fea tures, per for mance improve ments, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impact ful user-facing changes. The Service From the begin ning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not some thing it took advan tage of by default and was mostly used by power users. In 2.0 this server now auto mat i cally runs as a single back ground process on your machine. When you open up a TUI, the web inter face or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process. Terminal Fix flaky test Web Fix flaky test Desktop Add dark mode review.ts Review changes opencode pid 48213 Stopped Starting Running Sessions Fix flaky test Add dark mode Review changes If you're using the pro gram matic client @opencode/client to make your own scripts, they will autodis cover the local service and just work. This is par tic u larly useful for sched uled tasks. You can also call it via CLI by using opencode api com mands. You can expose it to other hosts and run /pair or opencode pair to connect it to other appli ca tions. We have native apps in the works that take advan tage of this flow. The API The old API grew hap haz ardly as we and the world col lec tively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad. We started from scratch and exam ined all the weird use cases across the mil lions of users who use OpenCode every day. It now sup ports nearly any thing you need to be able to do. OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git work tree when start ing new work. Session New session YOU Start rate limiting uploads in a new worktree. execute { code } âº opencode. worktree_create [name=rate-limit] âº opencode. session_rename [title=Rate limit uploads] âº opencode. session_move [directory=~/worktrees/rate-limit] YOU The flaky test session is stuck. Stop it, have it quarantine the test, and close my finished tabs. execute { code } âº opencode. session_list âº opencode. session_context [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a] â "Retrying uploads.test.ts againâ¦" execute { code } âº opencode. session_interrupt [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a] âº opencode. session_prompt [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a, text=Quarantine uploads.test.ts] âº opencode. tab_close [sessionID=ses_2f9d61b4] Stopped it, told it to quarantine the test, closed the config tab. OpenCode ~/app Fix flaky upload test interrupted Migrate config loader tab closed New session this session ~/worktrees/rate-limit We've also shipped a new client package @opencode/client that con tains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect. review.ts import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client" import { Service } from "@opencode/client/service" const endpoint = await Service. ensure () const client = OpenCode. make ({ baseUrl: endpoint.url, headers: Service. headers (endpoint), }) const session = await client.session. create ({ location: { directory: process. cwd () }, }) await client.session. prompt ({ sessionID: session.id, text: "Review the current changes" , }) Code Mode The models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advan tage of that more than any other coding agent. We've built a minimal JavaScript inter preter in the @opencode/codemode package. Session YOU File GitHub bugs in Linear. execute { code } tools.github.list_issues tools.linear.save_issue execute { code } ["OC-412", "OC-413", "OC-414"] Code Mode return [ search ({ query: "list github issues" }), search ({ query: "create linear issue" })] const { issues } = await tools.github. list_issues ({ owner: "anomalyco" , repo: "opencode" , labels: [ "bug" ], state: "OPEN" , }) const filed = await Promise . all (issues. map (({ title }) => tools.linear. save_issue ({ team: "OC" , title }))) return filed. map ( issue => issue.identifier) MCP servers github linear sentry This package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI end points, con vert ing them into func tions that the agent can call in a script. It can run these scripts natively without the com plex ity of Node.js VMs or embed ding com pli cated solu tions like QuickJS. This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool, map over the results and call another tool. Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time. All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into code mode by default. This means you can add a thou sand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will dis cover and compose them to get things done. Background Tasks The latest batch of models are incred i bly good at orches tra tion and it is impor tant for har nesses to let them express the full extent of that capa bil ity. Session YOU Spawn a background fable subagent to review this code. subagent review this code fable background 2 comments $ shell bun test background 148 passed edit src/retry.ts +12 $ $ shell bun run build background done Press ctrl b to move running work to the background YOU Update the changelog too. edit CHANGELOG.md +3 All done. The review left 2 comments, 148 tests passed, the build succeeded and the changelog is updated. Background review this code fable $ bun test $ bun run build ctrl b First, we've added back ground sub agents. This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it con tin ues. This happens auto mat i cally but you can also trigger it man u ally - even with a dif fer ent model. It lets you do things like âspawn a back ground fable sub agent to review this codeâ while you keep prompt ing. Second, we've added back ground shell com mands. The shell tool can be invoked asyn chronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent. It'll be noti fied when things are com plete. If any fore ground shell command or sub agent takes longer than you expect, you can hit a hotkey to move them to the back ground so you can keep prompt ing. Plugins Although OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system, it never got the atten tion it needed. To correct that, we forced our selves to imple ment nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an inter nal plugin and there are now 80+ of them. This guar an tees that the Plugin API stays well main tained. We've also pro moted TUI plugins from exper i men tal to stable. Since it is all powered by OpenTUI, you can build nearly any thing. Here is an example of some thing useless. We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded. So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away - we covered the design of this in a previous blogpost . You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to. But if you do want to read the docs, they are available here . The SDK OpenCode can also now be used as a library with the @opencode/sdk package. This is the exact same code that powers our CLI. This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in spe cial ized envi ron ments like Durable Objects. And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the stan dard OpenCode server pro to col. It also has an optional Effect-based API. This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can already use it . Upgrading To upgrade the CLI, make sure you're on the latest 1.x release, then run opencode upgrade --major . To upgrade your desktop app, download the latest here . There are some break ing changes. 1.0 plugins will not work in 2.0 Server API is completely different tui.json config is moved to json There are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible. It is worth pointing OpenCode at this doc so it can migrate things for you.
