title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
body_text: Americans’ Social Activity Has Steeply Declined in the Past 30 Years ⌃ Latest Polling Insights Issues Resources & Guides Newsletter About Donate Work With Us Back All Polling Briefs Reports Back All Issues Artificial Intelligence Climate Disability Economy Education Electoral Politics Family Care Foreign Policy Health Care Immigration Judiciary LGBTQ+ Rights Social Justice State & Local Polling Voting Rights & Democracy Workers' Rights Back Our Mission Our Impact Our Team Our Methodology Our Research Philosophy Media Jobs Latest Polling All Polling Briefs Reports Insights Issues All Issues Artificial Intelligence Climate Disability Economy Education Electoral Politics Family Care Foreign Policy Health Care Immigration Judiciary LGBTQ+ Rights Social Justice State & Local Polling Voting Rights & Democracy Workers' Rights Resources & Guides Newsletter About Our Mission Our Impact Our Team Our Methodology Our Research Philosophy Media Jobs Donate Work With Us Americans’ Social Activity Has Steeply Declined in the Past 30 Years In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.” Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points , from 63% to 38%. But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades. In a new survey , Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available. This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026 .  The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12). A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5). Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.     One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.     Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.     The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.     There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.     This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs. Methodology The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail. In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting. There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.  Lew Blank September 29, 2026 Facebook 0 Twitter LinkedIn 0 Reddit 0 Likes Previous Voter Support a Green New Deal for Public Housing Abby Springs October 7, 2026 Climate Next Unfavorable Views of Flock Surveillance Cameras Have Grown Since August Abby Springs September 23, 2026 Newsletter Block This newsletter signup form needs a storage option. title: Passkeys are not a trap
body_text: Passkeys Are Not a Trap Home Speaking Training Media Contact Sponsor 🌙 Subscribe Sponsored by:   Report URI - Passkeys protect login, not the session. Monitor what happens after authentication. Passkeys Passkeys Are Not a Trap Scott Helme Security researcher, entrepreneur and international speaker who specialises in web technologies. More posts by Scott Helme. Scott Helme 14 Oct 2026 • 4 min read A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords. The Argument The post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey. The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif> It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works... Your Passkeys Don't Attest The passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none . I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone. If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now. Attestation Isn't What You Think It Is The post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true. When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID , with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is. The YubiKey Recommendation This is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation". YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it! TOTP Is a Step Backwards The post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt . Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it. This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com . There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade... What You Should Do Keep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing. Sources I have some experience in this area: I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web. I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company. We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed. I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website . I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work . I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use. I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations. I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys. I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap. title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
body_text: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics. | CSO Online Topics Latest Newsletters Resources Buyer’s Guides Events Editions Search Menu Topics Close Analytics Application Security Artificial Intelligence Business Continuity Business Operations Careers Cloud Security Compliance Contributor Content Critical Infrastructure Cybercrime Enterprise Buyer’s Guides Generative AI Identity and Access Management Industry IT Leadership IT Management Network Security Physical Security Privacy Risk Management Security Security Infrastructure Software Development Vulnerabilities Back Close Search US - EN Topics Latest Newsletters Resources Buyer’s Guides Events More Awards Blogs BrandPosts Events Podcasts Videos Buyer’s Guides & Enterprise Spotlights Topics Topics Analytics Application Security Artificial Intelligence Business Continuity Business Operations Careers Cloud Security Compliance Contributor Content Critical Infrastructure Cybercrime Enterprise Buyer’s Guides Generative AI Identity and Access Management Industry IT Leadership IT Management Network Security Physical Security Privacy Risk Management Security Security Infrastructure Software Development Vulnerabilities Americas United States Asia ASEAN India Europe United Kingdom Oceania Australia Home Artificial Intelligence by Cynthia Brumfield Contributing Writer AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics. News Analysis Oct 14, 2026 9 mins Cyber experts say AI labs’ containment and monitoring failures — not agents with minds of their own — are to blame for recent alarming hacking reports. CISOs should vet their AI vendors and tighten security basics as safeguards. Credit: PeopleImages / Shutterstock Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. [ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ] Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires. First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.” For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.” But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’” “We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.” See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? She runs a cybersecurity news destination site, Metacurity.com , consults with companies through her firm DCT-Associates, and is the author of the book published by Wiley, Cybersecurity Risk Management: Mastering the Fundamentals Using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework . Cynthia holds a Master of Planning Degree from the University of Virginia and a Bachelor’s degree from The George Washington University. She has won multiple AZBEE awards for her work on CSO, including two in 2025. Style Aile Etoile Weight 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Slope Italic Oblique AMONG the many valuable contributions of William Dwight Whitney to linguistic science is one especially important and fundamental principle. It may be stated in these words. In explaining the prehistoric phenomena of language we must assume no other factors than those which we are able to observe and estimate in the historical period of language development. The factors that produced changes in human speech five thousand or ten thousand years ago cannot have been essentially different from those which are now operating to transform living languages. On the basis of this principle we look to-day at a much-discussed problem of Indo-European philology with views very different from the views held by the founders of Comparative Philology and their immediate successors. I refer to the problem, how the Indo-European people came to assign gender to nouns, to distinguish between masculine, feminine, and neuter. This question is of interest to others besides philologists. What man of culture who has learned languages such as the Greek, Latin, or French has not at times wondered that objects which have no possible connection with the natural gender of animals appear constantly in the language as male or female? In German, for example, it is der fuss, but die hand; der geist, but die seele; in Latin, hīc hortus, hīc animus, hīc amor, but haec planta, haec anima, haec felicitas; in Greek, ὁ πλοῦτος, ὁ οἶκος, but ἡ πενία, ἡ οἰκία. This gender distinction pervades all the older Indo-European languages, and must therefore be regarded as having its origin in the time of the pro-ethnic Indo-European community. Not only is the subject itself full of interest, but also the treatment it has received from the philological research of our century. The various efforts made to solve the problem may very aptly illustrate an essential difference which exists between the theories of language development held in the beginning and middle of this century and those which prevail to-day, — a difference of method existing not in comparative linguistics alone, but also in other fields of philological and historical research that border on it. 248 Explore the latest Slide 1 of 4 Solving frontier problems with experts Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are pairing with Argon to push the boundaries of science, math, robotics and cyber defense. Unlocking new scientific breakthroughs Argon is helping researchers at Google and the scientific community accelerate their path to discovery and real-world impact. Accelerating robotics Argon autonomously turns raw video to a physics-accurate simulation, estimating depth and physical boundaries, and writing the exact simulation code required to replicate those real-world environments. Scaling cybersecurity defense responsibly Argon ties for #1 on CWE-Bench (68%) for vulnerability remediation, is our most resilient model against indirect prompt injections, and is expanding to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners today. Hands-on Performance Safety Try Gemini 4 Argon Solving complex engineering tasks Across Google and our early access partners, Argon is quickly becoming the preferred model for engineers tackling long-horizon software engineering. Your browser does not support the video tag. Untangling browser feature code in Chrome Quantum chemistry open-source package optimization Optimizing a production Python codebase in hours Making our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast Migrating legacy code Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromiumâs 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes. xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official xTB repository on GitHub. Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their .agents/skills rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%. Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes. Argon in Antigravity migrated a backlog of 700+ Google Skills training labs off of hardcoded system images and runtimes spread across five code repositories, catching 16+ hidden timeout and race-condition bugs on the way. The work saved 955 engineering hours and reduced recurring cleanup sweeps from roughly 540 hours a year to a single 3-hour update. Delivering complex 3D visualizations Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models. Starting from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity, Argon drives Blender MCP in an autonomous loop, aligning camera grids, sculpting Gothic architecture, and staging audio-reactive lighting, to create a finished 3D scene. Transforming critical business and professional workflows Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to handle high-stakes professional workflows. title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
body_text: Jev: For the builders AND dreamers - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu âµ Back Company News Company News Jev: For the builders AND dreamers Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. ð¥ Our philosophy A huge debate weâve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity. To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally. On the other hand, thereâs no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We donât want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers. Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under âdanger zoneâ flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases! See these new capabilities as a continuation of what weâve built over 2 years of stealth. Theyâre less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. Theyâre also an early glimpse into what weâre focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards. Composable Images Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, weâre enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve. As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images Types Beyond Decisions Weâre introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. Itâs our first type thatâs not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support. We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so weâre enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers). Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box Size does matter, apparently ð Weâve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than weâve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod. We arenât your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length Opt-in to help us We love the communityâs desire to help make models better! Weâve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases. jev-1.14.0 Weâre also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything . Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support. Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but weâre well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while.  We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0 . Weâll release a deprecation policy prior to this. Measuring Intelligence As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks . However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers.  Weâre trying something new out here: weâre going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all. Some nuance This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, donât expect them to be consistent. Donât believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases. Weâre including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers. This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models. Whatâs next Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi weâre releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment. âµ â© â© âµ TypeSafe AI Â© 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI Â© 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
body_text: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. - yyhh.org Toggle navigation yyhh.org About Experience Notebook Opinion AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. Date Mon 12 October 2026 By Huahai Tags AI LLM Tools Clojure In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does. Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs. One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter. An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse. Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not? The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful. Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does. What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any. I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment. The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool. Status: alpha. Meant for testing, not production. Upgrading between prereleases may not be possible; plan to drop and recreate the extension and its indexes. See the changelog for known issues. PRISM index (100M+ vectors) — IVF-style, with hierarchical routing RaBitQ quantization with theoretical error bounds for two-stage search SIMD-optimized distance computation (AVX2, AVX512, NEON) Dynamic updates — inserts, updates and deletes, with posting-list splits via prism_rebalance (see Maintenance ) pgvector compatible — index existing vector and halfvec columns as-is (see Existing pgvector tables ) PRISM Index PRISM (Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching) is a PostgreSQL-native index access method that is conceptually similar to pgvector 's IVFFlat, but it is built around state-of-the-art quantization, routing, and partitioning techniques. It is implemented in C for high performance and seamless integration with PostgreSQL. The result: an index that is significantly faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW, for both querying and index building. In fact, compared to graph-based HNSW, PRISM is faster at equivalent recall on a 100-million-vector dataset, on an instance with a quarter of the memory. To achieve this performance, PRISM uses a hierarchical centroid tree to partition vectors into clusters, and relies on the PostgreSQL buffer cache to keep that tree warm in memory. Vectors are RaBitQ -quantized and stored in posting lists with a page layout optimized for SIMD distance computation. The RaBitQ encoding carries error bounds that let a search rule out vectors that cannot possibly be nearest neighbors, so far fewer of them need reranking against the full-precision vectors stored in the table. Query Flow: 1. Traverse centroid tree to find nearest clusters (buffer cache) 2. Scan posting lists for candidates (buffer cache, async I/O) 3. RaBitQ two-stage filtering: estimate → error bound → rerank 4. Full-precision reranking from heap 5. Return k nearest neighbors For detailed architecture, see docs/architecture.md . Usage Install the extension first; see Building . There are two ways to use a PRISM index. Pick the one that matches where your vectors live: Native types . Starting fresh, or not using pgvector? Store vectors in pg_vectorsearch 's own vec32 (float32) or vec16 (float16) columns. No other extension is needed. Existing pgvector tables . Already have vector or halfvec columns? Install pg_vectorsearch next to pgvector and build a PRISM index on those columns as they are. Your table and queries stay unchanged. Both paths build the same index and use the same operators ( <-> , <#> , <=> ) and tuning knobs. Native types CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; -- PLAIN keeps the vector inline. EXTERNAL (the default) toasts a value -- over ~2 kB, and rerank then pays an extra fetch the planner does not cost. CREATE TABLE items ( id serial PRIMARY KEY , embedding vec32( 3 ) STORAGE PLAIN ); -- Load first; the index is sized from the row count at CREATE INDEX. -- 500 rows is enough for the planner to use the index. INSERT INTO items (embedding) SELECT ARRAY[i:: real , (i % 7 ):: real , (i % 5 ):: real ]::vec32 FROM generate_series( 1 , 1000 ) i; -- For inner product or cosine, see Operator classes below. CREATE INDEX ON items USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- 0 = auto (~0.95 recall). Raise for recall, lower for speed. SET prism . nprobe = 40 ; SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding < - > ' [3,1,2] ' LIMIT 5 ; Use vec16 instead of vec32 to halve the space vectors take in the table, with the matching vec16_* operator classes . Existing pgvector tables If you already have a table with pgvector's vector or halfvec columns, you can build a PRISM index on it directly. Nothing about the table or your queries needs to change. vec32 and vec16 are binary-compatible with pgvector's vector and halfvec but have different names, so the two extensions can be installed side by side, even in the same schema. -- The table you already have, included so the example runs on its own. CREATE EXTENSION vector; CREATE TABLE documents ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY , body text , embedding vector( 384 ) ); CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops); -- Install pg_vectorsearch next to pgvector and build the index on the -- existing column. The column is not rewritten or copied. CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_prism ON documents USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- Your queries keep working as before. PRISM is normally faster, so -- the planner should prefer it over the HNSW index while both exist. -- Verify with an EXPLAIN: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id, body FROM documents ORDER BY embedding < - > ( SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id = 42 ) LIMIT 10 ; -- Limit -- InitPlan 1 -- -> Index Scan using documents_pkey on documents documents_1 -- Index Cond: (id = 42) -- -> Index Scan using documents_embedding_prism on documents -- Order By: (embedding <-> (InitPlan 1).col1) -- Once you are happy with it, drop the HNSW index. DROP INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw; Use the PRISM operator class for the same distance metric as your HNSW index. Operator classes Pick the operator class for your distance metric and column type. L2 is the default. Distance Operator vec32 / vector vec16 / halfvec L2 <-> vec32_l2_ops vec16_l2_ops Inner product <#> vec32_ip_ops vec16_ip_ops Cosine <=> vec32_cosine_ops vec16_cosine_ops When replacing an HNSW index, pgvector's vector_<metric>_ops maps to vec32_<metric>_ops and halfvec_<metric>_ops to vec16_<metric>_ops . Tuning Defaults are tuned from large-scale benchmarks; most deployments only ever adjust prism.nprobe . See the tuning guide for every index parameter and GUC, their tradeoffs, and when changing them makes sense. Maintenance An insert appends to whichever posting list its vector routes to, so lists grow as rows arrive and never split on their own. Besides REINDEX , the prism_rebalance procedure splits oversized lists in place. See the maintenance guide for how it works and its current limitations. Building Requirements: PostgreSQL 18+ (with development headers) GNU C11 compiler (GCC 11+ or Clang 14+) Meson build system Optional: CBLAS, for faster RaBitQ encoding. See Development . # Release build meson setup builddir --buildtype=release # Build and install to PostgreSQL meson install -C builddir See the development guide for build options. Documentation Tuning - Index parameters, GUCs, tradeoffs, defaults Maintenance - Rebalancing and splitting posting lists Architecture - High-level design and data structures SIMD - SIMD build options and distance computation Development - Build options, testing, CI scripts References Research RaBitQ - Binary quantization with theoretical error bounds (SIGMOD 2024) SPFresh - LIRE protocol for incremental updates (SOSP 2023) SPANN - Billion-scale ANN with boundary replication (NeurIPS 2021) ScaNN for AlloyDB - Hierarchical clustering (Google) Related Projects pgvector - Vector type and operators for PostgreSQL pgvectorscale - DiskANN-based vector index for PostgreSQL License The PostgreSQL License About High-performance vector search for PostgreSQL Resources Readme PostgreSQL license Activity Custom properties Stars 360 stars Watchers 2 watching Forks 13 forks Report repository Releases Packages Used by Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. The Early Years Apparatus Buckman Portraits Negative Copying Cartesians Loose Leaf The Lamp Posts of Alton Baker Park Animals and Insects Character Composites CHS1966 Dry Reading Store About Contact By Craig Hickman Ben: Dad, what have you been doing upstairs?   Dad: Writing a short history of Kid Pix.   Ben: Do you really think anyone is going to want to read that? Maynard and Joe Some people believe that humans are either analytical, rational and sensible or spontaneous, creative and intuitive. Having watched  too much TV  as a kid in the 50’s, I thought people were supposed to be  Sergeant Joe Friday (from Dragnet) or  Maynard G. Krebs (Dobie Gillis) . My problem was I always felt a little like both of these guys.   Sargent Joe Friday Maynard G. Krebs In college I decided to be a fine art photographer. But in 1972, when I was working in photography at  The Evergreen State College , I heard a clattering noise coming from what was labeled the "Terminal Room." Inside, a friend was sitting at what looked like a large typewriter. He said he was  programming  and asked if I would like to see how it was done. I said "yes" and have  never been the same since . Me next to the computer terminal shortly after I was introduced to programming, 1972. I bought a book explaining each command and how it was used. I started writing little programs that would use each of the commands. None of my programs tried to do anything useful, but they tended to be fun and surprising.  In 1974 I left Evergreen along with access to a computer and moved to Portland where some good friends and I started the non-profit photography  Blue Sky Gallery . Later I went to  graduate school in photography  at the  University of Washington , where  Paul Berger , a professor of mine, had just gotten an  Apple II computer . Microcomputers were new then and he explained what it could do.  Suddenly my craving to program came back . I had to have a computer of my own. My Atari in the darkroom A couple of months later I was busy  programming  at home with my own computer,  an Atari 400 . This was a  joyous experience . (My wife says that the day it arrived was the happiest she's ever seen me.) Despite its membrane keyboard and TV set monitor, it was loaded with graphics, sound capability, and programming challenges. I came up with endless projects. I can remember the thrill when I discovered how to input and output signals from the joystick ports. At one point I designed a  home surveillance system  for our apartment in Seattle that used little magnetic switches from Radio Shack. It displayed a representation of our apartment on the screen and showed when a door or window was open. It worked so well I expanded the system to include little tilt switches placed on bushes outside the windows. This also worked fine until one windy night when I was away from home and it set off the alarm every few minutes. The next day my wife told me to dismantle it. I began to be very interested in  user interface and program design . Articles that influenced me the most were ones by  Chris Crawford  in  Byte  Magazine and by  Alan Kay  in  Scientific American . I wanted to discover the simplest and most effective way to perform any task on the computer. This is when I began  my quest for software design beauty . My interest in photography began to wane at this time. The computer was just more interesting. I got one of those "Electronics Made Simple" books, figured out how to use the computer to control the enlarger, and made a rather nice program to control most of my darkroom timing and record-keeping tasks. I ended up using a "card" metaphor for this project that was sort of  HyperCard -like even though it predated HyperCard by several years. In 1984 Apple released the Macintosh . Up to this point I saw no reason to stop using my Atari (except for the fact that hardly anyone else used them and there was practically no audience for the software I was writing). For its day, it had great graphics and sound, and I knew a lot about programming it. Other computers had more serious reputations but they didn't seem as much fun to program. The Macintosh was different . It was totally graphical so the visual possibilities were much greater. Most of all, the Mac seemed to have people with a  consistent and enlightened vision behind it . The user interface was intelligent and beautiful. I got a Mac and began teaching myself to program on it. Originally I programmed in Rascal, a language developed at Reed College which was sort of a cross between C and Pascal. Later I switched to Pascal. Screen snapshot of Camera, 1988 My first Mac programs, which were given away, were designed to help me learn the Mac QuickDraw routines. They did nothing useful but were mildly entertaining.  Company  was a desk accessory that displayed an animated face and a game to keep you company.  Fido was an animated dog that talked in graphics. I also created two artist's books,  Signal to Noise  and  Dry Reading (Available on this site)  , that shared some of the graphics and aesthetics my software has. My most successful program from this time was Camera , an educational title that interactively demonstrated the relationship between f. stop and shutter speed. I put  Camera  in public domain and it was distributed widely on computer bulletin boards. One day in 1988 while I was using  MacPaint , the wonderful paint program that came with the Macintosh, my  3-year-old son Ben  asked to try using the program. I was surprised at how quickly he got the knack of using the mouse and how easily he was able to select tools. The problem was that he didn't have total control of the mouse and would occasionally (like every five minutes or so) pull down a menu and bring up a dialog box that he couldn't dismiss without being able to read. Everything was fine as long as I was in the room, but if I stepped out for a few minutes I would come back and find Ben kicking on the floor in  frustration . This was  not what I had in mind  for his introduction to the computer. As it turned out I was looking for a good programming project. I decided to write a simple paint program for Ben to use. I also decided that I would probably give it away for free. A few years earlier I had written what I thought was a rather nice darkroom timer program for the Atari computer and signed an agreement with a company to sell it. But few people used the Atari computer and almost no copies were sold. I always wished I had just  given the program  away so people could use it and I could have some satisfaction for the great deal of time I had spent writing it. Since I was going to give the program away I decided  I could design it exactly the way I wanted . These were its guiding principles: Screen snapshot of the original Kid Pix 1.  (The Prime Directive)  The program should be  extremely easy to use . No manual should be needed and program features should "explain themselves" through use. All tasks should be able to be performed in the simplest, most straightforward way. The program should go out of its way to meet the user. 2. As long as The Prime Directive is not violated, every opportunity should be taken to make the program  surprising and satisfying to use . No opportunity should be missed. The process of making a picture should be as important as the picture produced. 3. The program should, in some way,  expand  the concept of what computer paint programs are, as well as what mark making can be. 4. The program should be  open ended . Premade graphics should be modifiable by the user. 5. I wanted each tool to have a  large number of options  but I didn't want the user to be overwhelmed with options. I didn't want to use pull-down menus for this because, among other reasons, Ben had trouble with them. The system I developed involved displaying a selection of 14 options for each tool in a window at the bottom of the screen.  As the tool selection changed, the options changed . 6. The first Kid Pix was designed to run on the  original Macintosh with a 9-inch, black and white screen (512 X 342 pixels). All paint programs made for the Mac at that time displayed a virtual page showing only a portion of the potential drawing area at one time. I decided this was a bad idea for my program because it is essential to see your whole picture at the same time. So I made the drawing area on the screen as large as possible but did not have the contents of the screen scroll.  "What you saw is what you got." The Undo Guy 7. In addition to "traditional" computer paint program tools like the brush, pencil, eraser, circle and rectangle, my program would include tools that would be surprising and visually unusual . Most computer paint programs were designed in a way that made them seem like second class citizens, always attempting to mimic traditional art making tools, but never doing a particularly good job of it. In fact, the computer can make marks in a variety of interesting ways that traditional tools can't. It can also do a good job of creating comic tools. This is where the "wacky brushes" came from. 8. Undo is an extremely important function that deserves a button of its own instead of just being a menu item.  The Undo Guy was born.   Some of the stamps from the original Kid Pix. (Notice a relative of the Undo Guy here?) 9. Children love  stickers and rubber stamps . The program should allow for some pre-made iconic art. The stamps in the Original Kid Pix were taken from the Cairo font from Apple Computer designed by Susan Kare . Apple had stopped distributing Cairo with their computers and I thought the pictures were too good not to be seen. 10. Users are very smart and can tell quickly when someone is trying to cover up a lame program with flashy graphics. A poor program gets dull very soon no matter how trendy the interface is. 11. When Ben built something out of blocks, he enjoyed knocking his structure down almost as much as he did building it.  Getting rid of the picture should be fun.  Hence the exploding firecracker eraser. 12. Why not have an eraser that erases your picture but  displays a hidden picture  as you erase? 13. When small children are using the program, a parent should be able to  hide the menu bar  so desk accessories, etc. can't be selected accidentally. 14. The program should, in most ways,  act like a standard program  and have a standard user interface so users new to the computer learn basic principles. Kid Pix ended up being widely used to introduce children and adults to using the computer. 15. While on the surface the program should seem to be for children, open minded  adults should get a kick out of using it too . Program and document icons for the original Kid Pix As the program came closer to completion I needed to think of a name. After considerable thought I came up with  "Kid Pix."  It was easy to say , had a  nice punch to it  and was made up of simple three letter words. (This must be something I am attracted to: my wife's name is Kay and my children are Ben and Art). I liked the way "Pix" referred to " Pictures ," " Pixels ," and " to   Pick ," and I liked way the words looked graphically when stacked on top of each other. It also occurred to me that it would probably be easy to say in other languages, though at that time I never imagined that it would be sold around the world. Later, Broderbund decided to rename it and had a company-wide competition to come up with a new name. When none came up, they went to a professional name consultant. He told them that he could take their money and come up with a new name, but it wouldn't be any better than "Kid Pix." I could have run the Kid Pix name together to become KidPix, as was the style then for program names. I decided against it because I was afraid it was just a naming fad, although today if you do a search on the web the name appears as much one way as it does the other.  As I added new features to Kid Pix, I would try them out on Ben. Anything he had trouble with would be changed.  The customer was always right.  One day I took a number of computers to Ben's pre-school and tried it out on the children there, most of whom had not used computers before. Within ten minutes of having the children use the program I had accumulated a  long list of small user interface changes  for the program. Before I’d finished Kid Pix, Apple came out with the  color Macintosh . It seemed that the next logical step would be a color version of Kid Pix. My friend  Ken O'Connell  always supported my work and insisted that  I should sell the program rather than give it away . I felt that as it was, Kid Pix made a  great freeware  program but didn't yet have enough capability to be a commercial program. Before sending out the finished black and white version of Kid Pix I decided to commit to writing an expanded,  color version  of the program, which I would sell for $25. In  November 1989 I started distributing the black and white version , which included an ad for the color version stating that it would be done by June 1990. (The original black and white version of Kid Pix is still available for downloading  today from shareware web sites like  shareware.com .) Writing the black and white version was quite a challenge for me and I had no idea how to program color. I anticipated several months just to convert what I had done into color. As it turned out I figured out the basics of the conversion in about a day, which left lots of time to work on new features. Manual cover for Kid Pix Professional It was the style at that time to add the word "Professional" to new versions of software. To be humorous, I called the new version " Kid Pix Professional. " Besides adding color, I was  bursting with new ideas for the program . Here are a few of the changes and additions I made: 1. The program adjusts to  compensate for monitor size and displayable colors . You can make really big Kid Pix pictures if you have a large monitor, and all aspects of the program are customized to work in either black and white or color depending on the computer used. 2.  Sounds added  to the user interface make a more satisfying experience. The Alphabet tool now reads the letters. 3. There are twice as many  wacky brushes . 4. A new category of tool called "mixer" effects   makes  changes that affect the entire picture. 5. New, more interesting  hidden pictures  are added. 6. More  rubber stamps  are added. 7. Since my wife speaks Spanish, Kid Pix’s spoken Alphabet and menus become  bilingual .  8. There is now a  manual .   By June of 1990 I was starting to get $25 checks in the mail for Kid Pix Professional, and the program was actually done on time. It was a real  treat to walk out to the mailbox  every day and find checks and letters. I ended up  selling about 100 copies of Kid Pix Professional  and think that if vintage software is ever collected, it should make one of the really rare finds. Ben and me just after Kid Pix was released Many people had been  supportive of Kid Pix  when it was being developed, among them Paul Scott,  Bonnie Meltzer  ,  Anita Best  , Richard Wanderman  and  Judi Mathis.  Many were instrumental in helping make contacts that finally resulted in my sending a copy of Kid Pix to  Broderbund Software  in the summer of 1990. I really didn't expect that the program would be picked up by a major publisher, but when I received the name of someone at Broderbund to send it to, I dropped a copy in the mail anyway. About a week later I got a call from Harry Wilker of Broderbund, who said right off that he  wanted to publish Kid Pix . He also said that they receive a lot of paint program submissions and almost didn't even look at Kid Pix. A week later I flew to down to the corporate headquarters. There I also met  Leslie Wilson , Richard Whittaker and Rebecca Knievel. Rebecca had been a student of mine  at the University of Oregon a year earlier and the fact that she was working on the Kid Pix project was a total coincidence. Richard, the publisher, was very astute in his assessment of software. I ended up working extensively with Leslie over the next few years and found her to be a first-class software designer and extremely good at interpersonal relations. Before Kid Pix was released,  Broderbund wanted to make a number of changes . Fortunately, I agreed whole-heartedly with them and felt that the people I was working with  really understood the program.  One of the major changes was about sound. Kid Pix Professional had incorporated some user interface sounds, including the exploding eraser and alphabet sounds. I hadn't given everything a sound because, for one thing, I couldn't get some of the more sophisticated sound techniques to work, and for another, I quickly discovered that I didn't have the aptitude for sounds that I had for dealing with the visual aspects of the program. Fortunately Broderbund had an  exceptional sound department  which created a wonderful set of sound effects for Kid Pix tools. (I also figured out how to program sound without crashing the computer.) There were others from Broderbund and elsewhere who contributed to the final program. At the bottom of this document you will find the credits as they appeared in Kid Pix 1.0. Most  stressful  was dealing with  bugs . Broderbund had a large department of skilled people whose job it was to find things wrong with software. And they did. I had thought Kid Pix Professional was quite bug free: after all, I had been selling it. My  first   bug report was 30 pages long!  And each new feature that was added brought new bugs, which had to be fixed. Even the bug fixes often created new bugs. In the past I’d only had myself to please with my programming; now I was responsible for fixing all this myself. In the end each one got stomped out. This was also a stressful time because I was teaching full-time at the  University of Oregon  in a department that required many hours of teaching and committee work. Throughout this time I had many  long telephone calls with Leslie  discussing a wide variety of issues related to Kid Pix. Phillip Ivanier and John Sculley demonstrating Kid Pix at MacWorld, 1991 Even before the Broderbund version of Kid Pix was released,  the feedback I was getting was good . In December Stewart Alsop in P.C. Letter  had some kind things to say about a pre-release version of Kid Pix, and to my great surprise and shock, in January, 1991 John Sculley featured Kid Pix in his keynote speech at MacWorld.  In the following issue of  Macweek  a headline read, "Kid Pix Vrooms past Sculley at Expo." This was all before Kid Pix was released. At that time Broderbund started work on Kid Pix for DOS. Kid Pix 1.0 In March 1991  Kid Pix 1.0 was released,  and things started to get really good. Sales were significantly   above expectations   and the reviews were exceptional . Very positive reviews appeared in MacUser ,  The San Jose Mercury News ,  The Wall Street Journal ,  The New York Times  and  The Whole Earth Review . A  MacWorld Magazine review stated, " Pros: Brilliant; hilarious; innovative; inexpensive. Cons: None."  An article in the  Wall Street Journal referred to it as "a startling product for the Macintosh that uses color and sound." I couldn't believe what was happening! Kid Pix also won quite a number of awards, including the 1991  MacUser  Eddi for best Children's Program, the 1991  Software Publishers Association Awards for Best User Interface in a New Program and Best Early Learning Program (presented on stage by Bill Gates, who went on to create a competing product), and the  MacWorld  World-Class award for Best Education Program. Hebru Version of Kid Pix   Hebrew and Japanese versions of Kid Pix Japanese version of Kid Pix Kid Pix was also  sold around the world . There were versions in about a dozen languages, including Finnish and Hebrew. Since Kid Pix was already bilingual, it was rather easy to add another language.  I found that my life was changing significantly. I was regularly being interviewed and getting job offers. People were going out of their way to  shake my hand.  I even made a trip to Japan where I was honored, interviewed and offered much  sushi . It seemed that Kid Pix had touched people in a way the software seldom does. Later there were add-ons to the program, and a new version, Kid Pix Studio, but that should be the topic of another story.           Here are the credits as they appeared in Kid Pix 1.0, 1991. Program By Craig Hickman Product Manager Leslie Wilson Graphics Michelle Bushneff , Craig Hickman   Sound Jonelle Adkisson , Craig Hickman Tom Rettig Manual Susan Meyers Color printing technology Copyright © 1990 Equilibrium. title: Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland
body_text: Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland | dpa international Politics Economics Culture & Science Sports General News Trends & Features war medtop:20000062 conflict dpasubject:114 internet dpasubject:377 fire medtop:20000150 Bulgaria dpacountry:31 Russia dpacountry:139 Ukraine dpacountry:181 Poland dpacountry:135 updateme dpauserneed:updateme Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland 14.10.2026, 20:51 Uhr By Elena Lalowa, dpa Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Wednesday that there had been a fire at a facility of the Starlink satellite internet service near the capital Sofia last week. Two young men holding German passports have been taken into custody in connection with the suspected attack, Bulgarian media later reported, citing investigators. The satellite network is a strategically important part of Ukraine's defence in the war against Russia's invasion. The fire had previously been made public by the pro-Western opposition alliance Democratic Bulgaria (DB). Radev said he would not provide any further details in light of the ongoing investigations. According to DB, 11 of 17 antennas at a Starlink facility near Sofia were deliberately set on fire on October 9. The antennas were used in the war in Ukraine, DB said. Pro-Western opposition parties said they suspected Russia was linked to the attack. Two German passport holders in custody Two men aged 20 and 21, both holding German passports, were detained in Bulgaria on Monday in connection with the suspected attack, several Bulgarian media outlets reported on Wednesday evening, citing investigators. According to the news outlet Faktor.bg, the two suspects have migrant backgrounds and had legally entered Bulgaria from Greece through the Kulata border crossing. The website reported that investigators were examining whether the suspects belonged to a larger sabotage network potentially linked to two men arrested in Germany earlier this week over a recent attack on a Starlink facility in Poland. Sabotage suspected Bulgarian officials stressed that the Starlink facility near Sofia was privately owned. Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told parliament that additional security measures had been introduced at similar facilities, even though responsibility for their protection rested with their owners. Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria's State Agency for National Security (DANS), said he believed the fire at the Starlink facility was an act of sabotage. "Such acts of sabotage cannot be ruled out in the future either," he warned lawmakers. A fire also broke out at a Starlink ground terminal south of Warsaw on September 23. Two suspected saboteurs accused of carrying out that attack in Poland were arrested on Tuesday in NÃ¼rtingen, near Stuttgart in south-western Germany. The government in Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence services were behind the attack. (c) 2026 dpa Deutsche Presse Agentur GmbH powered by dpa-newslab | Legal Notice | About Us / Contact | Privacy

title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
body_text: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke · sunshowers sunshowers about work about work Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke 2026-10-14 · 2 min read vcs shorts Update 2026-10-15: I wrote a followup to answer questions and concerns. Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters . Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How Anthropic describes Scion’s derived data. Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How I described Mononoke’s derived data. I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.) I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.) But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke. Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse. For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti’s blog post for Cursor .  ↩︎ Read other posts ← More on Anthropic's Scion ripping off Mononoke iddqd, or the hardest kind of unsafe Rust → sunshowers Created with love in Oakland, CA. © Rain 2020-present.
