title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?
body_text: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long? - alex wennerberg Welcome to alex wennerberg 's website Why is every rationalist blog post way too long? October 13, 2026 For my piece on Catholic miracle apologetics , I read (correction: skimmed) a 25,000-word post by rationalist blogger Scott Alexander. My piece, which cited (but does not focus on) his, ended up being a cool 2,700 words. I don't think it would benefit from being longer, and it was the result of me cutting around 70% of the text I initially wrote. Rationalist bloggers do not generally appear to have this impulse. Eliezer Yudkowsky's "sequences" are over one million words long . Nearly every blog post I have read in this ecosystem, even the rare one that contains some good ideas, is painfully long and extremely tedious. These bloggers tend to spend their time on precisely the wrong things, i.e. adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating the one or two assumptions they make at the start or broadening their philosophical background beyond the collection of texts popular within their subculture. It seems to me that, in this community, verbosity is a substitute for thoroughness: surely, if someone wrote a lot about something, and is able to demonstrate that by producing a large volume of text, they must have something worthwhile to say about it? Consider when blogger Gwern explained that nicotine, actually, is not addictive, and is good for you, as long as you don't smoke it, over the course of 9,000 words, with over 100 references. It turns out, actually, nicotine is addictive, and is bad for you even if you don't smoke it, as you probably already obviously knew. In any case, what is missing from this endlessly verbose rationalist writing style is wisdom . Wisdom involves discretion: an intuition for what ideas are and are not worth seriously pursuing, and the ability to determine what does and does not need to be said. This community, broadly speaking, does not seem to value wisdom as a trait at all; the idea that something may be true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited tradition is anathema to them. Instead, there is a heavy bias towards that which is unconventional and counterculture, with the amount of ink spilled for heterodox ideas taken as evidence in itself that these ideas are worth taking seriously. live from beautiful san francisco, california normal mode

title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
body_text: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse - The Go Programming Language Skip to Main Content Why Go arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Case Studies Common problems companies solve with Go Use Cases Stories about how and why companies use Go Security How Go can help keep you secure by default Learn Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Docs arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Go Spec The official Go language specification Go User Manual A complete introduction to building software with Go Standard library Reference documentation for Go's standard library Release Notes Learn what's new in each Go release Effective Go Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code Packages Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Community arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Recorded Talks Videos from prior events Meetups open_in_new Meet other local Go developers Conferences open_in_new Learn and network with Go developers from around the world Go blog The Go project's official blog. Go project Get help and stay informed from Go Get connected Why Go navigate_next navigate_before Why Go Case Studies Use Cases Security Learn Docs navigate_next navigate_before Docs Go Spec Go User Manual Standard library Release Notes Effective Go Packages Community navigate_next navigate_before Community Recorded Talks Meetups open_in_new Conferences open_in_new Go blog Go project Get connected The Go Blog Better HTTP/1 connection reuse Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026 Take a look at the following function: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code. Using HTTP/1 ( GODEBUG=http2client=0 ), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds. That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible? The cost of establishing HTTP connections To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request. Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this: TCP handshake (1 RTT) : the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK , and the client replies with ACK . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT). TLS handshake (2 RTT) : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT. HTTP request : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT. These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small. Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org , which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable. Connection reuse To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version: HTTP/1.0 : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a Connection: close header. HTTP/1.1 : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a Connection: close header. HTTP/2 : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection. When connection reuse fails In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes: As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate net/http.Response , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from net/http.Response.Body . Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, net/http can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header). Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body : func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections. (HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.) Where failed connection reuse hurts This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code. As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"} . This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail. Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable. The manual solution The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body) return resp.StatusCode, nil } func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it. body.Close() } While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. body.Close() } However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1) go func() { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. drainDone <- struct{}{} }() // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body. select { case <-drainDone: case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond): // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks. } body.Close() } Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests: func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) { drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1) go func() { io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB. drainDone <- struct{}{} }() go func() { // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body. select { case <-drainDone: // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future // request. case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond): // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks. } body.Close() }() } As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary. The current state and conclusion Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent. As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example: func getStatus(url string) (int, error) { resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return 0, err } defer resp.Body.Close() return resp.StatusCode, nil } Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf. Ben Butcher Data Editor Updated 13 October 2026 5:22pm BST Published 13 October 2026 5:05pm BST Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed. Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics . There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly. Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”. He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.” The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health ”. Suicide rate highest on record Mr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.” The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people. The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population. Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981. For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk. Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024. Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”. She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.” The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44. Recommended Simon Reeve: 'I was a whisker away from taking my own life' Read more There were 19.5 deaths per 100,000 men aged 25 to 44 last year, which is the widest gap since 2009, when middle-aged male suicide rates overtook those of younger adults. The rate increased from 14 to 14.4 per 100,000 for those aged 65 to 74 and from 13.2 to 15.4 among those aged 75 or older. Marjorie Wallace, the chief executive of mental health charity Sane, said she was “not surprised” by the data. She said: “Analysis of the contact we receive reflects this – almost 60 per cent of our callers now talk about suicide or self-harm, a very different picture than 10 years ago. “While middle-aged men in their forties and fifties still remain at greatest risk, our other concern is the number of young people, particularly girls and women aged 16 to 24, who report anxiety and depression on a scale not experienced before.” Join the conversation Show comments The Telegraph values your comments but kindly requests all posts are on topic, constructive and respectful. body_text: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts News Featured Latest Anthropic warns self-replicating AI could spread to your smart devices Microsoft October 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 1,411 flaws, 3 zero-days Windows 11 KB5127648 & KB5126653 cumulative updates released Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts Hackers exploit Collabora RCE flaw to backdoor Nextcloud servers Android gets AI defenses against messaging scams, fake calls Hackers hijack D-Link, Ubiquiti devices to resell your stolen bandwidth Fake Arch Linux packages push malware with root privileges Tutorials Latest Popular How to access the Dark Web using the Tor Browser How to enable Kernel-mode Hardware-enforced Stack Protection in Windows 11 How to use the Windows Registry Editor How to backup and restore the Windows Registry How to start Windows in Safe Mode How to remove a Trojan, Virus, Worm, or other Malware How to show hidden files in Windows 7 How to see hidden files in Windows Webinars Downloads Latest Most Downloaded Qualys BrowserCheck STOPDecrypter AuroraDecrypter FilesLockerDecrypter AdwCleaner ComboFix RKill Junkware Removal Tool Deals Categories eLearning IT Certification Courses Gear + Gadgets Security VPNs Popular Best VPNs How to change IP address Access the dark web safely Best VPN for YouTube Forums More Virus Removal Guides Startup Database Uninstall Database Glossary Send us a Tip! Welcome Guide Home News Security Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts By Bill Toulas October 12, 2026 12:27 PM 2 Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets. The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia. Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware. Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions. On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices. The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with. "Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said. The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice. “[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger . Yesterday, Ledger provided another update , confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.” While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware. Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires. Hardware implant inside Ledger X device source:  Mark Karpelès The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong. According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM. "Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained . Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)." Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X. The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan. In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X. "Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices. For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out." In the second hardware wallet analyzed, Tibane researchers found that markings on both the MCU (Microcontroller Unit) and the eSIM had been scraped off to hide the part numbers. The second variant, which appears to be the same one that Karpelès described, is more advanced. It ran on the original battery and fit into the space normally occupied by the foam padding under the OLED display. In both cases, the tell tale was the antenna wire, which ran along the top edge in the case of the second implant. In the first implant, the antenna is taped across the top of the battery and the shielded LTE module. Hardware implant inside Ledger X source: Tibane Labs The researchers warned that the specimen above used "a designed, panelised flex PCB, the kind ordered from a board house, not a hand-built one-off." Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices. The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products. Ledger provides a ‘Genuine Check’ mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device’s original Secure Element remains intact. At this time, there’s no indication that any other Ledger resellers are shipping compromised wallets; however, the community’s trust in the resellers’ network has been compromised, with many now calling for its dismantling. Previous Article Next Article Comments tubrazysj - 2 days ago     A genuine-device verification check is not enough if a physical implant can bypass the user's security assumptions. Hardware wallet providers and distributors need robust anti-tampering controls, transparent incident reporting, and clear consumer remediation procedures. In crypto, security is not just a technical issue; it is also a matter of consumer protection and legal responsibility. PaoloA - 20 hours ago     Ah crypto! So useful - where else can you lose $100 million because someone intercepted your "unhackable" cold storage in a Malaysian warehouse and hot-wired a cellular spy chip to the screen ribbon? Surely "mass adoption" is just around the corner and then only up, right after the average person learns to weight their devices and X-ray their mail for spy implants. Ledger's official software still happily passes these bugged wallets through its "Genuine Check" with flying colors. So much for the utopian dream of being your own bank. Now, instead of dealing with incompetent tellers, the future of finance means you get to manage global supply chain threat modeling just to check your balance - all while praying you don't get targeted for a $5 wrench attack in your living room because a third-party shipping vendor leaked your home address. A list of how well "total self-custody" gets IRL, the master list of physical muggings and home invasions is right here: https://github.com/jlopp/physical-bitcoin-attacks [github.com] The only truly satisfied customers in this so called ecosystem appear to be ransomware syndicates, money launderers, and sanctioned regimes under putler and kim jong turd, who treat crypto drainers and multimillion-dollar exchange hacks as a lucrative "national export". title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
body_text: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet Subscribe! Not-Ship Charting the age of uncertainty. Subscribe! October 14, 2026 How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet Amanda Shendruk Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition. But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because... 💙 Amanda Support Not-Ship! Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over : the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop. In a nutshell, here's what's happening: This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon. Let's get into it. Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales . But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half! Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top. Where an Amazon sale goes Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising. There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article. Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice. Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options: In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising. So, sellers have to raise prices Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices. Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too. And they can't charge less elsewhere Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller , if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales. The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon. It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit , California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target. Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go. There's no easy way out For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales . For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option. At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final. After last week's piece , a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway. FULL DISCLOSURE I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy  dismantling the publication , so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom. CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining! FROM ELSEWHERE Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week: Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.) Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram . Endlessly inspirational. Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required! title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
body_text: Redesigning source control at Anthropic \ Anthropic Skip to main content Skip to footer Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Engineering at Anthropic Redesigning source control at Anthropic Published Oct 13, 2026 As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months. Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion. At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard. As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones. The typical setup for scaling git checkouts. Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like? Principles for agent-scale source control With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling , 2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are: Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it. Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally. A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control. Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed. Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem. The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads. How Scion works It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle. Data structures In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, 1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly. The shape of a changeset in Scion. This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets. A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents. This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search. Scaling Scion A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner. Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own. Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want. In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed. The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system. Scion’s checkout architecture. Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs. What we learned building Scion We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it. Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures. Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026. What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like. Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future. Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code. We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day. Observed performance improvements on native Scion repos. We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes. A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison. We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them. Contributing to the wider ecosystem We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case. Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities. Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful. However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well. Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential. Acknowledgements Written by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique. Footnotes Storing changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo. Specifically, the server component of Sapling, Mononoke . It pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion, in particular the Bonsai data model. title: Grace Hopper Celebration Cancelled
body_text: Press-Release About Events & Programs Support Our Cause Research Resources News & Stories Become a Member Donate Press Release An Important Update About Grace Hopper Celebration It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA. This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses. We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates. If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now: Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider. Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip. Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. AnitaB.org will contact registrants about registration fees by October 26. We recognize that each person’s circumstances may be different. For questions or assistance specifically related to the cancellation, please contact [ GHC@AnitaB.org ]. We ask that you use this address so we can centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible. To our attendees, sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and everyone who has invested in making Grace Hopper Celebration possible: we are profoundly grateful, and profoundly sorry. GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology. GHC has been central to our mission, and the circumstances leading to its cancellation have adversely affected our finances. We are evaluating strategic alternatives and the type of programming we can offer in the future. I anticipate further announcements will be made in the coming weeks as we gain greater clarity on key variables. Brenda Darden Wilkerson President & CEO AnitaB.org Frequently Asked Questions Why was this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration cancelled? AnitaB.org has determined that it will not have the funds required to pay the costs of producing the Celebration. This year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below prior years and, ultimately, below the level required to cover basic operating expenses. What happens to my in-person or virtual registration fee? Information regarding GHC registration and other financial matters will be communicated to you promptly once we obtain a clearer understanding of AnitaB.org ’s financial condition. Do I need to do anything right now? We encourage you to review cancellation and refund eligibility with your travel and accommodation provider. Many providers offer more flexibility the earlier a change is requested. My visa was approved for this trip. What does cancellation mean for me? AnitaB.org is unable to advise on immigration matters. Please consult a qualified immigration attorney or your sponsoring institution. I had interviews scheduled through the career fair. What now? Employers who had scheduled interviews are being notified, and we are asking them to continue those conversations directly where possible. We are a sponsor or exhibitor. Who should we contact? Your A nitaB.org contact is reaching out directly. Information regarding sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and related financial matters will be communicated to the organizations affected. For anything urgent, please use GHC@AnitaB.org . How will I hear about updates, and when is the next one? Updates will be posted on the GHC website, the most recent updates will appear at the top of the Press Release page. Who do I contact? Please use GHC@AnitaB.org , for anything related to the cancellation. Using one address allows us to centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible. Is Grace Hopper Celebration India still taking place? Yes, Grace Hopper Celebration India (GHCI) is still taking place in Bangalore, India, January 20-22, 2027. Learn more here: GHCI 27 - AnitaB.org India . We also encourage corporate sponsors to consider GHCI sponsorship inclusive of bulk registration opportunities to send your teams. Email corporate@anitabindia.org to learn more. I uploaded my resume through the GHC 26 platform. Will participating companies still have access to it? Yes. If you uploaded your resume through the GHC 26 Resume Hub, participating companies will continue to have access to your submitted resume. This service remains available to help connect attendees with potential career opportunities. Subscribe to our newsletter Get the latest news, articles, and resources from AnitaB.org. Why We’re Banning AI We urgently need to protect human thought and creativity. Our magazine is committing itself to remaining handmade. Ensure every publication you support does the same. Nathan J. Robinson filed 15 October 2026 in Editor’s Notes Iam proud to say that as part of our new union contract , Current Affairs recently adopted one of the strictest anti-AI policies in the publishing industry. No text that is AI-generated may be published in our magazine. No AI-generated art may be used as a Current Affairs illustration. When you read Current Affairs, you are going to be reading the thoughts of a human, and seeing the results of human artistry. We’re adopting this policy because we want to directly challenge the slopification of media. Newsrooms across the country are rushing to embrace AI and replace actual writers, public opinion be damned. The CEO of Business Insider, for instance, has said his publication is “all in on AI” (which is becoming an annoyingly common slogan ) and shamelessly publishes AI-written content. At least they’re honest about it. Some publications have deliberately tricked people; Sports Illustrated was caught publishing AI-written pieces by nonexistent journalists. Guest op-eds in all of the major newspapers have been found to be either partly or wholly written by AI. Sometimes publishing this work can happen inadvertently; here at Current Affairs, we have had plenty of freelance submissions that use suspicious numbers of em-dashes and “this is not an X, it’s a Y” sentences. (We can’t promise that nothing will ever slip through the cracks, but we’re vigilant!) Astonishingly, though, some editors have actually defended publishing the pieces even when writers have been caught. The Wall Street Journal published an op-ed from a hedge fund billionaire, Stan Druckenmiller, that turned out to have been AI-generated (probably because billionaires are inarticulate due to a lifetime of never having to craft arguments to persuade the yes-men around them), but the paper defended publishing the piece, since it reflected the billionaire’s genuine opinion . The trends are dire. But it’s obvious why these publications are rushing to replace writers. They are for-profit corporations, whose ultimate loyalty is to shareholders, not workers. AI is great for them, because it can produce “content” at a fraction of the expense that a writer costs. In fact, on the Milton Friedman theory that the only responsibility a business has is to increase its profits, CEOs are obligated to replace writers with AI if doing so is better for the bottom line. It’s a simple calculation: if producing 100 posts with AI costs almost nothing and takes four minutes, but paying a writer to produce 20 posts costs $5,000, well, why would you pay the writer? The calculation might hold even if the quality drops substantially, errors are introduced, and audience loyalty plummets. Even if you lost 60 percent of your readership, you might still make a lot more per story, because you can pump them out in seconds. Futurism reports that despite the common narrative that AI has not led to major job loss, creative industries are being “eviscerated” by AI, which is fueling “one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” with more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries being lost in four years. The situation is horrible for artists. Game studios are now designing their worlds and levels using “ art assets generated with full AI workflows. ” As Brian Merchant reported earlier this year :   Opportunities and pay rates declining as clients and employers embrace generative AI. Artists getting more touch-up jobs and fewer well-paying, sustainable gigs. Pessimism, anger, and even despair, growing common, if not universal, in the field.     This is especially galling given that all of the AI models that are being used to replace artists were trained through the mass theft of those very same artists’ work! Now here at Current Affairs, we’ve decided to say: fuck that! Over 62 beautiful print issues, we have commissioned hundreds of original, handmade artworks from brilliant artists around the world. We’ve published meticulously researched and edited articles, which often take weeks or months to go from the draft stage to publication. We spend ages working on our page layouts, poring over photographs for the magazine, tweaking sketches, moving sentences around in articles. The labor that goes into this magazine has been extensive from the start, and most of it is hidden from view. We do it because we care about quality. If you pick up a copy of our magazine, you’ll see the result. I think it’s clear when you read it that we actually care about what we’re putting out. It’s not just Content designed to farm clicks.       Current Affairs has always been a bit of an anachronism. We started a print magazine in 2016. Nobody thought this was a good idea. (The editor in chief of Vanity Fair told me to my face that this was a wholly misguided project and certain to fail. I remain grateful to him for giving me the resolve to prove the prediction wrong.) Everyone else was pivoting to video. We pivoted to ink and paper, sent via the U.S. Postal Service. Ten years later, we are still here, while a lot of other places that began with a lot more money have folded (see, e.g., the Messenger, which burned through $50 million in a year and then died). The reason we’ve survived is that there are still many people who don’t like that all media is now just transient images on a social media feed. They experience a thrill when they get a cool thing in the mail that they can unwrap and hold. They know that seeing a beautiful illustration on the printed page is different, and better, from seeing it as a JPEG on your phone. So we don’t really give a damn what the trends in the industry are. We located ourselves in New Orleans when everyone else is in New York. We defiantly publish on obscure topics that aren’t anywhere in the news cycle . (Have you read Alice Millar-Thompson’s article on eel smuggling ?) And we’re going to keep paying human artists to create elaborate, gorgeous works of handmade art that take ages to make. So our rule is simple: No AI generated articles or illustrations in the magazine! We are not going to feed you slop. And we think you should not give money to any publication that does feed you slop, because they’re both treating their audience with contempt, and avoiding paying workers so that their owners can get richer. This doesn’t mean nobody doing work here can ever use any of the softwares that are broadly lumped together as AI. Much as we respect the Luddites around here, we’re not against technological innovation. Nothing in our rules prohibits writers from using a new tool to help them research something, or prevents an artist from using a tool to, say, add a texture or change a color, or make some kind of small element. But we need, first, to ensure that technologies are a tool used by workers to help them, rather than a tool used to replace workers. And, second, we need to make sure that readers aren’t being fed things that look like people’s genuine thoughts and creative expression but are in fact the product of disembodied mathematical formulas. I’ll admit, I used to be excited by generative AI. I made goofy little images in DALL-E. I liked the dumb novelty songs. I thought it could be a cool tool for creative professionals to play around with. I forgot for a moment that we live under capitalism, where every new technology will be used by the ruling class to fuck over workers. As Garrison Lovely writes in his new book Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us—and How to Stop It , the developers of AI don’t see it as an asset for workers, but as a way to replace them. They’re trying to build a device whose success is literally measured by whether it successfully replaces people. It is not being designed to help the average person’s capacity to achieve their goals, but to help automate us all into obsolescence. That’s why it has to be fought aggressively. We at Current Affairs are not capitalists. There are no profits to be made here. We’re a unionized 501c3 organization, which means that we have no incentive to try to replace our workers with machines. So we’re going to demonstrate that you don’t have to do this, that there’s another way, and that it results in better media that is more pleasurable to read and more informative. It’s not going to be easy, because competitor publications are going to be able to produce immense quantities of writing in the time we are painstakingly correcting and adjusting a single article. But like John Henry , before we let that steam drill beat us, we will die with our hammer in our hand.     We need your help to keep putting out this handmade magazine. Subscribe or donate today. Your money pays real writers and real artists to make the world’s most beautiful printed publication. If you value authentic human thought and culture, get Current Affairs today. More from Nathan J. Description jsnell opened on Oct 13, 2026 Issue body actions Note Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context. Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver , the region constraint rework , and more generally Project Zero . It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones. This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high " is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit. Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. While it looks easy to trigger, to exploit this you need an intentionally malicious Drop implementation. ~ @lcnr In the following code: use std :: sync :: Mutex ; static KEPT : Mutex < Vec < Box < dyn std :: any :: Any + Send > > > = Mutex :: new ( Vec :: new ( ) ) ; struct Q < T : ' static + Send > ( Option < T > ) ; impl < T : ' static + Send > Drop for Q < T > { fn drop ( & mut self ) { if let Some ( t ) = self . 0 . take ( ) { KEPT . lock ( ) . unwrap ( ) . push ( Box :: new ( t ) ) ; } } } fn main ( ) { { let l = String :: from ( "hello world, this is long enough" ) ; let mut q = Q ( None ) ; q . 0 = Some ( & l ) ; } let _z = String :: from ( "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" ) ; let k = KEPT . lock ( ) . unwrap ( ) ; println ! ( "{}" , k [ 0 ] . downcast_ref :: < & ' static String > ( ) . unwrap ( ) ) ; } I expected to see this happen: program is not accepted Instead, this happened: program compiles and prints XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX .
