title: Show HN: Guitoro, a virtual guitar you strum with your keyboard
body_text: Virtual Guitar: Play Guitar Online Free | Guitoro in #stage, so the browser picks the same file. Browsers without AVIF skip this. --> Guitoro Online Virtual Guitar Loading guitar This guitar needs JavaScript to make sound. The most realistic virtual guitar online What is Guitoro? Guitoro is the most realistic and the most complete virtual guitar you can play online, free in your browser. Play it with your computer keyboard, your left hand on the chords and your right hand strumming, or swipe the strings with your finger on a phone or tablet. Choose a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar, an electric guitar or a four-string bass. It's also a way to learn chords and songs that a chord chart or a video lesson can't show you. Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it down to 20% and watch it being played: each string lights up the moment it's hit, the pick swings down and up with the strum, and the neck shows which finger goes where. Then it's your turn. No guitar? Play the song on the keys or the screen, and it waits for you at every chord change. Have a guitar? Pick it up and play along at your own speed, with the strings, the strum and the fingering right in front of you. Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument. There's nothing to download and no account to create. If you played the Google guitar doodle, Guitoro takes the idea further: six real strings, 15 chords in every key, and 51 songs to play along with. Start playing How you learn with it 4 instruments 15 chords in every key 51 songs to play along with 20% slowest song speed 56 strum and picking patterns 15 drum styles Play Play guitar with your keyboard or your fingers No guitar needed. Guitoro is built to be played, not just clicked, on whatever you have in front of you. Computer keyboard Your left hand holds a chord on the letter keys and your right hand strums with H and J , the way you'd play a real guitar. 15 chords sit under your fingers, plus keys for arpeggios, single strings, chucks and palm mutes. Touch screen On a phone or tablet, tap a chord pad and swipe the strings with your finger. Up to five fingers at once, and you can tap the frets on the neck to play single notes. Mouse Drag across the strings. A fast swipe plays louder, a slow drag rolls the notes one by one, and a click plucks a single string. Melodies in Solo On a computer, switch to Solo and every keyboard row becomes a string and every column a fret, with bends and vibrato on the arrow keys. Learn by watching See every string and every stroke, as slowly as you need In a video lesson the hand moves fast and hides the strings, so you can't tell which ones were really hit. Guitar apps teach the basic chords and stop there. Guitoro plays the song's real part on the guitar in front of you, at the speed you choose, and shows exactly what the hands do. Then you play it, on the virtual guitar or on your own. Played like the record Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it anywhere from 20% to full speed and the chords, the strum and the band slow down together. See which strings are hit Each string lights up the moment it sounds, then vibrates as it rings. You can see whether a stroke hits all six strings, just the bass strings or only the top three. Watch the strumming hand Over a strummed part, the pick swings down and up like a real strumming hand, once per step of the pattern. Solid swings hit the strings and faint ones miss them, so you see the hand keep moving through the gaps. Fingers on the neck While a chord rings, the neck shows it: finger numbers from 1 to 4, barres, muted strings and the capo. Copy the shape onto your own guitar. No guitar? The song waits for you Play a song's chords on the keys or the screen and it follows you. The keys show its chords in order, the next one lights green, and the song holds until you play it. No score and no rush. Have a guitar? Play along Watch a part slowly, copy it on your guitar, then play along as you raise the speed. On a computer, choose My guitar: the on-screen keys step aside and the song box shows the strum or picking pattern, a chord strip you can click to jump around, and the speed. Realism Why it sounds and feels like a real guitar Most online guitars only let you click single strings or frets, or play a synthesized tone when you click a chord. On Guitoro you strum: swipe across the strings or use the keys, and every string sounds as you cross it, from recordings of real instruments. Recorded, not synthesized Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument: a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar with nylon strings, a solid-body electric on its bridge pickup, and a four-string bass. Strums follow your hand Each string sounds as your finger or mouse crosses it. Swipe down or up, fast or slow, and you hear the difference, down to a slow roll across the strings. Real chord shapes Chords use the shapes guitarists play, with open strings, barres and muted strings, so a G sounds like a G on a guitar, not on a keyboard. Guitar techniques Chucks, palm mutes, hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato, while the strings vibrate on screen as they ring. Use cases What people use it for Playing without a guitar Strum real chords and play whole songs with your computer keyboard or your fingers, with a backing band behind you. On a train, at the office or on the sofa, a laptop or a phone and headphones are enough. Learning real songs Songs like Wonderwall, Hallelujah and Let It Be come set up with the right key, capo, tempo and the strum from the record. Lead the chords from the keys, or pick up your own guitar and play along at any speed. Getting a strum right Slow a song's strum down, watch which way the pick moves on every beat, then strum it yourself over a drum beat until it feels steady. Learning their first chords See where each finger goes, hear how the chord should sound, then copy the shape on a real guitar. Every chord also has its own page in the guitar chord chart . Checking a chord chart Paste the chords of a song from a chord site and hear how it goes before you sit down to play it. Writing a song Type a chord progression under My songs, loop it with the backing band, and record the idea before it's gone. Teaching Show a class a chord shape or a strum on a big screen, slowed down, with every string and every pick stroke visible. Other musicians Singers, keyboard players and songwriters can hear how guitar chords are voiced and see how a progression lies on the fretboard, without learning to hold a guitar first. Features Everything in the app The most complete virtual guitar online: four instruments, every key, real chord shapes, songs, a backing band and recording, all free in one place. Four real instruments Steel-string acoustic, classic guitar, electric and four-string bass, each built from recorded samples. Pick a recording for the acoustic (Warm, Bright or Mellow) and the classic (Natural or Concert), and presets for the electric, from Clean to Crunch, Classic Rock, Metal, Lead and Ambient. 15 chords in every key Pick any of the 24 major and minor keys and the chord keys fill with the chords that fit it: the main chords, sevenths, and sus, add9 or sus2 colors. Edit puts any chord you type, like F#m7 or Dsus2, on a key. Chord shapes on the neck While a chord rings, the neck shows finger numbers, barres, muted strings and the capo. Standard is the shape most players learn first, Easy swaps a barre chord for a smaller shape, and Up plays the same chord higher up the neck. Songs at any speed 51 songs and classical pieces come set up to play, from Wonderwall and Hotel California to Canon in D. Slow them to 20%, lead their chords from the keys, or play along on your own guitar. 56 strum and picking patterns 14 everyday strums from Steady downs and the pop staple D DU U DU to shuffle and 6/8, 4 styles (reggae, funk and country), 26 more rhythms drawn from real songs, and 12 picking patterns like Travis and classical p-i-m-a. Choose one and you hear it straight away. A backing band Drums, bass and strings that follow your chords: 15 drum styles, including rock, funk, reggae, bossa nova and cajon, and 25 bass lines. The Band switch next to Play turns them on. Tempo goes from 10 to 220 BPM, with a metronome. Your own songs Paste a song from a chord site or as ChordPro text, pick a strum, and Guitoro plays it with the band. Write "x2" to repeat a line or a part. Lyrics are left out, and your songs stay in your browser. Solo mode Play single notes and melodies on the neck from the computer keyboard, with hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato. Amp & FX Overdrive, distortion and fuzz on the electric, plus bass, mid and treble, room or hall reverb, and delay on every instrument. Press each one and watch the neck: the numbers are your fingers, from 1 for the index to 4 for the little finger. An X marks a string you don't play, and a bar across the strings is a barre. Listen to the difference Play C, then Am. The chord name above the guitar tells you which is major and which is minor, and your ear learns the bright and the sad sound. The trick is to keep your hand moving down on every number and up on every "and", even when it misses the strings. In Guitoro you can watch the pick do exactly that. Dismiss alert {{ message }} android ndk Repository navigation Code Issues 131 ( 131 ) Pull requests Discussions Actions Projects Wiki Security and quality Insights More items [BUG] bionic: wcscspn()/wcspbrk() treat every wchar_t >= 0x100 as a match (Android 17, CP3A.260905.009) #2260 New issue Copy link New issue Copy link Open Open [BUG] bionic: wcscspn()/wcspbrk() treat every wchar_t >= 0x100 as a match (Android 17, CP3A.260905.009) #2260 Copy link Labels bug Description francisdb opened on Oct 12, 2026 Issue body actions Description On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character of the string that is >= U+0100 whenever the reject set has two or more characters that are all < U+0100. The character is reported as a match even though it is not in the set. wcsspn() , wcschr() , wcsrchr() , wmemchr() and wcsstr() are correct. Any code that scans wide strings for ASCII delimiters, for example newline or wildcard characters, breaks as soon as the text contains an emoji, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek or Latin Extended character. Affected / unaffected Device Build Result Pixel 7 google/panther/panther:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys broken Pixel 8a google/akita/akita:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys (patch 2026-09-05) broken Nothing Phone 2 Nothing/PongEEA/Pong:16/BQ2A.250721.001-BP2A.250605.031.A3 (patch 2026-08-01) ok The public android17-release sources (android-17.0.0_r1, June 2026) build wcscspn / wcspbrk from external/llvm-libc, which is a plain nested loop over wchar_t and is correct. The code on the September builds is different (see "Mechanism"), so the regression was introduced between the June and September releases. Reproducer Build with the NDK ( aarch64-linux-android30-clang ), push to /data/local/tmp , run with adb shell : #include <stdio.h> #include <wchar.h> int main ( void ) { wchar_t s [] = { 'a' , 0x1F680 , 0x100 , 'b' , 'x' , '
' , 0 }; printf ( "wcscspn(s, L"x\n") = %zu (expected 4)
" , wcscspn ( s , L"x
" )); printf ( "wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") = index %ld (expected 4)
" , ( long )( wcspbrk ( s , L"x
" ) - s )); printf ( "wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = %zu (expected 2)
" , wcsspn ( s , L"a\U0001F680" )); return 0 ; } Output on CP3A.260905.009: wcscspn(s, L"x
") = 1 (expected 4) wcspbrk(s, L"x
") = index 1 (expected 4) wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = 2 (expected 2) A sweep of every code point from U+0001 to U+10FFFF (skipping surrogates and the two set members) with wcscspn(L"<cp>
", L"x
") returns 0 instead of 1 for 1,111,808 code points: every one from U+0100 to U+10FFFF. U+0001 to U+00FF are correct. Which set shapes trigger it (all measured on the Pixel 8a): Reject set Result one character ok two or more characters, all < U+0100 (e.g. L"x
" , L"\xe9
" ) broken two or more characters, at least one >= U+0100 ok haystack limited to U+0080..U+00FF ok Mechanism (from the shipped libc.so) Disassembly of wcscspn in /apex/com.android.runtime/lib64/bionic/libc.so on CP3A.260905.009 shows three paths selected by the set: One character: a plain compare loop. Correct. Two or more characters: a 256-byte bool table on the stack is filled from the set while the set characters are in 1..0xFF. If a set character >= 0x100 is seen, the function falls back to calling wcschr() for each haystack character. Correct. Otherwise the haystack is scanned against the table: a2564: ldrb w8, [x9, x8] ; table[c] a2568: tbnz w8, #0, a2578 ; in set -> stop (correct) a256c: ldr w8, [x22, #0x4]! ; next character a2570: cmp w8, #0x100 a2574: b.lo a2564 ; c < 0x100 -> keep scanning a2578: ... ; c >= 0x100 -> STOP, reported as a match A character >= 0x100 cannot be in a set whose members are all < 0x100, so for wcscspn the scan must continue past it. The code stops instead. wcsspn has the same structure, and there stopping is the correct answer (the character is not in the keep set), which is why only the complement functions are wrong. wcspbrk is implemented on top of this scan and inherits the bug. The existing bionic test TEST(wchar, wcspbrk) in tests/wchar_test.cpp only uses ASCII input, so it does not catch this. A test such as EXPECT_EQ(3u, wcscspn(L"aĀb
", L"x
")) would. Real-world impact Visual Pinball on Android (libwinevbs, a Unix build of Wine's vbscript engine) stopped loading any table whose VBScript source contains a comment with an emoji after the September update: the lexer uses wcspbrk(ptr, L"
") to skip comments, got the position of the first emoji instead of the line end, and reported "Invalid character". FileSystem.MoveFolder likewise treated every path containing a character >= U+0100 as a wildcard pattern via wcspbrk(src, L"*?><") . Worked around downstream by replacing the calls with plain loops: vpinball/libwinevbs#41 (shipped in vpinball/vpinball@ e7837322f4 ). Full disassembly of the affected functions and the probe sources are available on request. I am using a supported NDK I have checked and the NDK I'm using is currently supported Affected versions r29 Reactions are currently unavailable Activity francisdb added bug on Oct 12, 2026 enh-google commented on Oct 12, 2026 enh-google on Oct 12, 2026 Collaborator More actions yeah, that all sounds correct, and seems to still be an issue at ToT. (i was going to say "you know you can just look at the source?", but android-latest-release seems to still be too old to have any of these changes from april :-( ) wcspbrk() is affected because it's just __attribute__((__flatten__)) wchar_t* wcspbrk(const wchar_t* s, const wchar_t* delims) { size_t i = wcscspn(s, delims); if (s[i] != L'\0') return const_cast<wchar_t*>(s) + i; return nullptr; } but i'll add both missing tests, and ideally try to see if i can find everywhere else we're missing a test that actually uses non-ascii! i'll also see if i can get the fix backported to minimize the number of affected devices. (which is probably a reason to ensure any not-directly-related tests are added in a separate later change.) 👍 React with 👍 1 Reacted by Jagtesh Chadha 😕 React with 😕 20 Reacted by Joaquín Vacas Verísimo, Kunal Agrawal, Vinayak, Doug Lynch, Matheus Araújo, David Allison, LifeIsStrange, JannF, Alexander Pushkov, Oliver Krieg and 10 more 👀 React with 👀 5 Reacted by Joaquín Vacas Verísimo, Doug Lynch, David Allison, Stuart Axon and guiral lacotte enh-google commented on Oct 12, 2026 enh-google on Oct 12, 2026 Collaborator More actions gah, even more embarrassing is that we do have an existing test for wcscspn(), it's just wrong: [ RUN ] wchar.wcscspn bionic/tests/wchar_test.cpp:(1475) Failure in test wchar.wcscspn Expected equality of these values: 2u Which is: 2 wcscspn(L"he￾lo", L"lo") Which is: 3 wchar.wcscspn exited with exitcode 1. 🤦 👍 React with 👍 2 Reacted by lfuelling and Orlando 😕 React with 😕 1 Reacted by Joaquín Vacas Verísimo 👀 React with 👀 1 Reacted by Joaquín Vacas Verísimo francisdb commented on Oct 13, 2026 francisdb on Oct 13, 2026 Author More actions Thanks for the quick response. title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
body_text: Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak | Our World in Data Our World in Data Browse by topic Data Latest Resources About Subscribe Donate Data Insights Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak October 03, 2026 Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak Hannah Ritchie Download Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century. In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then. You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s. Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to. The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it. Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much. Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too. Explore how electricity generation has changed in your own country Related topic pages: Energy Copy link Our latest Data Insights See all Data Insights Yesterday A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria Max Roser According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000. The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000. Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible. Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress. If you want to be a part of this historic change, read my brief article on how you can contribute to humanity’s battle against malaria October 13 China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behind Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero. Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart. In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million. Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines . Explore progress against poverty across the world in our data explorer October 10 What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean? Hannah Ritchie Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean? In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from: A) Less than 1% B) Less than 36% C) Less than 66% Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third. The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean. The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered. From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place. People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way. Read my article, which looks at this question in more detail October 8 The new Living Planet Index reports a 73% average decline in studied wildlife populations Hannah Ritchie The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart. Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it. I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct. But it tells us none of that. It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index. When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable. As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most. Read my explainer on what the Living Planet Index captures, and what’s different in this report from previous ones October 6 Child mortality has declined in all world regions Max Roser In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died. The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined. In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold. Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history. And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day. Explore child mortality data for every country in our interactive data explorer October 1 Europe is older, but Latin America is aging faster Esteban Ortiz-Ospina The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises. That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates. The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42. But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation. Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter. title: Thunderbird for iOS
body_text: Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development - The Thunderbird Blog Product Development Mobile Community Tips & Guides Get Thunderbird Donate Search Product Development Mobile Community Tips & Guides RSS Feed Download Thunderbird Donate Mobile Thunderbird Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development October 1, 2026 Aly Blenkin 30 responses The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start. Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified.  Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future. Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS. Hassle-free setup Adding account user flow with options for email services like Google and Microsoft We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly.  Solid reliable connections Thunderbird inbox An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life. Core daily tools Formatting toolbar (highlighted to show the details) Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way. Designed for growth Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do. When can you try it? Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months. Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be? ➡️ Survey link Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded! A note to the community  Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience! Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience. title: 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692 (With Complete High-Res Scan)
body_text: A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan | Open Culture --> --> --> --> --> --> A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan --> The best free cultural & educational media on the web --> --> --> Online Courses Certificates Degrees & Mini-Degrees --> Audio Books Movies Languages --> Podcasts Textbooks --> K-12 K-12 --> eBooks Languages Donate --> --> Oct 12 --> A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan in Art | October 12th, 2026 Leave a Comment --> --> There’s ahead of its time, then there’s  Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau  — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title,  Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st , a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692 . Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his  Opticks  over a decade lat­er. It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810  The­o­ry of Col­ors  and Werner’s 1814  Nomen­cla­ture of Colour  to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963. But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy. Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,”  he writes , “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors. In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.” The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find  full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans . “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes  Refinery29 . “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here . Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
